maps.caption-2: Then: Troy (Hisarlık, Ottoman Empire), Türkiye - Now: Moscow, Russia

fun.short: Priam's Treasure is a hoard of gold jewellery, cups and weapons dug up at Troy in 1873 by Heinrich Schliemann. He thought it belonged to King Priam from Homer's stories, but it is about 1,000 years older! Fun fact: it disappeared in 1945 and turned up secretly in Moscow.
fun.medium: Heinrich Schliemann was a German businessman who loved Homer's Iliad, the story of the Trojan War. He was sure Troy was real, and he dug into a hill called Hisarlık in north-western Türkiye. In 1873 he found a hoard of gold diadems, earrings, necklaces with thousands of tiny beads, gold and silver cups, and bronze weapons. He announced that it was the treasure of King Priam of Troy! In fact, it comes from a much earlier city, built around 2500–2300 BCE. Schliemann secretly took it out of the Ottoman Empire and later gave it to Berlin. Fun fact: at the end of the Second World War, the treasure vanished from Berlin, and for almost 50 years nobody knew it was hidden in a museum in Moscow!
fun.long:
Around 2,700 years ago, the Greek poet Homer told the story of the Trojan War: the Greeks besieged the city of Troy, ruled by King Priam, for ten years, and finally tricked their way in with a wooden horse. For a long time, many people thought Troy was just a legend.

Heinrich Schliemann, a German businessman who had grown rich through trade, believed it was real. In 1870 he started digging at Hisarlık, a hill near the Dardanelles in the Ottoman Empire, today's Türkiye. His workers dug a huge trench right through the hill and discovered layer after layer of ancient cities built on top of each other.

In 1873 Schliemann announced that he had found a treasure: gold diadems with hanging chains, earrings, bracelets, cups of gold and silver and bronze weapons. He called it Priam's Treasure and even photographed his wife, Sophia, wearing the gold jewellery, which he named the "Jewels of Helen".

But Schliemann was wrong about the date. The treasure comes from the city archaeologists call Troy II, from around 2500–2300 BCE, more than a thousand years before the Trojan War could have happened.

Schliemann also broke his agreement with the Ottoman government, which was supposed to receive half of his finds. He smuggled the treasure to Athens. The Ottomans took him to court, and he paid them compensation. In 1881 he gave the treasure to Berlin.

Fun fact: in 1945, as the Soviet army captured Berlin, the treasure was handed over to Soviet officers and taken to Moscow. The Soviet Union kept this secret, and only in the 1990s did the world learn that the gold was in the Pushkin Museum.

basic.short: Priam's Treasure, a hoard of gold, silver and bronze objects from Troy II (c. 2500–2300 BCE), was found by Heinrich Schliemann in 1873 and smuggled out of the Ottoman Empire. Given to Berlin in 1881, it was taken by the Red Army in 1945 and revealed in the 1990s to be in Moscow's Pushkin Museum.
basic.medium: In 1873 Heinrich Schliemann uncovered a hoard of metal objects at Hisarlık, in north-western Anatolia, which he identified as the site of Homer's Troy. The hoard included gold diadems, earrings, bracelets and thousands of beads, vessels of gold, silver and electrum, and bronze weapons. Schliemann named it Priam's Treasure, but it belongs to the level known as Troy II, dated to about 2500–2300 BCE. Contrary to his permit, which required him to share his finds with the Ottoman state, Schliemann smuggled the treasure to Athens. After a lawsuit, he paid the Ottoman government compensation. In 1881 he donated his collection to Berlin. In 1945 the treasure was handed over to the Red Army and taken to Moscow. Its existence there was kept secret until the early 1990s, and it has been displayed at the Pushkin Museum since 1996. Germany and Türkiye both claim it.
basic.long:
Hisarlık, a mound near the entrance to the Dardanelles in north-western Anatolia, had been proposed as the site of Troy before Heinrich Schliemann began excavating there in 1870. Schliemann, a merchant who had made a fortune in trade, was determined to prove that Homer's Troy was historical. His excavations, with large trenches cut through the mound, revealed a sequence of superimposed cities, but also destroyed much of their archaeological context.

In 1873 Schliemann found a hoard of objects near a wall of the early city, which he announced as the treasure of King Priam. It included gold diadems, earrings, bracelets, pins and thousands of small gold beads, as well as vessels of gold, silver, electrum and bronze, and bronze weapons. The hoard belongs to the level now called Troy II, around 2500–2300 BCE, far earlier than any possible historical Trojan War. Schliemann's account of how it was found has also been questioned.

Schliemann's permit required him to give half of his finds to the Imperial Museum in Constantinople. Instead, he smuggled the treasure to Athens. The Ottoman government sued him in a Greek court, and in 1875 the case was settled when Schliemann paid compensation to the Imperial Museum. In 1881 he donated the treasure and his other Trojan finds to the city of Berlin.

During the Second World War, the treasure was stored in a flak tower at the Berlin Zoo. In 1945 museum officials handed it over to the Soviet army, and it was taken to Moscow. For decades the Soviet authorities denied knowing where it was. In the early 1990s, after investigations by journalists, Russia confirmed that it was in the Pushkin Museum, where it has been on display since 1996. Germany claims it as illegally removed wartime property; Türkiye argues that it was illegally exported from the Ottoman Empire.

expert.short: Priam's Treasure has been displaced three times: smuggled from the Ottoman Empire by Schliemann in 1873, removed from Berlin as Soviet trophy art in 1945, and claimed by both Germany and Türkiye. Russia's 1998 law on displaced cultural valuables makes it, in Russian law, state property.
expert.medium: The hoard from Troy II, variously interpreted as a single deposit or an assemblage compiled from several finds, was misidentified by Schliemann with Homer's Troy, a claim his collaborator Wilhelm Dörpfeld later corrected. Its export breached the terms of Schliemann's firman and the Ottoman regulations then in force; the Athens lawsuit ended in 1875 with a settlement that the Ottoman side accepted but that later Turkish claims regard as incomplete redress. Donated to Berlin in 1881, the treasure was surrendered by Wilhelm Unverzagt to Soviet forces in May 1945 and taken to Moscow by a trophy brigade. Its location was concealed until the revelations of Konstantin Akinsha and Grigorii Kozlov in 1991. Germany invokes the 1990 German–Soviet treaty and international law on wartime removals; Russia relies on the 1998 Federal Law on cultural valuables displaced as a result of the Second World War, which treats such property as compensatory restitution. Türkiye's claim rests on the original illicit export, producing a layered dispute with three claimants.
expert.long:
The treasure found by Heinrich Schliemann in 1873 belongs to the level of Troy II, dated to the mid-third millennium BCE. Whether it was a single hoard or an assemblage of objects from several contexts combined by Schliemann remains debated, as does his account of its discovery. Its identification with Priam's Troy, central to Schliemann's self-presentation, was abandoned after his collaborator Wilhelm Dörpfeld demonstrated that the Late Bronze Age levels were much later.

The first displacement was the illicit export from the Ottoman Empire. Schliemann's firman required him to share finds with the Imperial Museum, whose director Philipp Anton Dethier sought to enforce Ottoman regulations. Schliemann smuggled the treasure to Athens, and the Ottoman government sued him before a Greek court. In 1875 the parties settled: Schliemann paid compensation to the Imperial Museum and retained the treasure. The episode contributed to the stricter Ottoman antiquities law of 1884, drafted under Osman Hamdi Bey. Turkish claimants have since argued that the settlement did not legitimise an export contrary to Ottoman law.

The second displacement was wartime removal. Donated to Berlin in 1881, the treasure was stored during the Second World War in the flak tower at the Zoo. In May 1945 the prehistorian Wilhelm Unverzagt surrendered it to Soviet forces, and trophy brigades transported it to Moscow, part of a systematic removal of cultural property from Germany as compensation for Nazi destruction in the Soviet Union. Its whereabouts were concealed for nearly half a century until Konstantin Akinsha and Grigorii Kozlov revealed in 1991 that it was held in the Pushkin Museum; Russia confirmed this in 1993, and the treasure has been exhibited there since 1996.

The third layer is the current legal dispute. Germany claims the treasure under the 1990 Treaty on Good-Neighbourliness with the Soviet Union and the 1992 cultural agreement with Russia, which provide for the return of unlawfully removed cultural property, and under the Hague Regulations prohibiting the seizure of cultural property. Russia's Federal Law of 1998 on cultural valuables displaced to the USSR as a result of the Second World War declares such property Russian state property, as compensatory restitution for wartime losses. Türkiye has asserted that, if the treasure were to leave Russia, its claim would take precedence as the state of origin.

The case is thus a layered dispute in which each claimant relies on a different historical moment: the illicit export of 1873, the donation of 1881, the removal of 1945. It illustrates how successive displacements can generate competing legitimacies, and how restitution requires choosing which past to repair.

maps.caption-2: Then: Amarna, Egypt - Now: Berlin, Germany

fun.short: Meet Queen Nefertiti! Her bust shows off her royal beauty, and it’s over 3,000 years old. German archaeologists took this sculpture to Berlin, and it’s been there for more than 100 years. Fun fact: Queen Nefertiti was famous for her beauty—and she’s still a star today!
fun.medium: Meet Queen Nefertiti, one of ancient Egypt’s most famous and beautiful figures! The Bust of Nefertiti, over 3,000 years old, captures the elegance of this iconic queen who ruled alongside Pharaoh Akhenaten during the Amarna Period. The bust was uncovered in 1912 by German archaeologists and was taken to Berlin, where it remains a star attraction at the Neues Museum. Her perfectly symmetrical face and serene expression are a testament to the artistic mastery of Egyptian sculptors, showcasing the height of royal portraiture at the time.  - Fun fact: Queen Nefertiti was so renowned for her beauty that even today, her bust is seen as a global icon, and she continues to inspire modern fashion and art! While this sculpture immortalizes her royal beauty, its presence in Berlin rather than Egypt has sparked a century of controversy. Egypt has repeatedly asked for the bust’s return, yet it remains in Europe, a relic of the colonial era’s power imbalance in archaeology.
fun.long: The Bust of Nefertiti is one of the most iconic masterpieces of ancient Egyptian art, embodying the height of artistic expression during the Amarna Period, around 1345 BCE. Crafted from limestone and stucco, the bust is a remarkable example of royal portraiture and was designed to capture the elegance, beauty, and divine status of Queen Nefertiti, wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten. Nefertiti’s reign was a pivotal moment in Egyptian history, marked by sweeping religious reforms as Akhenaten sought to elevate the worship of Aten, the sun god, over traditional polytheism. This period, known for its artistic innovations, including a shift toward more naturalistic representations in art, produced some of the finest sculptures, with Nefertiti’s bust standing as a crowning achievement. The bust is celebrated not only for its depiction of Nefertiti’s symmetrical, serene face but also for the intricacies of her iconic tall blue crown and the delicate rendering of her features, which were carefully enhanced with vibrant pigments. Egyptian sculptors of the time were masters of their craft, using materials like limestone to create lifelike portraits that embodied both physical beauty and divine attributes. Nefertiti’s bust, however, stands apart for its unprecedented refinement, with its perfectly proportioned features and subtle expressions reflecting an unparalleled level of artistic sophistication. Discovered in the ruins of Amarna in 1912 by a team led by German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt, the bust was immediately recognized as a treasure of immense historical and artistic value. Its removal from Egypt and subsequent transport to Berlin, where it remains on display at the Neues Museum, has sparked over a century of controversy. Egypt has long demanded the bust’s repatriation, arguing that such a significant cultural artifact should be returned to its homeland. Despite this, the bust has remained one of the most prized exhibits in Germany, raising ongoing ethical debates about the ownership and location of culturally significant artworks, especially those taken during periods of colonial rule. The Bust of Nefertiti thus not only captures the grandeur of ancient Egyptian art but also serves as a symbol of the complex and contested legacy of archaeological discoveries in the modern world.

basic.short: The Bust of Nefertiti, carved around 1345 BCE, is a symbol of ancient Egyptian royalty. German archaeologists uncovered the bust in 1912, and since then, it has been housed in the Neues Museum in Berlin. Egypt has repeatedly requested its return.
basic.medium: The Bust of Nefertiti, carved around 1345 BCE, is a stunning representation of one of Egypt’s most famous queens. Nefertiti’s reign marked a unique period in Egyptian history—the Amarna Period—during which her husband, Pharaoh Akhenaten, instituted sweeping religious reforms, focusing worship on the sun god Aten. The bust, discovered in the ancient city of Amarna, was found in 1912 by German archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt. Despite its Egyptian origins, the bust was swiftly transported to Berlin, where it has remained ever since, becoming one of the most famous pieces of ancient art housed outside of Egypt.   Nefertiti’s bust exemplifies the incredible skill of ancient Egyptian sculptors, with its precise detailing of the queen’s facial features and the intricate headdress she wears. Its relocation to Europe, however, has been a source of tension, as Egypt has consistently requested its repatriation. Despite international discussions, the bust continues to reside in Germany, sparking ongoing debates about the legacy of colonial-era archaeology and cultural heritage ownership.
basic.long: The Bust of Nefertiti, created around 1345 BCE, is one of the most celebrated works of ancient Egyptian art, embodying both the artistic skill of its creators and the political and religious transformations of the Amarna Period. This period saw the radical religious reforms introduced by Pharaoh Akhenaten, who elevated the worship of the sun god Aten, dismantling centuries of polytheistic tradition. Nefertiti, as Akhenaten’s queen, played a prominent role during this era, not only in religious rituals but also in the political life of Egypt, where she was depicted with near-equal status to her husband, an unprecedented portrayal for a queen in Egyptian history. The bust itself is a masterpiece of Egyptian craftsmanship. Carved from a single piece of limestone, it was meticulously coated in stucco and painted with natural pigments, some of which still survive today, offering insight into the sophisticated techniques used by ancient artisans. The fine detailing of Nefertiti’s facial features—her high cheekbones, elegantly arched brows, and distinctive long neck—exemplifies the transition toward more realistic and naturalistic portrayals of the human form during this period. Her large blue crown, adorned with the sacred uraeus (the symbol of royal authority), further emphasizes her divine and royal stature, underscoring the blend of political and religious symbolism inherent in her portrayal. The bust’s discovery in 1912 by the German archaeological team led by Ludwig Borchardt in Amarna was a major find, providing an unparalleled look into the art and culture of one of Egypt’s most unique historical periods. The circumstances of its removal from Egypt, however, remain a source of controversy. While Borchardt legally obtained the bust under the agreements of the time, which allowed foreign powers to remove artifacts from their excavation sites, the ethics of such practices have since come under significant scrutiny. Nefertiti’s bust was transported to Berlin, where it was hidden from public view for several years before becoming one of the most famous exhibits in the Neues Museum.<r>Today, the bust is a symbol of both Egypt’s rich artistic heritage and the broader issues surrounding the ownership of cultural artifacts. Egypt has persistently called for its return, citing its importance not only as a national treasure but also as an integral piece of their historical identity. Germany, on the other hand, argues that the bust was legally acquired and has been better preserved under their care. This ongoing debate is emblematic of larger conversations about cultural restitution, colonialism, and the role of museums in housing artifacts that originated in other nations.

expert.short: The iconic Bust of Nefertiti, crafted in the Amarna period of ancient Egypt around 1345 BCE, represents one of the most famous symbols of Egyptian cultural heritage. Removed by German archaeologists in 1912, the bust’s placement in Berlin has sparked long-standing debates about cultural restitution and the ethics of colonial-era excavations.
expert.medium: The Bust of Nefertiti, crafted in 1345 BCE during the height of the Amarna Period, stands as one of the most recognizable and iconic pieces of ancient Egyptian art. Its nearly flawless depiction of the queen’s features reflects both the artistic sophistication of the time and the political significance of Nefertiti herself. As the wife of Pharaoh Akhenaten, Nefertiti played a central role in his religious revolution, and her bust was likely created to emphasize her divine status alongside her husband. The bust, made of limestone and covered with a thin layer of stucco and paint, displays a level of craftsmanship that has fascinated historians and artists alike for over a century. Discovered by German archaeologists in 1912, the bust was removed from Egypt and taken to Berlin, where it has remained despite numerous requests for its repatriation. The removal of the bust from Egypt represents the broader patterns of cultural appropriation that occurred during the height of Western archaeological expeditions in the 19th and 20th centuries. Nefertiti’s bust has since become a symbol of the ongoing struggle between nations to reclaim their cultural heritage, raising questions about the ethical responsibilities of museums in the modern world.
expert.long: The Bust of Nefertiti, sculpted around 1345 BCE, is a quintessential representation of the artistic excellence of ancient Egypt, crafted during the transformative Amarna Period. This era, marked by radical shifts in religious and political structures under Pharaoh Akhenaten, introduced a more humanistic and individualized approach to royal portraiture. The bust itself stands as a visual testament to this period’s departure from traditional Egyptian art, which had long emphasized idealized, stoic representations of the divine and royal figures. Nefertiti’s bust, however, captures a sense of both regal authority and personal beauty, reflective of the queen’s elevated status as both a political and religious figure alongside Akhenaten. Nefertiti’s role during the Amarna Period went far beyond that of a typical queen. She was often depicted in positions of power traditionally reserved for pharaohs—leading religious ceremonies, engaging in diplomacy, and acting as a central figure in the Atenist monotheistic worship introduced by Akhenaten. Her portrayal in the bust, with its perfectly symmetrical face, elongated neck, and distinctive blue crown, symbolizes not only her beauty but also her divine and political authority. The sculpture, attributed to the master sculptor Thutmose, exemplifies a fusion of realism and idealization that was revolutionary for its time. The fine detailing of her facial features, including the soft contours of her cheekbones, the delicate arch of her eyebrows, and the hint of a serene smile, reflects the highly skilled craftsmanship and the artistic innovations of the period. The materials used to create the bust are equally significant. The limestone core was covered with a thin layer of stucco, allowing for precise details to be modeled. Natural pigments were applied to bring life to the figure, most notably the striking use of blue for her crown and the vibrant red for her lips. This emphasis on color and material contrasts is reflective of the symbolic importance of Nefertiti’s role as a living goddess, embodying both earthly and divine qualities. Moreover, the missing inlaid quartz in one of her eyes has fueled much speculation, with some suggesting it was never completed, while others argue it symbolically represents the mystery surrounding her life and reign. The bust’s discovery by Ludwig Borchardt and his team in 1912 during excavations at Amarna, the capital city built by Akhenaten, was a landmark event in the history of Egyptology. Borchardt recognized its significance immediately, describing it as a piece of unparalleled beauty. However, its removal from Egypt to Germany soon became a point of contention. The excavation and subsequent export of the bust were conducted under the prevailing laws of the time, which allowed foreign archaeologists to divide their finds with local authorities. Nonetheless, this practice reflected the unequal power dynamics of the colonial era, during which Western powers exerted considerable influence over the cultural and historical heritage of countries under their control or influence. Since its relocation to Berlin, the bust has been at the center of ongoing repatriation debates. Egypt has made multiple formal requests for the return of Nefertiti, arguing that the bust is a national treasure of immense cultural and historical significance. Germany, on the other hand, has maintained that the bust was acquired legally and that its conservation and display in the Neues Museum have preserved it for the world to appreciate. This dispute is emblematic of broader discussions about the legacy of colonial-era archaeology, the ethics of artifact acquisition, and the rights of nations to reclaim their cultural heritage. The Bust of Nefertiti, therefore, is not only an extraordinary piece of art but also a symbol of the complex entanglements of history, power, and identity. Its story raises critical questions about the responsibilities of modern museums, the long-standing impact of colonialism, and the ongoing struggles for cultural restitution in a post-colonial world.

maps.caption-2: Then: Babylon, Iraq - Now: Berlin, Germany

fun.short: The Ishtar Gate was the shining blue entrance to ancient Babylon, covered in dragons and bulls made of glazed bricks. German archaeologists dug it up and rebuilt it in a museum in Berlin! Fun fact: the gate you see in Berlin is only the smaller front part.
fun.medium: About 2,600 years ago, King Nebuchadnezzar II made Babylon one of the most magnificent cities in the world. Its main gate, dedicated to the goddess Ishtar, was covered in bricks glazed a deep, shining blue, with rows of golden-brown bulls and strange dragons called mušḫuššu, part snake, part lion, part eagle. A long street lined with lions led through it. Over the centuries Babylon fell into ruins, and the gate was buried. Between 1902 and 1914 the German archaeologist Robert Koldewey dug up thousands of broken glazed bricks. They were shipped to Berlin, where experts pieced them together like a gigantic puzzle. Fun fact: the rebuilt gate opened in the Pergamon Museum in 1930, and it is so big that the museum had to be built around it!
fun.long:
Around 575 BCE, Babylon, in today's Iraq, was ruled by King Nebuchadnezzar II, one of the most powerful kings of the ancient world. He rebuilt his capital to show off his power and to honour the gods, with huge walls, palaces and temples.

The most spectacular entrance to the city was the Ishtar Gate, dedicated to the goddess of love and war. Its walls were covered in bricks glazed a brilliant blue, and on them marched rows of animals in relief: aurochs, a kind of wild bull linked to the storm god Adad, and mušḫuššu dragons, the animal of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon. A wide road, the Processional Way, passed through the gate, lined with lions, the animals of Ishtar. Every New Year, statues of the gods were carried along it in a great festival.

After Babylon's glory faded, its buildings crumbled and were buried under earth and rubble. People took bricks away to build their houses.

In 1899 the German archaeologist Robert Koldewey started digging at Babylon, and from 1902 he uncovered the Ishtar Gate. The lower parts of the walls were still standing, but the glazed bricks from above had fallen and broken into countless pieces. His team collected them in boxes.

Many years later, in 1927, the fragments were shipped to Berlin. There, the archaeologist Walter Andrae and his team spent years sorting the pieces and filling the gaps with new bricks. In 1930 the reconstructed gate and part of the Processional Way opened in the new Pergamon Museum. Fun fact: in Babylon itself, visitors today can see the original foundations with their unglazed animal reliefs, and a smaller replica of the gate.

basic.short: The Ishtar Gate, built of glazed bricks for Nebuchadnezzar II around 575 BCE, was excavated at Babylon by Robert Koldewey from 1902. Its fragments were shipped to Berlin, where it was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum from 1928.
basic.medium: The Ishtar Gate was the northern entrance to the inner city of Babylon, built around 575 BCE under Nebuchadnezzar II and dedicated to the goddess Ishtar. Its walls were faced with blue glazed bricks decorated with moulded reliefs of aurochs and mušḫuššu dragons, symbols of the gods Adad and Marduk, while the Processional Way that ran through it was lined with lions. The German Oriental Society's excavations at Babylon, directed by Robert Koldewey from 1899 to 1917, uncovered the gate from 1902. The glazed bricks survived only as fragments. After the First World War, an agreement with the Iraqi antiquities authorities under the British mandate allowed their shipment to Berlin in 1927, where Walter Andrae reconstructed the front gate and part of the Processional Way in the Pergamon Museum. It opened in 1930. Iraqi officials have called for its return.
basic.long:
Babylon, on the Euphrates in central Iraq, was one of the great cities of the ancient world. Under Nebuchadnezzar II (reigned 605–562 BCE) it was rebuilt on a monumental scale, with double walls, palaces and the temple of Marduk with its ziggurat, the Etemenanki.

The Ishtar Gate, completed around 575 BCE, was the northernmost of the eight gates of the inner city. It consisted of a smaller outer gate and a larger inner one, faced with bricks glazed in deep blue. On them alternated moulded reliefs of aurochs, sacred to the weather god Adad, and mušḫuššu dragons, the emblem of Marduk. Through the gate ran the Processional Way, lined with glazed lions, along which the statues of the gods were carried during the New Year festival.

The German Oriental Society began excavating Babylon in 1899 under Robert Koldewey. From 1902 his team uncovered the gate, whose lower courses, with unglazed reliefs, still stood in place, while the glazed upper parts had collapsed into fragments. Tens of thousands of fragments were collected and packed.

The First World War interrupted the work. After the war Iraq came under a British mandate, and in 1926 the Iraqi antiquities service agreed to a division of finds that allowed most of the glazed brick fragments to go to Berlin. They arrived in 1927, and Walter Andrae directed their reconstruction. In 1930 the outer gate and part of the Processional Way opened in the Pergamon Museum. Other panels went to museums in Istanbul, Paris, New York, Chicago and elsewhere.

Iraqi officials have called for the gate's return. Berlin has not agreed, and the Pergamon Museum has been closed for renovation since 2023.

expert.short: Excavated by Koldewey from 1902 and reconstructed in Berlin from fragments divided under the British mandate in 1926, the Ishtar Gate is both an archaeological reconstruction and a product of the partage system. Iraqi calls for its return question that system's legitimacy.
expert.medium: The Ishtar Gate formed part of Nebuchadnezzar II's reconstruction of Babylon as a cosmic capital, its imagery of aurochs and mušḫuššu embodying the protective presence of Adad and Marduk at the city's ritual threshold. The Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft's excavation under Robert Koldewey (1899–1917) combined architectural archaeology with the recovery of glazed brick fragments whose reassembly required decades of work. The fragments' division in 1926, negotiated with the Iraqi Department of Antiquities under British mandatory authority, exemplifies the partage system, in which excavated finds were shared between host countries and foreign excavators. Walter Andrae's reconstruction of the outer gate in the Pergamon Museum, opened in 1930, is an interpretive reassembly incorporating substantial modern material. Iraqi calls for return challenge a division concluded under mandate conditions, while German institutions point to its legality and to the gate's fragility and composite character.
expert.long:
The Ishtar Gate belongs to Nebuchadnezzar II's reconstruction of Babylon as the centre of the cosmos, a programme recorded in the king's building inscriptions. As the northern gate of the inner city, it marked the threshold through which the Processional Way entered the sacred precinct during the akītu, or New Year festival, when the statue of Marduk was carried to the festival house outside the walls. Its imagery of aurochs and mušḫuššu dragons, rendered in moulded and glazed brick, placed the city under the protection of Adad and Marduk, while the lions of the Processional Way evoked Ishtar.

The Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft, founded in 1898 with imperial patronage, sponsored excavations at Babylon under Robert Koldewey from 1899. The project expressed German imperial ambitions in the Ottoman Empire, in the era of the Baghdad Railway, and developed innovative techniques of architectural excavation. From 1902 Koldewey's team uncovered the gate, recording its unglazed foundation reliefs in situ and collecting the fragments of its glazed superstructure.

The removal of the fragments was delayed by Ottoman antiquities law and then by the war. After 1918, Iraq came under British mandatory administration. In 1926 the Iraqi Department of Antiquities, headed by British officials in accordance with a law drafted under Gertrude Bell's influence, agreed to a division that allowed the majority of the glazed brick fragments to go to Berlin, with a share remaining in Iraq. This was an instance of partage, the system by which finds were divided between host countries and foreign expeditions, common in the Middle East until the mid-twentieth century.

In Berlin, Walter Andrae directed the desalination, sorting and reassembly of the fragments, reconstructing the smaller outer gate and a section of the Processional Way in the Pergamon Museum, which opened in 1930. The result is an interpretive reconstruction in which original glazed bricks are combined with modern replacements. Surplus panels were exchanged or sold to museums in Istanbul, Paris, New York, Chicago, Detroit and elsewhere.

Iraqi officials have called for the gate's return, arguing that a division negotiated under mandate conditions did not reflect Iraqi sovereignty. German institutions consider the division lawful and emphasise the gate's fragility and composite character. Meanwhile Babylon, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019 after damage caused by twentieth-century reconstruction and military occupation, displays the gate's foundations in situ. The case illustrates how partage, often presented as a legal and equitable arrangement, is now reassessed in light of the unequal political conditions under which it operated.

maps.caption-2: Then: Persepolis, Fars, Iran - Now: London, UK, and other museums

fun.short: The Achaemenid reliefs are stone carvings from the Persian Empire, over 2,500 years ago! They tell stories about ancient kings and warriors. Explorers took them in the 1800s, and today, they’re displayed far away in Europe. Fun fact: Persia was one of the most powerful empires ever, and these carvings show off its greatness!
fun.medium: The Achaemenid Reliefs are magnificent stone carvings created over 2,500 years ago during the reign of the Persian Empire. These detailed carvings, found primarily in Persepolis, depict the grandeur of Persian kings, warriors, and court officials. The reliefs were designed to celebrate the might of the empire, showcasing the power and influence of rulers like Darius the Great. Carved into the stone walls of palaces and ceremonial structures, these reliefs once welcomed foreign dignitaries and impressed visitors with their intricacy.  - Fun fact: Persia was one of the most powerful empires of the ancient world, stretching from Egypt to India, and these carvings serve as a visual testament to its greatness! Sadly, in the 19th century, European explorers took these cultural treasures during their expeditions, and today they are displayed in museums far from their original context. The removal of these artifacts from Persepolis, the heart of the Persian Empire, means they have lost much of their historical connection to the land where they were created.
fun.long: The Achaemenid reliefs, carved over 2,500 years ago during the reign of the mighty Persian Empire, are some of the most impressive stone carvings from the ancient world! These intricate works of art, found on the walls of Persepolis, depict processions of noblemen, soldiers, and ambassadors from different nations paying tribute to Persian kings. The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great, was one of the largest and most powerful empires in ancient history, stretching from the Mediterranean Sea all the way to the Indus River. These reliefs give us a glimpse into the grandeur of this empire, illustrating scenes of diplomacy, royal ceremonies, and military might. One of the most famous of these carvings is the depiction of King Darius I, seated on his throne, surrounded by attendants and soldiers. The figures are shown in a highly stylized manner, with impressive attention to detail, from their elaborate clothing to the weapons they carry. This artistry demonstrates the Achaemenid’s ability to use reliefs not just as decoration, but also as propaganda, showcasing the power and stability of their rule. The reliefs weren’t just art; they were designed to impress visitors and subjects with the empire’s might, as well as to reinforce the idea of Persian superiority and unity. But while these reliefs are now admired in museums, they were never meant to be viewed so far from home. In the 19th century, European explorers and archaeologists began to excavate ancient Persian sites, including Persepolis, during the great wave of imperial exploration. In the process, they removed many of these reliefs and transported them to European museums, far from their original locations. These reliefs, once part of the monumental architecture of Persepolis, are now on display in countries like the UK and France, where they are admired as examples of ancient Persian craftsmanship. However, their removal raises serious ethical questions about the legacy of colonialism and the ways in which artifacts were taken from their places of origin. For many Iranians, these reliefs represent an important part of their cultural heritage, and their absence from Iran is a reminder of the losses endured during colonial times. The Achaemenid reliefs are not just ancient stone carvings; they are symbols of a rich cultural history that was disrupted by the colonial ambitions of European powers.

basic.short: The Achaemenid Reliefs, dating to the 5th century BCE, are intricate carvings from the heart of the Persian Empire. European explorers looted them in the 19th century, and now they reside in museums outside of Iran, far from their historical context.
basic.medium: The Achaemenid Reliefs, dating to the 5th century BCE, are masterful examples of Persian stonework from one of the world’s most powerful ancient civilizations. These reliefs were carved into the walls of Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, which once ruled over a vast territory stretching across the Middle East and Central Asia. The detailed scenes depict processions of dignitaries, soldiers, and tribute bearers, highlighting the empire's diplomatic reach and military prowess. Scholars believe these carvings were intended to reinforce the divine right of the Persian kings and their role as global rulers. In the 19th century, European explorers, driven by a fascination with Persia's ancient past, removed many of these reliefs, taking them back to Europe. Their extraction disrupted the historical landscape of Persepolis, and today, the reliefs are dispersed across various museums in Europe and North America. This loss not only removed key pieces of Iran's cultural history but also deprived the world of experiencing these artworks within their original, majestic setting.
basic.long: The Achaemenid reliefs, created during the 5th century BCE in the heart of the Persian Empire, are a masterful representation of Persian art and imperial power. These elaborate carvings, primarily found at Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid dynasty, depict processions of soldiers, officials, and emissaries from subject nations paying tribute to the Persian king. The reliefs are not just decorative but serve a deeper purpose—highlighting the empire’s vast reach and the unity among the diverse peoples it ruled. The level of detail, from the flowing robes of the ambassadors to the intricate patterns on their armor and headgear, reflects the sophistication of Persian craftsmanship and the grandeur of their imperial narrative. Persepolis itself was a masterpiece of ancient architecture, and these reliefs formed an integral part of its monumental staircases, gateways, and palaces. The empire’s greatest rulers, including Darius the Great and Xerxes, oversaw the construction of these buildings and their adornment with intricate carvings that conveyed Persian dominance over its subjects. The reliefs were designed to reinforce the political and cultural ideology of the Achaemenid Empire, emphasizing loyalty, submission, and the prosperity that came from being part of such a vast and powerful empire. They also offered a visual record of the empire’s might, showcasing warriors, tribute bearers, and royal figures in stylized but highly symbolic scenes. However, during the 19th century, when European explorers began to delve into the ancient world, they uncovered the ruins of Persepolis and its stunning reliefs. Archaeologists and treasure hunters alike took interest in these artifacts, which were seen as trophies of a bygone era. Many of the reliefs were looted and shipped to Europe, where they now reside in museums such as the British Museum and the Louvre. These museums celebrated their acquisition as evidence of the West’s cultural dominance, placing the reliefs among other trophies from non-Western civilizations. Removed from their original context, these reliefs are admired today as isolated works of art, rather than as integral parts of the grand structures they once adorned. The looting and removal of the Achaemenid reliefs are emblematic of the larger trend during the colonial period, where Western powers appropriated valuable artifacts from the Middle East and beyond. The displacement of these cultural treasures from Iran has sparked ongoing debates about the ethics of retaining them in European collections. The Achaemenid reliefs, which once stood as proud symbols of Persian imperial authority, now symbolize the cultural exploitation and material loss that accompanied the spread of Western imperialism. Iran has long sought the return of these pieces, arguing that they are crucial elements of its cultural heritage and historical identity. Despite these calls, the reliefs remain in Europe, where they continue to be viewed through a lens of imperial legacy and colonial acquisition.

expert.short: These reliefs from Persepolis, created during the height of the Achaemenid Empire in the 5th century BCE, are significant artefacts of Persian art and history. Their removal by European explorers in the 19th century exemplifies the cultural losses endured by non-Western nations during the age of imperial exploration and looting.

These reliefs adorned the grand palaces of Persepolis, depicting rulers like Darius the Great receiving tributes from the vast territories under their control. Each figure is intricately detailed, showcasing the artistic sophistication of Achaemenid craftsmanship and their advanced stone carving techniques. The reliefs provide invaluable insights into the social and political structure of the empire, depicting delegations from various nations, each bringing offerings to the Persian king in a show of loyalty and submission. In the 19th century, these reliefs were removed from Persepolis by European explorers, a common practice at the time as Western nations sought to claim cultural artifacts from around the world. expert.long: The Achaemenid reliefs, meticulously carved in the 5th century BCE at the height of the Persian Empire, stand as powerful symbols of the empire’s grandeur and the artistic achievements of the ancient Near East. These reliefs, primarily found at the palace complex of Persepolis, depict ceremonial processions, royal audiences, and the presentation of tribute from subject nations. They serve as both artistic and political statements, reinforcing the legitimacy and dominance of the Achaemenid rulers over their vast empire, which stretched from Egypt to India. The reliefs were not just ornamental; they were integral to the architectural and ideological design of Persepolis, designed to glorify the Persian monarchy and communicate the unity and diversity of the empire's people. Crafted with remarkable precision, the reliefs depict emissaries from different parts of the empire, identifiable by their unique clothing, hairstyles, and gifts, which represent the distinct cultures within the Persian realm. This visual portrayal of the empire's breadth and the loyalty of its subjects to the Persian king was a deliberate strategy to convey the empire's power and stability. Furthermore, the representations of Persian guards, with their disciplined posture and finely detailed armor, highlight the militaristic strength that underpinned the empire's political dominance. The reliefs also provide insight into the Achaemenid worldview, emphasizing order, hierarchy, and divine kingship, with the king often depicted as a larger-than-life figure presiding over the procession of lesser dignitaries. During the 19th century, however, European explorers and archaeologists, spurred by a growing fascination with the ancient world and a desire to expand museum collections, descended upon sites like Persepolis. These reliefs, seen as exceptional examples of ancient craftsmanship and imperial power, became prime targets for removal. Archaeologists, often backed by imperial powers, saw the acquisition of these artifacts as both a scholarly pursuit and a form of cultural conquest. As a result, many Achaemenid reliefs were removed from their original locations and transported to European museums, where they were displayed as evidence of the greatness of ancient civilizations—civilizations that had long been subdued or forgotten. The removal of these reliefs, particularly from Persepolis, signifies more than just the loss of valuable artifacts; it reflects the broader trend of cultural extraction that occurred during the age of imperialism. The reliefs, once integral to the architectural and ceremonial space of Persepolis, were stripped from their historical and cultural contexts, reducing their significance to mere artistic objects in foreign lands. European museums, particularly the British Museum and the Louvre, became the new homes for these Persian treasures, where they were celebrated as symbols of Western exploration and intellectual achievement. However, in the process, the cultural and historical continuity of the reliefs was broken, and their meaning within the Persian imperial context was lost to the audiences that now viewed them in distant European capitals.  The continued presence of these reliefs in European museums has fueled ongoing debates about the ethics of cultural restitution and the responsibilities of museums to return looted artifacts. Iran, like many countries that experienced colonial or imperial exploitation, has made repeated requests for the return of these pieces, arguing that they are essential to the nation’s cultural heritage and identity. The reliefs, once a source of pride for the Achaemenid Empire, now serve as reminders of the cultural losses suffered by non-Western nations during the 19th century. They exemplify the complex legacy of imperialism, where the artistic and historical achievements of ancient civilizations were appropriated by imperial powers, leading to long-lasting tensions over the ownership and rightful place of cultural treasures.

maps.caption-2: Then: Nok culture sites, Kaduna State, Nigeria - Now: Various museums and private collections

fun.short: More than 2,000 years ago, people of the Nok culture in central Nigeria made amazing clay figures with big eyes and fancy hairstyles. They were forgotten until tin miners found one in 1943. Fun fact: since the 1990s so many were dug up and sold illegally that Nigeria had to ban their export!
fun.medium: The Nok people lived in the hills and valleys of central Nigeria more than 2,000 years ago. They farmed, they were among the first in West Africa to make iron, and they modelled clay into figures of people and animals, with huge eyes, elegant hairstyles and jewellery. In 1943 tin miners dug up a clay head near the village of Nok, and archaeologists realised that a whole ancient culture had been found. Many of the first finds went to Nigerian museums. But from the 1990s collectors abroad paid high prices for Nok figures, and looters dug up hundreds of sites. Fun fact: when looters dig without recording anything, we lose the clues that could tell us what the figures meant!
fun.long:
Imagine a clay head with enormous triangular eyes, a pierced nose and a hairstyle of rolls and buns, made more than 2,000 years ago. That is a Nok terracotta, from one of the oldest sculptural traditions in Africa south of the Sahara.

The Nok culture lived in central Nigeria, around the Jos Plateau, from about the first millennium BCE. Nok farmers grew millet and other crops, and they were among the earliest people in West Africa to smelt iron. They also made clay figures, some almost life-size, of people with detailed jewellery, clothes and hairstyles, and sometimes animals.

For a very long time nobody outside the region knew about them. Then, in 1943, tin miners working near the village of Nok found a clay head. A British archaeologist working for the Nigerian antiquities service, Bernard Fagg, collected more and more finds, and many went into Nigerian museums, such as the museum in Jos.

The trouble began later. From the 1990s art collectors in Europe and North America paid high prices for Nok figures. Looters dug up hundreds of sites, breaking and smuggling the figures out of Nigeria, even though the law forbids it. Every time a site is dug without archaeologists, we lose the information about how and why the figures were buried.

Fun fact: in 2000 the International Council of Museums put Nok terracottas on a "Red List" of objects at risk, to warn museums and collectors not to buy them. Some looted figures have since been seized by customs officers and sent back to Nigeria.

basic.short: Nok terracottas, made in central Nigeria in the first millennium BCE and early centuries CE, are among the oldest sculptures of sub-Saharan Africa. First found in 1943, they were dug up illegally in large numbers from the 1990s for the international art market.
basic.medium: The Nok culture flourished in central Nigeria, on and around the Jos Plateau, from the first millennium BCE into the early centuries CE. Its farmers were among the first ironworkers in West Africa, and its artists modelled terracotta figures with triangular eyes, elaborate hairstyles and jewellery. The first figure was found by tin miners at Nok in 1943, and the archaeologist Bernard Fagg, of the colonial antiquities service, gathered many finds for Nigerian museums. The great losses came later: from the 1990s the demand of collectors abroad led to the looting of hundreds of sites. Nigerian law bans the export of antiquities, and in 2000 Nok terracottas were placed on the ICOM Red List of objects at risk. Looted figures are now in private collections and some museums abroad; a few have been seized and returned.
basic.long:
The Nok culture takes its name from the village in central Nigeria where the first of its terracottas was found. Archaeologists now date it from the first millennium BCE into the early centuries CE, in a region around the Jos Plateau that spans today's Kaduna, Plateau and Nasarawa states. Its people farmed pearl millet and other crops and were among the earliest iron smelters in West Africa.

Nok artists made terracotta figures of remarkable skill: heads and bodies with triangular or D-shaped eyes, pierced pupils, elaborate hairstyles, beads and clothing. Many were broken and deliberately buried, which suggests a ritual use that is still debated; they may have represented ancestors or important people.

The first Nok head was found in 1943 by tin miners. Bernard Fagg, an archaeologist of the colonial antiquities service, recognised its importance and built up a collection, much of which stayed in Nigeria and formed the basis of the Jos Museum, opened in 1952.

The major loss of Nok heritage happened after independence. From the 1990s the international art market's demand for African antiquities made Nok figures valuable, and looters dug up hundreds of sites. The figures were smuggled out through regional networks to dealers in Europe and North America. Nigerian law forbids the export of antiquities, and in 2000 the International Council of Museums placed Nok terracottas on its Red List for Africa.

The case is also a museum story. In 1998 France bought three looted Nok figures for the new gallery of African art at the Louvre; after criticism, an agreement of 2002 recognised Nigeria's ownership while leaving them in Paris on loan. Customs authorities in several countries have since seized looted figures and returned them to Nigeria.

expert.short: Nok terracottas, products of a central Nigerian culture of the first millennium BCE, entered scholarship in 1943 and the international market mainly from the 1990s. Their loss is less a matter of colonial seizure than of post-colonial looting driven by demand in Europe and North America.
expert.medium: The Nok culture, dated by recent research at Goethe University Frankfurt and elsewhere from the late second or first millennium BCE into the early first millennium CE, is known for terracotta sculpture of great formal complexity and for early iron metallurgy. Its archaeology began in 1943, when tin miners found a head at Nok, and Bernard Fagg of the colonial Antiquities Service built a collection that largely remained in Nigeria. The destruction of the Nok record occurred mostly after independence: from the 1990s, market demand for 'authentic' African antiquities fuelled systematic looting, destroying stratigraphic contexts at hundreds of sites. Nigerian law vests antiquities in the state and bans their export, and ICOM's Red List for Africa (2000) includes Nok terracottas. The French acquisition of three looted figures for the Louvre in 1998, regularised by a 2002 agreement recognising Nigerian ownership, illustrates how Western institutions participated in and then accommodated this trade.
expert.long:
The Nok culture occupies a central place in the archaeology of West Africa. Recent research, notably the long-term project of Goethe University Frankfurt, places it from the late second or first millennium BCE into the early first millennium CE, in a region around the Jos Plateau of central Nigeria. Its communities practised farming, including pearl millet, and were among the earliest iron smelters in the region. Their terracotta sculpture, ranging from small figures to near life-size heads, displays a sophisticated formal language of stylised eyes, coiffures, jewellery and posture.

Nok entered scholarship in 1943, when tin miners discovered a terracotta head at Nok. Bernard Fagg, of the colonial Antiquities Service, identified further finds from the tin fields and founded the Jos Museum, which opened in 1952. In contrast to many objects in this collection, the early Nok finds were largely retained in Nigeria, forming part of the country's national collections at independence.

The destruction of the Nok record took place mainly after independence and was driven by international demand. From the 1990s the market for African antiquities in Europe and North America placed high values on Nok terracottas. Looting spread across hundreds of sites, often organised through local labour and regional middlemen, and the figures were exported illegally, frequently with restorations or forgeries mixed in. The loss is above all epistemic: without stratigraphic context, the function of the figures, often found broken and buried, is far harder to reconstruct.

Legal and institutional responses followed. Nigerian law vests antiquities in the state and prohibits their export, and ICOM's Red List for Africa (2000) included Nok terracottas. Yet Western institutions also took part in the trade. In 1998 France acquired three looted Nok figures for the gallery of African art at the Louvre; after public criticism, an agreement of 2002 recognised Nigeria's ownership while allowing the figures to remain in Paris on loan. Seizures and returns by customs authorities, including in the United States and Europe, have repatriated some pieces.

The case thus requires a different frame from colonial seizure. It shows how the post-colonial art market, legitimised by the aesthetic canon of 'African art' built during the colonial period, produced losses on a scale comparable to earlier removals, and how restitution depends on controlling demand as well as on returning objects.

maps.caption-2: Then: Acropolis, Athens (Ottoman Greece), Greece - Now: London, UK

fun.short: The Parthenon Marbles are sculptures that used to decorate an amazing temple in ancient Athens! Imagine walking around a giant building with statues of gods and heroes everywhere. Lord Elgin took these sculptures, and now they live in the British Museum instead of Greece. Fun fact: Greece has been asking for these marbles back for over 200 years!
fun.medium: The Parthenon Marbles are magnificent sculptures that once adorned the Parthenon in Athens, a grand temple built for the goddess Athena. These masterpieces were crafted by the finest artists of ancient Greece and depicted gods, heroes, and mythological battles in incredible detail. However, during the early 19th century, Lord Elgin, a British nobleman, removed many of these sculptures and transported them to the UK. Today, they reside in the British Museum, far from their original home in Greece.  - Fun fact: Greece has been asking for these marbles back for over 200 years, starting one of the longest-running cultural heritage disputes! The Parthenon was more than just a religious building—it was a symbol of Athens' power and culture. The marbles, carved in 447-438 BCE, reflect the artistic and intellectual achievements of the city during its Golden Age. Their removal by Elgin has sparked centuries of debate, as Greece continues to campaign for their return.
fun.long: The Parthenon Marbles, masterpieces of classical Greek sculpture, were once part of the architectural and artistic grandeur of the Parthenon in Athens, a temple dedicated to Athena, the city’s patron goddess. Created between 447 and 438 BCE under the direction of the sculptor Phidias, these sculptures are celebrated for their detailed depiction of gods, heroes, and mythological events. Carved from Pentelic marble, they adorned the Parthenon’s frieze, metopes, and pediments, showcasing scenes such as the battle between the Lapiths and Centaurs, the gods of Olympus, and the legendary Panathenaic procession. These artworks reflect not only the technical mastery of Greek sculptors but also the city-state’s cultural dominance during the Golden Age of Athens. The Parthenon itself symbolized the power and prestige of Athens, a beacon of art, philosophy, and democracy in the ancient world. In the early 19th century, Lord Elgin, then serving as the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, arranged for the removal of a large portion of these sculptures. His actions, while approved by the Ottoman authorities, were highly controversial, both in Greece and across Europe. Elgin’s shipment of the marbles to Britain sparked widespread debate about the ethics of their removal, with many in Greece and abroad criticizing the transfer as an act of cultural theft. For over two centuries, the marbles have been housed in the British Museum in London, where they remain a centerpiece of the museum’s collection. Greece, however, has continuously demanded their return, making the Parthenon Marbles one of the most contested cultural artifacts in the world. Fun fact: Greece’s campaign to recover the Parthenon Marbles has spanned more than 200 years, making it one of the longest-running cultural heritage disputes in history! Since gaining independence in 1832, Greece has maintained that these sculptures are an integral part of its national heritage and should be reunited with the remaining fragments that are still housed in the Acropolis Museum in Athens. Despite international support for their repatriation, the British Museum has consistently resisted these claims, citing the legality of Elgin’s acquisition and the global significance of the marbles. This ongoing struggle highlights not only the artistic value of the Parthenon Marbles but also the profound cultural and political significance they hold for Greece.

basic.short: The Parthenon Marbles, created in the 5th century BCE, were part of the Parthenon in Athens. In the early 1800s, Lord Elgin removed them and took them to the UK, where they are now housed in the British Museum. Their removal has sparked on-going debates between Greece and the UK over who rightfully owns them.
basic.medium: The Parthenon Marbles, crafted in the mid-5th century BCE, represent a pinnacle of ancient Greek art and architecture. They formed part of the decoration of the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to Athena, the protector of Athens. The sculptures capture dynamic scenes of gods and humans, including the famous frieze that shows the Panathenaic procession, an important religious festival. In the early 1800s, Lord Elgin, then the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire (which controlled Greece at the time), obtained permission to remove a significant portion of the marbles. The marbles were transported to the UK and eventually sold to the British Museum, where they remain. The removal, however, has been a subject of dispute, with Greece calling for their return ever since. The debate is not only about ownership but also about the preservation of cultural identity, with the marbles seen as a vital part of Greece’s heritage.
basic.long: The Parthenon Marbles, created during the height of Athens' Golden Age in the mid-5th century BCE, represent a pinnacle of ancient Greek artistic achievement. Commissioned by the statesman Pericles and designed by the renowned sculptor Phidias, these marble sculptures were integral to the Parthenon, a temple dedicated to Athena, the patron deity of Athens. The marbles consist of intricate depictions of mythological scenes and historical events that celebrated Athens’ military victories and its cultural supremacy. Notable sections include the metopes showing the legendary battle between the Lapiths and Centaurs, a violent struggle symbolizing the triumph of civilization over barbarism. The continuous frieze, which ran around the inner colonnade of the Parthenon, depicted the Panathenaic procession—a grand religious and civic festival held in honor of Athena. Together, these sculptures encapsulate the ideals of Athenian democracy, civic pride, and religious devotion. In the early 19th century, when Greece was under Ottoman rule, Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, negotiated for the removal of many of these sculptures. Between 1801 and 1812, Elgin’s agents stripped approximately half of the surviving marbles from the Parthenon and shipped them to Britain. His motivations were complex—he claimed to be preserving the marbles from further damage or neglect, as the Parthenon had been partially destroyed during centuries of conflict and natural disasters. However, critics at the time and ever since have questioned both the legality and morality of his actions. The marbles were eventually purchased by the British government and placed in the British Museum, where they remain on display to this day. This transfer of the Parthenon Marbles to Britain has been the subject of heated debate for over two centuries. Greece argues that the marbles are an essential part of its cultural and historical heritage and should be returned to their original context, especially since the opening of the Acropolis Museum in 2009, which has space specifically designed to house them. The British Museum, however, maintains that the marbles were acquired legally under the laws of the time and that they are better preserved and more accessible to a global audience in London. The ongoing controversy has raised important questions about the ethics of museum collections, particularly regarding artifacts removed during periods of foreign domination and conflict. The marbles, therefore, are not only a reflection of ancient Athens’ artistic brilliance but also a symbol of the complex relationship between cultural heritage and national identity.

expert.short: These sculptures, taken by Lord Elgin in the early 19th century, are emblematic of the complex history of cultural property disputes. Created in the 5th century BCE for the Parthenon, the marbles are central to the heritage of Greece. Their removal has raised legal and ethical debates about cultural ownership and repatriation.
expert.medium: The Parthenon Marbles are among the most contested cultural artifacts in modern history, taken by Lord Elgin between 1801 and 1812 from Greece, under the rule of the Ottoman Empire. Their creation, nearly 2,500 years ago, coincided with Athens' height as a cultural and political power. These sculptures, designed by the famous artist Phidias, adorned the Parthenon, one of the most revered buildings of the ancient world. The marbles include figures of gods, humans, and mythological creatures, symbolizing the harmony between mortals and the divine. Since their arrival in Britain, the marbles have been at the heart of a contentious legal and moral debate. Greece argues that they are a part of its national identity and should be returned to their original context in Athens. The British Museum, however, maintains that they acquired the marbles legally and that they are better preserved and accessible in London. This ongoing dispute touches on broader questions of cultural restitution, the ethics of museum collections, and the responsibilities of former colonial powers. The legacy of the Parthenon Marbles thus transcends the boundaries of time and geography, raising questions about how nations reclaim their cultural history.
expert.long: The Parthenon Marbles stand as some of the most significant and contentious artifacts in the narrative of cultural heritage, removed by Lord Elgin during a period of great upheaval between 1801 and 1812, when Greece was under Ottoman control. Created nearly 2,500 years ago, these marbles symbolize the zenith of classical Greek civilization, embodying the aesthetic values, religious beliefs, and political aspirations of Athens during its Golden Age. Commissioned by the Athenian democracy, the sculptures were designed by Phidias, whose artistic vision shaped not just the Parthenon but also the ideals of beauty and harmony that would influence Western art for centuries. The removal of the Parthenon Marbles is emblematic of the broader colonial dynamics that characterized European expansion during the 19th century. Lord Elgin's actions were framed as an attempt to preserve these ancient treasures from the ravages of time and neglect, yet they also reflected a paternalistic attitude common among imperial powers, who often viewed artifacts from colonized regions as spoils to be collected and displayed. The marbles' presence in the British Museum challenges the narrative of preservation versus plunder, raising ethical questions about the legitimacy of their acquisition and the rights of nations to reclaim their cultural patrimony. The ongoing dispute over the Parthenon Marbles has evolved into a complex dialogue about cultural identity and national heritage. Greece’s sustained efforts to have the marbles returned underscore the importance of these artifacts in contemporary discussions about colonial legacies and restitution. The marbles are more than mere artistic achievements; they are critical symbols of a national identity that has struggled for recognition in the face of historical trauma and cultural erasure. The debates surrounding their return reflect a growing awareness of the need for reparative justice in the field of cultural heritage, as countries grapple with the ramifications of past injustices perpetrated during colonial rule. The legacy of the Parthenon Marbles thus transcends their physical form; they are a reminder of the enduring impact of imperialism on cultural identity and memory. As Greece continues its campaign for repatriation, the case of the Parthenon Marbles has catalyzed broader discussions about the ownership of cultural artifacts worldwide, highlighting the necessity for museums and nations to address the historical injustices that underlie their collections. Ultimately, the story of the Parthenon Marbles reflects a larger narrative about the relationship between art, history, and identity, illustrating the challenges and complexities of reclaiming cultural heritage in an increasingly interconnected world.

maps.caption-2: Then: Paracas peninsula, Ica, Peru - Now: Peru (returned 2014–2021)

fun.short: More than 2,000 years ago, people on the desert coast of Peru wrapped their dead in beautiful embroidered cloaks. In the 1930s a Swedish diplomat smuggled some of them to Sweden, but they have now gone home! Fun fact: the dry desert kept the colours bright for two thousand years.
fun.medium: On the Paracas peninsula, where the desert meets the Pacific Ocean in southern Peru, the Paracas people buried important people wrapped in many layers of cloth. The finest were big mantles embroidered with tiny, colourful figures: flying beings, animals, warriors and masked dancers. Because it almost never rains there, the textiles survived for about 2,000 years. In 1927 the Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello found hundreds of these bundles. A few years later, in the 1930s, the Swedish consul in Peru, Sven Karell, secretly sent a collection of Paracas textiles to Gothenburg in Sweden. Fun fact: between 2014 and 2021 the museum in Gothenburg sent all 89 textiles back to Peru!
fun.long:
Imagine a desert so dry that a piece of cloth can survive for two thousand years without rotting. That is the Paracas peninsula, on the southern coast of Peru. Between about 200 BCE and 200 CE, the people who lived there buried their most important dead sitting up, wrapped in layer after layer of cotton and wool cloth, like a giant bundle.

The most precious layers were mantles embroidered with hundreds of little figures in red, blue, yellow and green. Some are birds or cats, some are dancers or warriors carrying heads, and some are strange flying beings with long tongues and streaming hair. Each mantle took an enormous amount of work, and some were never worn by the living: they were made to go into the tomb.

In 1927 the Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello discovered a huge cemetery at Paracas, with more than 400 bundles. The discovery was famous, and collectors wanted the textiles too. In the 1930s Sven Karell, the Swedish consul in Lima, took a collection of Paracas textiles out of Peru and sent them to the Ethnographic Museum in Gothenburg. Peruvian law already protected such objects, so the export was illegal.

For decades the textiles stayed in Sweden. Then Peru asked for them back, and in 2013 Sweden agreed. The textiles were carefully studied and packed, and they returned home in several shipments between 2014 and 2021. Fun fact: they travelled in special boxes to protect them from changes in temperature and humidity, because after 2,000 years in the desert, the damp Swedish air was their biggest danger!

basic.short: Embroidered textiles from the Paracas Necropolis on Peru's south coast (c. 200 BCE–200 CE) were exported illegally to Sweden in the 1930s by the Swedish consul Sven Karell. Gothenburg's Museum of World Culture returned all 89 to Peru between 2014 and 2021.
basic.medium: The Paracas culture flourished on the southern coast of Peru in the late first millennium BCE. At the Paracas Necropolis, excavated by Julio C. Tello from 1927, the dead were buried in large funerary bundles wrapped in textiles, including mantles embroidered with complex figures of supernatural beings, animals and ritual performers. The arid climate preserved their colours. In the 1930s the Swedish consul in Peru, Sven Karell, exported a group of Paracas textiles to the Ethnographic Museum in Gothenburg, in breach of Peruvian protection of archaeological heritage. After Peru requested their return, Sweden agreed in 2013, and the Museum of World Culture in Gothenburg sent all 89 textiles back in stages between 2014 and 2021. Their return is one of the clearest examples of a complete restitution of an illegally exported collection.
basic.long:
The Paracas culture developed on the southern coast of Peru, around the peninsula of the same name, from about 800 BCE. Its later phase, known from the Paracas Necropolis (also called Wari Kayan), is famous for some of the finest textiles of the ancient Americas.

Between roughly 200 BCE and 200 CE, the Paracas buried high-status individuals in large funerary bundles. The body, seated, was wrapped in successive layers of cloth, among them mantles of cotton and camelid wool embroidered with repeated figures: flying beings with streaming hair, felines, birds, and ritual performers holding staffs, fans or trophy heads. Such mantles represent thousands of hours of work, and some appear to have been made specifically for burial.

The Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello excavated the Necropolis from 1927, recovering more than 400 bundles, now the core of Peru's national collections. The discovery also attracted collectors. In the 1930s Sven Karell, Sweden's consul in Peru, sent a collection of Paracas textiles to the Ethnographic Museum in Gothenburg. Peru had already enacted laws protecting its archaeological heritage, and the export was illegal.

The textiles remained in Gothenburg for about eighty years. After Peru requested their return, the Swedish government agreed in 2013. The Museum of World Culture, successor to the Ethnographic Museum, worked with Peruvian specialists to document and pack the fragile textiles, and returned them in several shipments between 2014 and 2021, completing the return of all 89 pieces.

The case shows that full returns are possible when an export was illegal at the time, when the requesting state is clearly the rightful owner and when the holder agrees. It also shows the care needed to move fragile objects safely.

expert.short: Removed from Peru in the 1930s by Sweden's consul Sven Karell, in breach of Peruvian heritage law, the Paracas textiles of Gothenburg were returned in full between 2014 and 2021. Their restitution is an example of a negotiated, complete return based on illegal export.
expert.medium: The textiles belong to the Paracas Necropolis phase (c. 200 BCE–200 CE), known principally from the funerary bundles excavated by Julio C. Tello at Wari Kayan from 1927. Their embroidered mantles, with their repetitive iconography of anthropomorphic flying beings and ritual performers, are among the most complex textile works of the ancient Andes. The Gothenburg collection was assembled in the 1930s by the Swedish consul Sven Karell and exported contrary to Peru's heritage legislation, which had placed archaeological remains under state protection. After a Peruvian request, the Swedish government decided in 2013 to return the collection, and the Museum of World Culture repatriated all 89 textiles in successive shipments between 2014 and 2021, accompanied by joint documentation and conservation. The case illustrates restitution grounded in illegality at the time of export, which avoids the retrospective moral arguments that complicate colonial-era claims.
expert.long:
The Paracas textiles of Gothenburg belong to the Necropolis phase of the Paracas tradition on the southern coast of Peru, dated roughly between 200 BCE and 200 CE and sometimes associated with the early Nasca period. At Wari Kayan, on the Paracas peninsula, Julio C. Tello and his team excavated from 1927 onwards more than 400 funerary bundles, in which seated individuals were enveloped in dozens of textiles. The most elaborate are mantles of cotton and camelid fibre embroidered in stem stitch with repeated figures, whose variations of colour and posture form complex visual systems. Their iconography of flying anthropomorphic beings, ritual performers and trophy heads has been read as evidence of shamanic practice and ancestor veneration.

Tello's excavation was a landmark in the creation of a Peruvian national archaeology, but it coincided with a thriving market for Andean antiquities. In the 1930s Sven Karell, Sweden's consul in Lima, acquired a group of Paracas textiles and exported them to the Ethnographic Museum in Gothenburg. The export was contrary to Peruvian legislation that had brought archaeological heritage under state protection, a point the Swedish side later accepted.

The textiles remained in Gothenburg for about eighty years, where they were studied and occasionally exhibited. After a request from Peru, the Swedish government decided in 2013 to return the collection. The Museum of World Culture, working with Peruvian conservators, undertook documentation and conservation and returned all 89 textiles in successive shipments between 2014 and 2021. The staging reflected both conservation needs and the logistical difficulty of moving fragile archaeological textiles across climates.

The case is instructive in several respects. First, its legal basis was clear: the illegality of the export at the time allowed restitution without recourse to retrospective arguments about colonial injustice. Second, it was negotiated between states and carried out through professional cooperation rather than litigation. Third, it was complete, returning the whole collection rather than a selection. In this sense it offers a model for returns in which the question is not whether an object should go back, but how to move it safely, and it contrasts with cases, like many in this collection, where the lawfulness of the original acquisition is itself in dispute.

maps.caption-2: Then: Rashid (Rosetta), Egypt - Now: London, UK

fun.short: The Rosetta Stone is a broken slab of dark stone with the same message written three times, in three different scripts. Thanks to it, people learned to read Egyptian hieroglyphs again! Fun fact: it was found by French soldiers but ended up in London.
fun.medium: More than 2,200 years ago, in 196 BCE, Egyptian priests wrote a decree praising the young king Ptolemy V. They had it carved on stone slabs in three scripts: hieroglyphs for the gods, Demotic for everyday use, and Greek for the rulers of the time. One of those slabs was found in 1799 by French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta. Because scholars could read the Greek, they could slowly work out the hieroglyphs, and in 1822 the Frenchman Jean-François Champollion cracked the code! Fun fact: after the British defeated the French in Egypt, the stone was handed over to them in 1801, and it has been in the British Museum ever since.
fun.long:
Imagine a secret code that nobody in the world could read for more than a thousand years. That was Egyptian hieroglyphs! After the end of ancient Egypt, people forgot how to read the pictures of birds, eyes and snakes carved on temples and tombs.

The key to the code was a broken slab of dark granodiorite. In 196 BCE, priests gathered in Memphis wrote a decree honouring the king Ptolemy V, and it was carved on stone in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic (a quicker Egyptian script) and ancient Greek. The slab was later reused as building material, and it lay forgotten for centuries.

In 1799, during Napoleon's expedition to Egypt, French soldiers were strengthening an old fort near Rashid, called Rosetta by Europeans, when they found it in a wall. The officers realised at once that it was important, because the Greek text said the same message was written in the other two scripts.

But the French did not keep it for long. In 1801 the British defeated them in Egypt, and under the peace agreement, the Capitulation of Alexandria, the French had to hand over the antiquities they had collected. The stone sailed to England and was put on show in the British Museum in 1802.

Scholars across Europe raced to decipher it. The Englishman Thomas Young made progress, but it was Jean-François Champollion who, in 1822, showed how hieroglyphs really worked. Fun fact: you can still see words painted on the side of the stone by the British: "Captured in Egypt by the British Army in 1801".

basic.short: The Rosetta Stone carries a decree of 196 BCE in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, the key to deciphering hieroglyphs. Found by French soldiers in 1799, it was handed to the British in 1801 and has been in the British Museum since 1802.
