basic.medium: The Rosetta Stone is a fragment of a granodiorite stele inscribed in 196 BCE with a decree issued by a council of priests at Memphis in honour of Ptolemy V. The text is written three times: in hieroglyphs, in Demotic and in ancient Greek. In July 1799, soldiers of Napoleon's army in Egypt found it built into a wall while working on a fort near Rashid (Rosetta). After the French defeat, Article 16 of the Capitulation of Alexandria (1801) transferred the antiquities collected by the French scholars to the British. The stone reached London in 1802 and was placed in the British Museum. Because the Greek text could be read, the stone allowed Thomas Young and, decisively, Jean-François Champollion in 1822 to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
basic.long:
The Rosetta Stone is part of a larger stele of dark granodiorite. Its text is a decree passed in 196 BCE by a council of Egyptian priests at Memphis, confirming the royal cult of the young king Ptolemy V a year after his coronation. Copies were set up in temples across Egypt, written in three scripts: hieroglyphs, the traditional script of temples; Demotic, the everyday Egyptian script; and ancient Greek, the language of the Ptolemaic administration.

Centuries later the stele was broken and reused as building material. In July 1799, during Napoleon Bonaparte's expedition to Egypt, French soldiers found it in the walls of a fort near Rashid, in the Nile Delta. The expedition's scholars recognised its importance and made copies of the inscription.

The stone's fate was decided by war. In 1801 British and Ottoman forces defeated the French army in Egypt. The Capitulation of Alexandria required the French to hand over the antiquities they had gathered, and after some dispute the stone was surrendered. It arrived in England in 1802 and was presented to the British Museum in the name of King George III. The words "Captured in Egypt by the British Army in 1801" were painted on its side.

The decipherment took another two decades. The English scholar Thomas Young identified the names of rulers written in cartouches, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion showed that hieroglyphs combined sound signs and meaning signs, opening the whole of ancient Egyptian writing to modern readers.

Today the Rosetta Stone is the most visited object in the British Museum. Egyptian scholars and former officials have called for its return, arguing that it was taken as a spoil of war between two foreign armies occupying Egypt.

expert.short: A fragment of a stele recording the Memphis decree of 196 BCE in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, the Rosetta Stone was found by the French army in 1799 and transferred to Britain under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801. Its status as a spoil of war between occupying powers underlies Egyptian calls for its return.
expert.medium: The Rosetta Stone preserves the lower part of a copy of the Memphis decree of 196 BCE, issued by a synod of Egyptian priests to confirm the cult of Ptolemy V and set up in temples throughout the country. Its trilingual text, in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, made it central to the decipherment achieved by Thomas Young and above all Jean-François Champollion, whose Lettre à M. Dacier (1822) laid the foundations of Egyptology. The stone was discovered in 1799 by soldiers of the Armée d'Orient at Fort Julien near Rashid and, after the defeat of the French, was ceded to Britain under Article 16 of the Capitulation of Alexandria (1801). Displayed in the British Museum since 1802, it has become emblematic of debates on restitution; Egyptian scholars, including Zahi Hawass, have led petitions for its return, arguing that neither party to the capitulation had a right to Egypt's heritage.
expert.long:
The Rosetta Stone is a fragment of a granodiorite stele bearing a copy of the decree issued in 196 BCE by a synod of priests at Memphis. The decree confirmed the royal cult of Ptolemy V Epiphanes, recorded the tax remissions granted to the temples and ordered that copies be set up in temples of the first, second and third rank, in the 'sacred', 'native' and 'Greek' scripts. It is thus a document of the negotiation between the Macedonian dynasty and the Egyptian priesthood.

The stone was found in July 1799 by soldiers of the Armée d'Orient, under the engineer officer Pierre-François Bouchard, during work on Fort Julien near Rashid. The Commission des Sciences et des Arts accompanying Bonaparte's expedition recognised its significance and circulated copies of the inscription in Europe. After the defeat of the French army in 1801, the antiquities collected by the scholars became a point of contention. Article 16 of the Capitulation of Alexandria obliged the French to surrender them, and the stone was shipped to England, where it entered the British Museum in 1802 as a 'gift' of George III. The inscriptions painted on its sides, 'Captured in Egypt by the British Army in 1801' and 'Presented by King George III', record the conditions of its acquisition.

The decipherment unfolded as a scholarly rivalry that paralleled the military one. Thomas Young identified royal names in cartouches and several phonetic values; Champollion, drawing on Coptic, demonstrated in 1822 that hieroglyphic writing combined phonetic and ideographic signs, and extended the reading to the whole system.

The stone's significance for restitution debates lies in its double displacement: removed by one occupying army and transferred to another under a treaty to which Egypt was not a party. Zahi Hawass and other Egyptian scholars have argued that the capitulation cannot confer legitimate title, and in 2022, the bicentenary of the decipherment, petitions calling for its return gathered well over 100,000 signatures. The British Museum maintains that the stone was acquired under the 1801 treaty and that it is legally unable to deaccession objects under the British Museum Act 1963, offering instead collaboration and replicas.

maps.caption-2: Then: Pergamon (Bergama), Türkiye - Now: Berlin, Germany

fun.short: The Altar of Pergamon is like an ancient Greek temple! German archaeologists took it to Berlin, where it still stands today. It’s huge, and Turkey has been asking for it to come back. Fun fact: Imagine having to move an entire building—that’s how big this altar is!
fun.medium: The Altar of Pergamon is a massive structure, built more than 2,000 years ago in what is now modern-day Turkey. This altar was dedicated to Zeus and Athena, showcasing the power and prestige of the Hellenistic city of Pergamon. German archaeologists unearthed it in the 19th century and transported it, piece by piece, to Berlin, where it still stands today. It’s an incredible example of ancient Greek architecture, with its monumental frieze depicting the battle between gods and giants (the Gigantomachy).  - Fun fact: The altar is so large that when it was moved to Berlin, it required the construction of an entire wing of the Pergamon Museum just to house it! However, the removal of the altar from its original location in Turkey has caused controversy for decades. Turkey has made repeated requests for its return, but the altar remains in Berlin, symbolizing a broader issue of cultural heritage and repatriation.
fun.long: The Altar of Pergamon, created in the 2nd century BCE, stands as one of the most extraordinary examples of Hellenistic art and architecture. Erected on the acropolis of Pergamon, a major city in ancient Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey), this monumental altar was dedicated to Zeus and Athena, the city’s chief deities. The altar was designed not only as a place of religious significance but also as a symbol of the city’s power, cultural prestige, and artistic prowess. The architectural scale of the altar is breathtaking—it was a massive structure that could be approached by an imposing staircase, with a monumental colonnade surrounding the central altar space. Perhaps the most iconic feature of the Altar of Pergamon is its sculptural frieze, which stretches over 110 meters and depicts the Gigantomachy, the mythological battle between the Olympian gods and the giants. This frieze is one of the most vivid representations of Hellenistic sculpture, illustrating the clash of divine forces with a level of drama and intensity that had never been seen before. The figures are carved in high relief, with deep undercutting that creates a play of light and shadow, giving the scene a sense of movement and life. Gods like Zeus, Athena, and Nike are shown in dynamic poses, their drapery swirling as they engage in combat, while the defeated giants writhe in agony below. This focus on motion, emotion, and realism marks a significant shift from the more rigid and idealized forms of earlier Greek art, highlighting the artistic innovations of the Hellenistic period. German archaeologists unearthed the altar in the late 19th century, and it was transported, in sections, to Berlin, where it remains today in the Pergamon Museum. The logistics of moving such a colossal structure were unprecedented at the time—so much so that an entire wing of the museum had to be built specifically to house it. This relocation sparked considerable interest in Hellenistic art and brought the altar to the attention of a global audience. However, its removal from Turkey has been a source of controversy for over a century. The altar's presence in Berlin is often seen as emblematic of the broader issues surrounding the relocation of cultural treasures during periods of colonial expansion and imperial ambition. One fascinating aspect of the Altar of Pergamon is its reflection of the political and religious atmosphere of the Hellenistic world. The choice of the Gigantomachy as a subject was no accident—it symbolized the triumph of civilization over chaos, a message that aligned with the city of Pergamon’s aspirations to be seen as a cultural and political leader in the region. The altar also served as a means of asserting the city’s divine protection under Zeus and Athena, reinforcing its legitimacy and power. The artistic mastery and symbolic weight of the altar made it a masterpiece of its time, one that continues to captivate audiences and scholars alike. However, the controversy surrounding its removal cannot be ignored. Turkey has made repeated claims for the return of the altar, arguing that it is a vital part of their cultural heritage. The altar’s story is thus not just one of ancient craftsmanship but also one of modern-day debates over the ownership and repatriation of cultural artifacts. This ongoing dispute highlights the complex relationship between archaeology, national identity, and the legacy of historical injustices.

basic.short: The Altar of Pergamon, built in the 2nd century BCE, is a monumental structure from ancient Greece, located in modern-day Turkey. In the 19th century, German archaeologists transported it to Berlin, where it remains. Turkey continues to request its repatriation.
basic.medium: The Altar of Pergamon, built in the 2nd century BCE, is one of the finest examples of Hellenistic art and architecture. Originally located in the ancient city of Pergamon (in present-day Turkey), the altar was designed to celebrate the gods Zeus and Athena. Its monumental size and elaborate frieze, which depicts the Gigantomachy (the battle between gods and giants), make it an extraordinary feat of ancient engineering and artistic creativity. The frieze is renowned for its dynamic composition, with figures twisting and writhing in dramatic poses, highlighting the skill of Hellenistic sculptors in creating vivid, lifelike scenes. In the late 19th century, German archaeologists excavated the altar and transported it to Berlin, where it has remained in the Pergamon Museum. The removal of such a large and significant structure has fueled ongoing debates about the ethics of removing cultural artifacts, especially monumental structures, from their original locations. Despite numerous calls from Turkey for its return, the altar remains one of Berlin’s most famous attractions, continuing to raise questions about cultural ownership and the responsibilities of modern museums.
basic.long: The Altar of Pergamon, constructed in the 2nd century BCE, is one of the most significant artistic and architectural achievements of the Hellenistic world. Built atop the acropolis of Pergamon, a prominent city in Asia Minor, the altar was dedicated to Zeus and Athena, the protectors of the city. This colossal structure served not only as a religious monument but also as a visual representation of the city’s status as a political and cultural hub in the Hellenistic world. Standing over 9 meters high and adorned with a monumental sculptural frieze, the altar was a testament to the technical and creative brilliance of Hellenistic artists. The centerpiece of the altar’s design is the Gigantomachy frieze, a dynamic depiction of the mythological battle between the gods and the giants. Spanning over 110 meters in length, this frieze is an unparalleled example of Hellenistic sculpture, with its deeply carved reliefs and intricate compositions that create a dramatic interplay of light and shadow. The figures in the frieze are shown in intense motion, their expressions conveying a range of emotions from divine wrath to the agony of defeat. The gods, led by Zeus and Athena, are depicted in triumphant poses, their divine power evident in their muscular forms and flowing garments. The defeated giants, on the other hand, are shown writhing in pain, their twisted bodies a striking contrast to the poised, controlled figures of the gods. The artistic innovations of the frieze are emblematic of the Hellenistic era’s departure from the more restrained, idealized forms of Classical Greek art. Hellenistic artists sought to capture movement, emotion, and drama in their works, reflecting the broader cultural and political shifts of the time. The Altar of Pergamon, with its theatrical composition and attention to detail, exemplifies this artistic trend. The depiction of the Gigantomachy was not just an artistic choice but a symbolic one, representing the triumph of order over chaos, a theme that resonated deeply with the city of Pergamon’s identity as a center of power and learning. In 1878, German archaeologists, led by Carl Humann, began the excavation of the altar, and by the end of the century, large sections of it had been transported to Berlin. The scale and grandeur of the altar posed significant challenges in its relocation, requiring advanced techniques to dismantle and move such a vast structure. Once in Germany, the altar became the centerpiece of the Pergamon Museum, where an entire wing was constructed to house it. The frieze, with its powerful depiction of the battle between gods and giants, became one of the most famous examples of ancient Greek art housed outside of its country of origin. The removal of the altar from Turkey has been a point of contention ever since. Turkish authorities have repeatedly called for its return, seeing it as a significant part of their cultural and historical heritage. This debate reflects the broader issues surrounding the acquisition of cultural treasures during the 19th century, a period when European powers, through their imperial ambitions, frequently removed artifacts from their original contexts. The Altar of Pergamon’s journey from Turkey to Germany serves as a reminder of the complex and often contentious relationship between archaeology, cultural heritage, and national identity.

expert.short: The Altar of Pergamon, a monumental work of Hellenistic architecture and art, was removed from its site in the late 19th century by German archaeologists. Its relocation to Berlin sparked on-going debates about the ethics of removing large cultural structures and Turkey’s demands for its return.
expert.medium: The Altar of Pergamon, constructed in the 2nd century BCE, is a monumental testament to the power and artistic achievements of the Hellenistic world. Dedicated to the gods Zeus and Athena, the altar was the centerpiece of the acropolis in Pergamon, a city renowned for its intellectual and cultural contributions during the Hellenistic period. The frieze, which encircles the altar, is one of the most dramatic examples of Hellenistic sculpture, portraying the gods in a fierce battle against the giants in what is known as the Gigantomachy. The dynamic movement and intricate details of the figures exemplify the Hellenistic artistic style, which sought to evoke strong emotions and convey movement through stone. The altar’s removal to Berlin by German archaeologists in the 19th century remains a contentious issue. Turkey has made several attempts to negotiate the return of the altar, seeing it as a crucial piece of their cultural heritage. The debate surrounding the Altar of Pergamon is part of a larger global conversation about the ethical implications of transporting cultural artifacts to foreign museums, especially those acquired during periods of colonialism or imperial expansion. As such, the altar stands not only as a relic of ancient history but as a symbol of the ongoing struggle for cultural restitution in the modern era.
expert.long: The Altar of Pergamon, created in the 2nd century BCE, is a masterful representation of the fusion of art, religion, and politics in the Hellenistic world. This monumental structure stood as a focal point on the acropolis of Pergamon, one of the leading cities of Asia Minor, and its sheer size and elaborate decoration were a testament to the city's wealth and influence. Built under the reign of King Eumenes II, the altar was not merely a religious site but also a symbol of Pergamon’s military victories and the city’s cultural dominance in the region. Its dedication to Zeus, the king of the gods, and Athena, the goddess of wisdom and warfare, reinforced the divine protection that Pergamon's rulers claimed to enjoy. The most striking feature of the altar is the Gigantomachy frieze, which runs around the base of the altar and vividly depicts the mythological battle between the gods of Olympus and the giants, a common theme in Greek art symbolizing the triumph of order over chaos. This frieze is renowned for its complexity and artistic innovation. Measuring nearly 2.3 meters in height and stretching over 110 meters in length, the frieze is filled with more than 100 larger-than-life figures, each intricately detailed. The deep carving of the relief creates a powerful interplay of light and shadow, enhancing the dramatic effect of the battle scene. The figures are shown in extreme motion, their bodies twisting and contorting in the heat of combat, a style characteristic of Hellenistic art, which favored dynamic poses and emotional intensity over the more static, idealized forms of earlier Classical art. The technical skill involved in crafting such a monumental work cannot be overstated. The sculptors employed advanced techniques to give the figures a sense of depth and movement, using the contours of the marble to suggest the tension of muscles and the flow of drapery. The faces of the gods and giants are rendered with remarkable detail, each expression carefully crafted to convey the emotional weight of the battle—ranging from the serene power of the gods to the desperate anguish of the defeated giants. This attention to emotion and physicality marks a significant evolution in Greek sculpture, reflecting broader changes in Hellenistic art that embraced realism and psychological complexity. Discovered in fragments by German archaeologists led by Carl Humann in the late 19th century, the altar was transported to Berlin, where it was painstakingly reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum. The decision to move such a significant monument from its original site in Turkey to Europe was emblematic of the imperialist attitudes of the time, when Western nations frequently appropriated cultural treasures from their colonies or other regions. The reconstruction of the altar in Berlin required the construction of a dedicated museum space, highlighting the scale and importance of the structure. However, this removal has been the subject of long-standing controversy. Turkey has made several formal requests for the return of the altar, arguing that its place is in its original context, as part of the ancient site of Pergamon. The debates surrounding the Altar of Pergamon reflect broader issues in the field of archaeology and cultural heritage. The removal of artifacts from their original locations, especially during periods of imperial expansion, raises complex questions about ownership, preservation, and the ethical responsibilities of museums. In the case of the Altar of Pergamon, German archaeologists justified their actions by pointing to the neglect of the site under Ottoman rule and the risks of damage or loss if the altar remained in situ. However, critics argue that such justifications are rooted in colonialist attitudes that privileged European scholarship and institutions over the rights of the countries from which these artifacts were taken. Today, the Altar of Pergamon remains one of the most celebrated exhibits in the Pergamon Museum, drawing visitors from around the world. Yet, its presence in Berlin serves as a stark reminder of the power dynamics that have shaped the field of archaeology and continue to influence debates over cultural restitution. The ongoing discussions about the return of the altar highlight the need for museums to engage with the legacies of colonialism and to reconsider the role they play in preserving, but also possessing, the cultural heritage of other nations.

maps.caption-2: Then: Temple of Hathor, Dendera, Egypt - Now: Paris, France

fun.short: The Dendera Zodiac is a map of the sky carved on the ceiling of an Egyptian temple about 2,000 years ago. In 1820 a Frenchman cut it out with saws and gunpowder and took it to Paris! Fun fact: in Egypt a copy now hangs in its place.
fun.medium: Look up! On the ceiling of a small chapel on the roof of the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, Egyptian artists carved a round map of the sky around 50 BCE. You can find the lion, the scorpion, the fish and other zodiac signs we still use, mixed with Egyptian gods and stars. French scholars drew it during Napoleon's expedition in 1799, and everyone in Europe wanted to see it. In 1820 a team sent by a French collector cut the whole ceiling out, using saws, chisels and even gunpowder, and shipped it to France. The king of France bought it, and today it is in the Louvre. Fun fact: some people once believed it was tens of thousands of years old, until Champollion read the names in it and showed it was from the time of the Ptolemies and Romans!
fun.long:
Around 2,000 years ago, in the town of Dendera in southern Egypt, people rebuilt a great temple for the goddess Hathor. On its roof they made small chapels for the god Osiris, and on the ceiling of one of them, around 50 BCE, sculptors carved a circle full of stars.

This is the Dendera Zodiac. It shows the sky as the Egyptians saw it: the thirty-six groups of stars they used to count the hours of the night, planets, constellations, and the twelve signs of the zodiac that the Egyptians had learned from Babylon through the Greeks. You can spot the bull, the twins, the crab and the scales, held up by four goddesses and falcon-headed spirits.

In 1799 French scholars travelling with Napoleon's army reached Dendera, and the artist Vivant Denon drew the zodiac. When his drawings were published, all of Europe became curious. Some people even thought it proved that the world was much older than the Bible said!

In 1820 a French collector, Sébastien Saulnier, sent a man called Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain to Egypt to bring the ceiling back. Lelorrain cut through the stone with saws and chisels and used gunpowder to loosen it. The block was dragged to the Nile and shipped to France, where King Louis XVIII bought it in 1821.

In 1822 Champollion read the word "autocrator" in the hieroglyphs, a title of the Roman emperors, and showed that the zodiac was not so ancient after all. Fun fact: the zodiac moved to the Louvre in 1922, exactly a hundred years later, and a plaster copy now fills the hole in the chapel ceiling at Dendera.

basic.short: The Dendera Zodiac, a circular sky map carved around 50 BCE on a chapel ceiling in the Temple of Hathor, was cut out and taken to France in 1820–1821. In the Louvre since 1922, it is the subject of Egyptian requests for return.
basic.medium: The Dendera Zodiac is a sandstone relief from the ceiling of a chapel dedicated to Osiris on the roof of the Temple of Hathor at Dendera, carved in the late Ptolemaic period, around 50 BCE. It is a map of the sky combining the Egyptian decans and constellations with the twelve signs of the zodiac, which had reached Egypt from Mesopotamia through the Greek world. After it was drawn by Vivant Denon in 1799, it became famous in Europe, and in 1820 the collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier had it removed by Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain, who used saws, chisels and gunpowder. Louis XVIII bought it in 1821. First shown in the royal library, it was moved to the Louvre in 1922. Zahi Hawass included it in a 2022 petition asking for the return of major Egyptian antiquities from Europe.
basic.long:
Dendera, on the west bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, was the cult centre of the goddess Hathor. The temple visible today was rebuilt from the late Ptolemaic period into Roman times. On its roof stand chapels dedicated to the mysteries of Osiris, and one of them had a ceiling carved with a circular representation of the sky, dated to around 50 BCE.

The Dendera Zodiac shows the thirty-six decans, groups of stars that the Egyptians used to divide the night, together with planets, Egyptian constellations and the twelve signs of the zodiac, a system that had come to Egypt from Babylon through Greek astronomy. The disc is supported by four standing goddesses and by kneeling figures with falcon heads.

The relief became famous after Napoleon's expedition. Vivant Denon drew it in 1799, and its publication started a debate: some scholars dated it to many thousands of years ago, which seemed to challenge the chronology of the Bible. In 1820 the Parisian collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier commissioned Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain to remove it. Lelorrain cut the ceiling out with saws and chisels, using gunpowder to break up the stone around it, and brought it to France in 1821. King Louis XVIII bought it for the royal library.

In 1822 Champollion read Greek and Roman titles in its cartouches and dated it correctly to the Ptolemaic-Roman period, ending the controversy.

The zodiac entered the Louvre in 1922. A cast now fills its place at Dendera. The Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass has asked for its return, including in a 2022 petition, and in France a framework law to make returns from public collections easier passed the Senate in January 2026, although it is not yet clear whether it could apply to the zodiac.

expert.short: Carved c. 50 BCE for an Osirian chapel on the roof of the Temple of Hathor, the Dendera Zodiac was removed in 1820 on the commission of a Parisian collector and acquired by Louis XVIII. Its extraction, the 'Dendera affair' and Egyptian claims make it a case study in the market-driven removal of monuments.
expert.medium: The zodiac of Dendera is a sandstone ceiling relief from the eastern Osirian chapel on the roof of the Temple of Hathor, securely dated to the mid-first century BCE. It is the earliest complete circular representation of the sky from Egypt, integrating the decans, Egyptian constellations and planets with the Mesopotamian zodiac transmitted through Hellenistic astronomy. Published from Denon's drawings, it fuelled the 'Dendera affair', in which dates proposed by Dupuis and others were read as a challenge to biblical chronology, until Champollion's reading of the cartouches in 1822. Its removal in 1820, carried out by Lelorrain for the dealer Saulnier with the permission of Muhammad Ali's administration and with the use of explosives, was a commercial operation. Bought by Louis XVIII for 150,000 francs, it has been in the Louvre since 1922; Egyptian scholars question the validity of the permission and call for its return.
expert.long:
The zodiac of Dendera is a sandstone relief that formed the ceiling of the eastern of the two chapels dedicated to the mysteries of Osiris on the roof of the Temple of Hathor at Dendera. Its astronomical configuration and the style of the reliefs date it to around 50 BCE, under the last Ptolemies. It is the earliest complete circular map of the sky known from Egypt, and it synthesises two traditions: the Egyptian system of thirty-six decans and indigenous constellations, and the zodiac of Mesopotamian origin transmitted through Hellenistic astronomy. The disc is supported by four goddesses at the cardinal points and by falcon-headed figures, a composition that also embodies cosmological ideas about the sky as the body of the goddess Nut.

The relief entered European consciousness through Napoleon's expedition. Vivant Denon's drawing, published in 1802, and the more precise renderings of the Description de l'Égypte provoked the 'Dendera affair'. Scholars such as Charles-François Dupuis, reading the zodiac as a record of the sky at the time of its carving, proposed dates thousands of years in the past, which were taken up in polemics against the biblical chronology. The controversy was resolved in 1822 when Champollion identified the Greek title 'autocrator' in a cartouche, placing the monument in the Ptolemaic-Roman period.

The removal itself was a commercial undertaking. In 1820 the collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier commissioned the engineer Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain, who obtained permission from the administration of Muhammad Ali and cut the ceiling out with saws, chisels and gunpowder, damaging the surrounding structure. Transported down the Nile and shipped to Marseille, the relief was bought in 1821 by Louis XVIII for 150,000 francs and displayed in the Bibliothèque royale, before its transfer to the Louvre in 1922. A plaster cast now fills the chapel ceiling.

The case illustrates how the permission of an Ottoman-era ruler, eager to secure European goodwill, enabled the extraction of monuments for the European market. Egyptian scholars, led by Zahi Hawass, reject that permission as a legitimate basis for title and included the zodiac in a 2022 petition for the return of key antiquities. The Louvre, bound by the principle of the inalienability of French public collections, has not agreed to return it. A French framework law intended to ease restitutions from public collections was passed by the Senate in January 2026 and was pending before the National Assembly in spring 2026; its scope with respect to objects such as the zodiac remains to be seen.

item11.title: Horses of Saint Mark – 2nd–3rd century CE (disputed)

maps.caption-2: Then: Constantinople (Byzantine Empire), Türkiye - Now: Venice, Italy (returned from Paris 1815)

fun.short: The four bronze Horses of Saint Mark have been stolen twice! Venetians took them from Constantinople in 1204, and Napoleon took them from Venice in 1797. Fun fact: they came back to Venice in 1815, and today the ones outside the church are copies.
fun.medium: Nobody knows exactly who made the four bronze horses, or when: perhaps in Roman times, around the 2nd or 3rd century CE. They are covered in a thin layer of gold, and they look as if they are about to trot off! For centuries they stood in the Hippodrome of Constantinople, the great racetrack of the Byzantine capital. In 1204 the knights of the Fourth Crusade, together with the Venetians, attacked and looted Constantinople. The Venetians shipped the horses home and put them on the front of St Mark's Basilica. In 1797 Napoleon conquered Venice and took them to Paris, where they stood on a triumphal arch. Fun fact: after Napoleon's defeat, they returned to Venice in 1815, and since the 1980s the originals have been kept safely inside the basilica.
fun.long:
Imagine four life-size bronze horses, glinting with gold, prancing side by side as if pulling an invisible chariot. They are one of the only groups of ancient horses of this kind that have survived. Nobody knows who made them. Some experts think they are Greek, from the 4th century BCE; others think they are Roman, from the 2nd or 3rd century CE.

For many centuries they stood in Constantinople, today's Istanbul, the capital of the Byzantine Empire. They probably decorated the Hippodrome, a huge stadium for chariot races.

In 1204 an army of crusaders, who had set out to fight in the Holy Land, turned against Constantinople instead, helped by the powerful city of Venice, which had supplied their ships. They captured the city and looted its churches and palaces. The Venetian leader, the doge Enrico Dandolo, sent the horses back to Venice. They were placed on the terrace above the main door of St Mark's Basilica, where they became a symbol of the city's power.

Almost 600 years later, in 1797, Napoleon Bonaparte conquered Venice and ended its independence. He took the horses to Paris, and in 1808 they were placed on top of the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, near the Louvre.

When Napoleon was defeated, the Austrian emperor made sure the horses went back to Venice, and they arrived on 13 December 1815.

Fun fact: because air pollution was damaging the bronze, the original horses were moved inside the basilica's museum in the 1980s, and copies now stand on the terrace. So the horses you see from St Mark's Square are replicas!

basic.short: The gilded bronze Horses of Saint Mark were taken from Constantinople by the Venetians in the Fourth Crusade (1204) and from Venice by Napoleon in 1797. Returned in 1815, the originals are now inside St Mark's Basilica, replaced outside by copies.
basic.medium: The Horses of Saint Mark, also called the Triumphal Quadriga, are four gilded copper-alloy horses of classical antiquity. Their date and origin are debated: proposals range from Greece in the fourth century BCE to Rome in the second or third century CE. They stood in Constantinople, probably in the Hippodrome, until the Fourth Crusade. In 1204 crusaders and Venetians sacked the city, and the horses were taken to Venice and installed on the loggia of St Mark's Basilica, probably around the middle of the thirteenth century. In 1797 Napoleon ended the Venetian Republic and removed the horses to Paris, where they crowned the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel. After his fall, they were returned to Venice on 13 December 1815. Since the 1980s the originals have been kept in the Museum of St Mark, while replicas stand on the façade.
basic.long:
The Horses of Saint Mark are the only surviving quadriga, or team of four horses from a chariot group, from classical antiquity. Cast in a copper alloy with a high copper content and then gilded, they show traces of scratches applied to soften the brilliance of the gold. Their date is uncertain: some scholars attribute them to a Greek sculptor of the fourth century BCE, others to Roman workshops of the second or third century CE.

They are known to have stood in Constantinople, where they are thought to have decorated the Hippodrome, the centre of the city's public life and chariot racing.

In 1204 the army of the Fourth Crusade, transported by the Venetian fleet, diverted from its goal and attacked Constantinople. The city was sacked for three days, and its treasures were divided among the crusaders. The Venetians took relics, precious objects and the four horses. They were installed on the loggia of St Mark's Basilica, where they came to symbolise the power and independence of the Venetian Republic.

In 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte's army occupied Venice, ending more than a thousand years of independence. The horses were taken to Paris as spoils of war, displayed in triumph and, from 1808, placed on the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel.

After Napoleon's defeat, the Allies required the return of many works taken by the French. Under Austrian supervision, the horses were taken down and returned to Venice, where they arrived on 13 December 1815 and were reinstalled on the basilica.

In the late twentieth century, pollution threatened the bronze. After restoration, the originals were moved into the Museum of St Mark inside the basilica, and replicas were placed on the loggia in 1982.

expert.short: Spoils of the Fourth Crusade and of Napoleon's Italian campaign, the Horses of Saint Mark embody successive regimes of looting and return. Their restitution in 1815 is often cited as a founding precedent, but their original seizure from Constantinople has never been redressed.
expert.medium: The quadriga of San Marco is the only surviving classical quadriga, its dating contested between the fourth century BCE and the Roman imperial period. Its removal from Constantinople after the sack of 1204 exemplifies the Venetian appropriation of Byzantine spolia, which, installed on the façade of the basilica, legitimised the Republic's claim to the heritage of Rome and Byzantium. Napoleon's removal in 1797, formalised through the treaties of the Italian campaign, integrated the horses into the Parisian display of conquest on the Arc du Carrousel. Their return in 1815, following the Allied demand for restitution of works taken by France, is frequently cited as a precedent in the history of the law of cultural property, marking the emergence of the principle that works of art are not legitimate spoils of war. Yet restitution restored the horses to Venice, itself the beneficiary of an earlier looting, illustrating the selective temporality of restitution norms.
expert.long:
The quadriga of San Marco occupies a unique place in the history of cultural displacement. Its origins are uncertain, with attributions ranging from Lysippos in the fourth century BCE to Roman imperial workshops of the second or third century CE, and its presence in Constantinople, probably in the Hippodrome, is attested by later sources. It was displaced at least three times, each time as a spoil of conquest.

The sack of Constantinople in 1204 by the Fourth Crusade was one of the largest transfers of works of art in the Middle Ages. The Venetians, who had financed and transported the expedition, secured a large share of the spoils, including relics, liturgical objects and architectural elements. Installed on the loggia of San Marco, probably in the mid-thirteenth century, the horses joined a façade assembled from Byzantine spolia that proclaimed Venice as heir to the imperial legacy of Rome and Constantinople.

In 1797 Napoleon's Italian campaign ended the Venetian Republic. The horses were removed to Paris, where they featured in the triumphal entry of the spoils of Italy in 1798 and were placed, in 1808, on the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel. Their removal was part of a systematic policy of appropriation, legitimised by treaty clauses and by the revolutionary ideology that presented Paris as the proper home of the masterpieces of liberty.

After Napoleon's defeat, the Allies demanded the restitution of works removed by France, and the horses were returned to Venice, then under Austrian rule, arriving on 13 December 1815. The restitutions of 1815, supported by Wellington and Castlereagh and carried out despite French resistance, are often cited as a precedent for the principle that cultural property is not a legitimate object of war booty, later codified in the Hague Conventions of 1899 and 1907 and the Hague Convention of 1954.

The horses' case, however, also exposes the selectivity of restitution. The return of 1815 restored them to Venice, the beneficiary of the sack of 1204, without questioning that earlier looting. No claim for their return to Istanbul has been pursued, and Pope John Paul II's apology in 2001 and 2004 for the sack of Constantinople did not extend to its spoils. Since 1982 the originals have been displayed in the Museum of St Mark, with replicas on the loggia, a solution driven by conservation that has also, in effect, turned the horses into museum objects. Their history thus demonstrates that restitution norms apply to some historical moments and not to others.

maps.caption-2: Then: Filandia, Quindío, Colombia - Now: Madrid, Spain

fun.short: The Quimbaya Treasure is a group of 122 shining gold objects, like helmets, bottles and little seated figures, made in Colombia about 1,700 years ago. In 1893 Colombia's president gave it to the Queen of Spain! Fun fact: today Colombia's highest court says it should come back.
fun.medium: Around 1,700 years ago, in the green mountains of what is now Colombia, goldsmiths made beautiful objects by melting gold mixed with copper and pouring it into clay moulds. Some are bottles in the shape of calm, seated people with closed eyes; others are helmets, necklaces and ear ornaments. They were buried with important people in their tombs. In 1890 treasure hunters dug up two tombs near Filandia, in the region of Quindío, and found 122 gold objects. The Colombian government bought them, and in 1893 President Carlos Holguín gave them as a present to Queen Maria Cristina of Spain. Fun fact: the treasure is now in the Museo de América in Madrid, and in 2017 Colombia's Constitutional Court told the government to try to bring it home!
fun.long:
In the middle of Colombia, in the Cauca River valley and the coffee-growing mountains of today's Quindío region, lived people whose goldsmiths were among the best in the ancient Americas. Archaeologists call their style Quimbaya, after a people who lived in the area when the Spanish arrived, although the objects are much older, made roughly between 250 and 430 CE.

The goldsmiths used a technique called lost-wax casting. They modelled an object in wax around a clay core, covered it with more clay, heated it so the wax melted away, and poured in molten tumbaga, a mixture of gold and copper. Then they treated the surface so it shone like pure gold. They made bottles shaped like seated men and women, called poporos, which held lime for chewing coca leaves, as well as helmets, pins and jewellery.

In 1890 treasure hunters, called guaqueros, opened two tombs at a place called La Soledad, near Filandia, and found an extraordinary group of gold objects. The Colombian government bought 122 of them.

In 1892 Spain celebrated 400 years since Columbus reached the Americas with a big exhibition in Madrid, and Colombia sent the treasure. Spain had also helped settle a border dispute between Colombia and Venezuela. To thank Spain, in 1893 President Carlos Holguín gave the treasure to the Queen Regent, Maria Cristina.

Fun fact: many Colombians say that the president had no right to give away the nation's heritage. In 2017 Colombia's Constitutional Court agreed that the government must ask Spain for it back. Spain has refused, and the treasure is still in the Museo de América in Madrid.

basic.short: The Quimbaya Treasure, 122 gold objects from two tombs found at Filandia in 1890, was given by Colombia's president Carlos Holguín to Queen Maria Cristina of Spain in 1893. It is in the Museo de América, Madrid; in 2017 Colombia's Constitutional Court ordered the government to seek its return.
basic.medium: The Quimbaya Treasure consists of 122 objects of gold and tumbaga, a gold-copper alloy, from two tombs found by guaqueros in 1890 at La Soledad, near Filandia in today's Quindío department. Made in the Quimbaya Classic style, around 250–430 CE, it includes seated figures used as lime containers (poporos), helmets, pins, necklaces and ear ornaments, cast by the lost-wax method. The Colombian government acquired the objects and exhibited them in Madrid in 1892 at the Historical American Exposition for the fourth centenary of Columbus's voyage. In 1893 President Carlos Holguín gave them to the Queen Regent of Spain, Maria Cristina, as a gesture of gratitude, in part for Spain's arbitration of Colombia's border with Venezuela. The collection is now in the Museo de América. In 2017 Colombia's Constitutional Court ruled that the gift was irregular and ordered the government to seek its return. Spain has declined.
basic.long:
The Quimbaya style of goldwork developed in the middle Cauca valley of Colombia, in a region of mountains, rivers and fertile volcanic soils now famous for coffee. The objects of the Quimbaya Treasure date from the Classic period, around 250–430 CE, long before the arrival of the Quimbaya people encountered by the Spanish, who gave the style its name.

The goldsmiths worked tumbaga, an alloy of gold and copper, using lost-wax casting to produce complex hollow forms. They then enriched the surface, removing copper to leave a layer of pure gold. The treasure includes seated human figures, some of which served as poporos, containers for lime used when chewing coca leaves, as well as helmets, nose and ear ornaments, pins and beads. The figures, with closed eyes and serene faces, may represent ancestors or people in a trance.

In 1890 guaqueros, people who dig for grave goods, opened two tombs at La Soledad, near Filandia. The Colombian government bought 122 of the objects. At that time Colombia was preparing to take part in the Historical American Exposition in Madrid in 1892, for the fourth centenary of Columbus's first voyage, and the treasure was shown there.

In 1893 President Carlos Holguín presented the collection to Queen Regent Maria Cristina of Spain. The gift was a gesture of gratitude, partly for the Spanish Crown's arbitration of the border between Colombia and Venezuela in 1891. The treasure entered the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid and later the Museo de América.

In 2006 a Colombian lawyer, Felipe Rincón, began legal action arguing that the president had no authority to give away national heritage. In 2017 the Constitutional Court agreed and ordered the government to seek the treasure's return. Spain considers the gift valid, and has given the collection the protected status of a Bien de Interés Cultural.

expert.short: Given by President Carlos Holguín to the Spanish Crown in 1893, the Quimbaya Treasure raises the question of whether a head of state could alienate national heritage. Colombia's Constitutional Court answered no in 2017; Spain maintains that the gift was valid.
expert.medium: The treasure belongs to the Quimbaya Classic tradition of the middle Cauca valley, whose tumbaga castings, including seated figures functioning as poporos, are among the most accomplished of the ancient Americas. Excavated by guaqueros at La Soledad in 1890, the 122 objects were bought by the state and exhibited at the Historical American Exposition in Madrid in 1892. Holguín's gift to Maria Cristina in 1893 reflected the diplomacy of the Regeneration, which emphasised Colombia's Hispanic, Catholic identity and sought Spain's goodwill, notably after its 1891 arbitral award on the Venezuelan border. The Constitutional Court's ruling SU-649 of 19 October 2017, arising from a popular action filed in 2006, held that the gift contravened norms protecting public property and ordered the government to pursue the collection's return through diplomatic channels. Spain regards the donation as a lawful act of a sovereign state and has declared the collection a Bien de Interés Cultural, further restricting its export.
expert.long:
The Quimbaya Treasure belongs to the Quimbaya Classic tradition, which flourished in the middle Cauca valley between roughly the first and seventh centuries CE. Its goldsmiths worked tumbaga through lost-wax casting and depletion gilding, producing hollow figures of exceptional refinement. Seated figures with closed eyes, some functioning as poporos for the lime used in coca chewing, have been interpreted as representations of ancestors or of individuals in altered states of consciousness, linking the objects to funerary and ritual practice.

The objects were excavated in 1890 by guaqueros at La Soledad, near Filandia, from two tombs, a context that, as with much Colombian goldwork, was lost to systematic documentation. The Colombian state purchased 122 pieces, and in 1892 displayed them at the Historical American Exposition in Madrid, part of the celebrations of the fourth centenary of Columbus's voyage, which staged the Hispanic world's shared heritage under Spanish leadership.

The donation of 1893 must be understood in the context of the Regeneration, the conservative political project led by Rafael Núñez and his allies, including Carlos Holguín. Its ideology emphasised Colombia's Hispanic and Catholic identity and sought rapprochement with Spain. The Spanish Crown's arbitral award of 1891 on the Colombian-Venezuelan border provided an occasion for a diplomatic gesture, and Holguín presented the collection to the Queen Regent Maria Cristina. The treasure entered the Museo Arqueológico Nacional and later the Museo de América.

In 2006 the lawyer Felipe Rincón filed a popular action arguing that the gift was unlawful, since national property could not be alienated without congressional authorisation. After lower-court rulings, the Constitutional Court, in its judgment SU-649 of 19 October 2017, held that the donation had disregarded norms protecting public property and ordered the government to take diplomatic steps to seek the treasure's return. Spain has rejected the request, regarding the donation as a valid act of a sovereign state, and has declared the collection a Bien de Interés Cultural, reinforcing its protection under Spanish law.

The case is unusual among restitution disputes in that the object was neither looted nor sold, but given by the government of the country of origin. It thus raises the question of the limits of a state's power to dispose of heritage, and of whether a gift made in a context of post-colonial deference to the former metropole can bind later generations. It also highlights a gap between the domestic law of the country of origin, which may deem the transfer irregular, and that of the holder, which recognises it.

maps.caption-2: Then: Sultanganj, Bihar, India - Now: Birmingham, UK

fun.short: This giant copper Buddha statue, made about 1,500 years ago in India, weighs over 500 kilograms! It was found by British workers while they were building a railway. Today, you can visit it in Birmingham, UK. Fun fact: This statue is so big, it had to be transported in pieces!
fun.medium: This massive copper Buddha statue, known as the Sultanganj Buddha, is an incredible 1,500 years old! Discovered in India during the British colonial period, it weighs more than 500 kilograms, making it one of the largest metal Buddhist statues ever found. British workers came across it while building a railway in 1861, and it was later sent to Birmingham in the UK, where it has been displayed for over a century. The statue is an extraordinary example of early Buddhist art, representing the serenity and wisdom of the Buddha.  - Fun fact: The statue is so enormous that it had to be carefully disassembled and transported in pieces, all the way from India to England! The relocation of the Sultanganj Buddha highlights the vast scale of colonial-era artifact removal. Although it is admired in Birmingham today, many feel that it should be returned to India, where it was originally created and venerated.
fun.long: The Sultanganj Buddha, a massive copper statue from the 5th-7th centuries CE, stands as a monumental representation of early Indian Buddhist art. Crafted during the Gupta period, often hailed as a golden age of Indian culture, this statue captures the essence of serenity and spiritual grace. The Buddha is depicted in a meditative pose, symbolizing enlightenment and inner peace. At over 2 meters tall and weighing more than 500 kilograms, it is one of the largest early Buddhist sculptures ever found, exemplifying the technical and artistic brilliance of ancient Indian copper casting. The statue was discovered by British engineers in 1861 during the construction of a railway near Sultanganj in Bihar, a region that was once home to thriving Buddhist communities. It was created using the lost-wax casting technique, a sophisticated method that allowed for detailed features, such as the smooth flowing drapery of the Buddha's robe and the delicate rendering of his serene expression. The craftsmanship and scale of the statue make it a unique example of early Indian metallurgy, reflecting the spiritual ideals of Buddhism at the time. The Sultanganj Buddha was transported to Birmingham shortly after its discovery, where it has been displayed at the Birmingham Museum ever since. Its relocation, like many artifacts taken during the British colonial period, has sparked debates about cultural heritage and the ethics of artifact removal. While admired for its artistry in the UK, many believe the statue should return to India, where it once held deep religious significance. Fun fact: The Sultanganj Buddha is so large that it had to be disassembled and shipped in parts, a logistical feat for the time! The statue’s journey from a quiet corner of India to a museum in Birmingham is part of a broader story about colonialism and the displacement of cultural treasures.

basic.short: The Sultanganj Buddha, dating back to the 5th-7th centuries, is one of India’s largest surviving early Buddhist sculptures. Discovered during railway construction in 1861, a British railway engineer sent it to Birmingham Museum, where it remains.
basic.medium: The Sultanganj Buddha, one of India’s largest early Buddhist sculptures, dates back to the 5th-7th centuries. Discovered during the British colonial period, it was unearthed in 1861 by British railway workers near the town of Sultanganj in present-day Bihar. Standing at over 2 meters tall and weighing more than 500 kilograms, this copper statue is a significant representation of the Buddha in the Gupta style, a period known for its artistic and spiritual achievements in India. The statue was transported to the UK shortly after its discovery and has been housed at the Birmingham Museum ever since. This enormous statue reflects the technical skill and religious devotion of early Indian sculptors. However, its removal to the UK during the height of British colonialism is a reminder of how sacred and culturally significant objects were often taken from their original settings and placed in European museums, far from the communities that created them. The Sultanganj Buddha remains an important symbol of India’s rich Buddhist heritage, and its presence in Birmingham continues to raise questions about the ethics of colonial-era artifact removal.
basic.long: The Sultanganj Buddha, created between the 5th and 7th centuries CE during India’s Gupta period, represents one of the largest surviving examples of early Indian copper statuary. Standing over two meters tall and weighing more than 500 kilograms, this copper masterpiece embodies the spiritual and artistic zenith of Gupta art. The Gupta Empire is often celebrated as a golden age in Indian history, marked by cultural prosperity and religious devotion, particularly within Buddhist and Hindu traditions. The statue depicts the Buddha in a classic meditative pose, with stylized drapery that flows naturally around his body, embodying the balance and serenity associated with the enlightened state. Its serene facial expression and symmetrical form are characteristic of the period’s artistic ideals, which emphasized harmony and spiritual calmness. The Sultanganj Buddha was unearthed accidentally in 1861 by British engineers working on a railway line near the town of Sultanganj, Bihar. Its discovery came at a time when British colonial efforts were rapidly expanding India’s rail infrastructure, linking distant parts of the empire. The statue was shipped to the UK shortly after its discovery and has since resided in the Birmingham Museum, where it remains a major draw for visitors. The statue’s removal highlights the broader impact of British colonialism on India’s cultural heritage, with many significant artifacts transported to European museums during this period. Technically, the statue is a marvel of copper casting. It was likely created using the lost-wax method, a technique that allowed for intricate details and a smooth, polished finish. The craftsmanship of the statue reflects not only the religious devotion of its creators but also the highly developed metallurgical skills of ancient Indian artisans. While the exact origins of the statue remain uncertain, it is believed to have been commissioned by Buddhist monks or royalty during a time when Buddhist monasteries flourished in the region. The removal of the Sultanganj Buddha to the UK during the colonial period has raised significant ethical questions regarding the displacement of sacred and culturally significant objects. As with many artifacts taken during colonial times, there are ongoing discussions about the rightful ownership of the statue. India has occasionally requested the return of such significant pieces of its cultural heritage, citing the need to restore sacred artifacts to their original context. The presence of the Sultanganj Buddha in Birmingham symbolizes the wider issue of cultural dislocation brought about by imperialism, and the continuing debate over the restitution of artifacts displaced during colonial rule.

expert.short: The Sultanganj Buddha is a remarkable piece of early Buddhist art, dug up by British railway engineers in the 19th century during a railway project. Its relocation to Birmingham reflects the disconnect between sacred objects and their original cultural and religious contexts.
expert.medium: The Sultanganj Buddha is a monumental example of early Indian Buddhist art, created during the Gupta period, which is often regarded as a golden age for Indian culture. Crafted in the 5th-7th centuries, this copper statue stands as a testament to the religious devotion and artistic achievements of ancient India. The Buddha is depicted in a meditative pose, symbolizing inner peace and enlightenment, key aspects of Buddhist philosophy. This remarkable statue was discovered by British engineers in 1861 while constructing a railway line near the town of Sultanganj. Its excavation and subsequent removal to the UK are emblematic of the ways in which sacred and cultural objects were taken from colonized lands during the British Empire’s expansion. The relocation of the Sultanganj Buddha to Birmingham Museum exemplifies the broader issue of cultural dislocation caused by colonial infrastructure projects, such as the building of railways. Although it remains a popular attraction in Birmingham, its removal from India has sparked ongoing debates about cultural restitution and the return of sacred objects to their places of origin. The Sultanganj Buddha’s journey from India to England reflects the tensions between colonialism and cultural heritage, raising important questions about the legacy of colonialism in modern museums.
expert.long: The Sultanganj Buddha, crafted between the 5th and 7th centuries CE, is an extraordinary representation of Gupta-period art, a time known for its flourishing culture, spirituality, and artistic innovation in ancient India. This copper statue, standing over 2 meters tall and weighing more than half a ton, is one of the largest surviving early Buddhist sculptures. Created using the lost-wax casting technique, it is a masterwork of ancient Indian metallurgy, showcasing intricate details like the flowing robe and the serene, meditative expression of the Buddha. These features exemplify the artistic refinement achieved during the Gupta era, which is often considered the pinnacle of Indian sculpture for its blend of naturalism, spirituality, and technical precision. The statue was unearthed in 1861 by British engineers near the town of Sultanganj, Bihar, during the construction of a railway line—a symbol of colonial expansion into India's interior. The excavation and subsequent removal of the Buddha to Birmingham, where it has been housed since 1867, highlight the larger pattern of cultural displacement during British rule. Sacred objects like the Sultanganj Buddha were not only removed from their religious and cultural context but also from the societies that created and revered them. This displacement reflects the imbalance of power in colonial archaeology, where decisions about cultural heritage were often made without the consent of local communities. The Sultanganj Buddha’s removal to the UK, like many artifacts taken during the British colonial period, has sparked ongoing debates about cultural repatriation. In the context of religious art, the statue's relocation is particularly poignant, as it was originally a deeply spiritual object meant to inspire contemplation and reverence in its homeland. Today, while the statue is a significant feature of the Birmingham Museum, its presence there raises important ethical questions about the legacy of colonialism, cultural restitution, and the modern responsibilities of museums. As calls for repatriation grow stronger, the Sultanganj Buddha stands as a reminder of the complex histories that surround ancient art and its modern custodianship.

maps.caption-2: Then: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang (Qing China), China - Now: London, UK

fun.short: The Diamond Sutra is the oldest printed book in the world that tells us exactly when it was made: 868 CE! It was hidden in a sealed cave in China for about 900 years. Fun fact: in 1907 it was sold to a British explorer and is now in London.
fun.medium: Long before printing presses in Europe, people in China printed books by carving a whole page into a wooden block, covering it with ink and pressing paper onto it. The Diamond Sutra is a Buddhist text printed this way on a scroll about five metres long, with a beautiful picture of the Buddha at the start. At the end, a note says it was made by a man called Wang Jie for his parents in the year we call 868 CE. Around the year 1000, the scroll was sealed in a small cave at Mogao, near the desert town of Dunhuang, together with tens of thousands of other manuscripts. Fun fact: when the cave was opened again in 1900, the scroll was still in great condition, and in 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein bought it and took it to London!
fun.long:
Imagine finding a secret room full of books that nobody had seen for 900 years. That is what happened at Mogao, near the town of Dunhuang in western China, where Buddhist monks carved hundreds of caves into a cliff and painted them with bright pictures.

Around the year 1000, someone filled one small cave with tens of thousands of scrolls, paintings and documents, and sealed the entrance with a wall. Nobody knows exactly why. The desert air kept everything dry and safe.

In 1900 a Daoist monk called Wang Yuanlu, who looked after the caves, noticed a crack in a wall and discovered the hidden library. Among the treasures was a scroll of a Buddhist text called the Diamond Sutra. It had been printed from carved wooden blocks, and at the beginning there is a picture of the Buddha teaching his disciple Subhuti, surrounded by monks, guardians and lions.

What makes it so special is a short note at the end. It says that the scroll was made by Wang Jie for his two parents, to be given away for free, on a day in the year we call 868 CE. That makes it the oldest printed book in the world with a date, almost 600 years before Gutenberg printed his Bible in Europe!

In 1907 the British-Hungarian explorer Aurel Stein arrived in Dunhuang. He persuaded Wang Yuanlu to sell him thousands of manuscripts for a small sum of money, and the Diamond Sutra was among them. Fun fact: today it is in the British Library in London, but you can look at every inch of it online, thanks to the International Dunhuang Project.

basic.short: The Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang, printed in 868 CE, is the world's earliest dated printed book. Found in the sealed Library Cave at Mogao, it was sold by Wang Yuanlu to Aurel Stein in 1907 and is now in the British Library.
basic.medium: The Diamond Sutra is one of the most important texts of Mahayana Buddhism. The copy from Dunhuang is a scroll about five metres long, made of sheets of paper printed from woodblocks, with a frontispiece showing the Buddha preaching to his disciple Subhuti. Its colophon states that it was made for free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his parents in the ninth year of the Xiantong era, which corresponds to 868 CE, making it the earliest dated printed book known. The scroll was deposited in the Library Cave (Cave 17) at the Mogao Caves, which was sealed around the early eleventh century. The Daoist monk Wang Yuanlu rediscovered the cave in 1900, and in 1907 he sold the scroll, with thousands of other manuscripts, to the explorer Aurel Stein. It is now in the British Library in London.
basic.long:
The Mogao Caves, carved into a cliff near the oasis town of Dunhuang in Gansu province, are one of the greatest sites of Buddhist art in the world. From the fourth to the fourteenth century, monks and patrons created hundreds of cave temples decorated with wall paintings and sculptures.

One small cave, now known as Cave 17 or the Library Cave, was filled with manuscripts, printed texts, paintings and textiles and walled up around the early eleventh century. Its contents, some 50,000 items in Chinese, Tibetan, Sanskrit, Uyghur and other languages, remained hidden for nine centuries.

Among them was a printed copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist text on the nature of perception and emptiness. It is a scroll about five metres long, printed from carved woodblocks on seven sheets of paper, and it opens with a finely detailed picture of the Buddha preaching. The colophon at the end states that Wang Jie had it made for free distribution on behalf of his parents on a date equivalent to 11 May 868. It is thus the earliest complete printed book with a date, showing that printing was already a mature craft in Tang China.

In 1900 Wang Yuanlu, a Daoist monk who had appointed himself guardian of the caves, found the Library Cave. He reported it to local officials, who did little. In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein, working for British India, persuaded him to part with thousands of manuscripts and paintings in exchange for a donation towards restoring the caves. Stein's collection went to the British Museum and later the British Library.

Today the Diamond Sutra is one of the treasures of the British Library. Since 1994, the International Dunhuang Project has digitised Dunhuang manuscripts held around the world and made them available online.

expert.short: The Dunhuang Diamond Sutra (868 CE), the earliest dated printed book, left China in 1907 when Aurel Stein acquired it from Wang Yuanlu. Its dispersal with the Library Cave's contents across London, Paris, St Petersburg, Kyoto and Beijing remains a sensitive chapter in Chinese memory.
expert.medium: The Dunhuang copy of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation, is a woodblock-printed scroll with a colophon dated to the thirteenth day of the fourth month of Xiantong 9 (868 CE), recording its commission by Wang Jie for universal distribution on behalf of his parents. Its technical sophistication, particularly the frontispiece, implies a long prior development of xylography. The scroll was deposited in Cave 17 at Mogao, sealed in the early eleventh century. After Wang Yuanlu's discovery in 1900, Aurel Stein acquired it in 1907 as part of several thousand manuscripts; it is now in the British Library (Or.8210/P.2). Paul Pelliot, Japanese, Russian and other expeditions followed, and the remainder was transferred to Beijing in 1910. The historian Chen Yinke's description of Dunhuang as a 'history of sorrow' for Chinese scholarship captures the enduring perception of this dispersal.
expert.long:
The printed Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang is a copy of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in the Chinese translation of Kumārajīva, a key text of Mahayana Buddhism, particularly in the Chan tradition. The scroll, about five metres long, consists of seven sheets printed from woodblocks. Its frontispiece, showing the Buddha preaching to the elderly disciple Subhūti amid bodhisattvas, guardians and donors, is a highly accomplished work of block-cutting, which implies that xylography was by then a mature technique. The colophon states that it was reverently made for universal free distribution by Wang Jie on behalf of his two parents on the thirteenth day of the fourth month of the ninth year of Xiantong, corresponding to 868 CE. The practice of producing sūtras for merit explains both its creation and its distribution.

The scroll was deposited in Cave 17 at Mogao, the so-called Library Cave, which was sealed around the early eleventh century for reasons that remain debated. Its contents constitute the largest cache of medieval manuscripts ever found in Asia and have given rise to the field of Dunhuang studies.

The cave was opened in 1900 by the Daoist Wang Yuanlu, who informed local officials without prompting effective intervention. In 1907 Aurel Stein, conducting his second expedition for the government of British India, obtained several thousand manuscripts and paintings, including the Diamond Sutra, in exchange for donations to Wang's restoration work, a transaction Stein himself described in terms of persuasion and secrecy. Paul Pelliot followed in 1908, selecting manuscripts for Paris; Japanese, Russian and other expeditions acquired further material; and the Qing government transferred the remainder to Beijing in 1910. Today Dunhuang material is held principally in London, Paris, St Petersburg, Kyoto and Beijing, with smaller holdings elsewhere.

In China, the dispersal is remembered as a national loss. The historian Chen Yinke described Dunhuang as a 'history of sorrow' of Chinese scholarship, and Wang Yuanlu has been cast as a figure of betrayal, although recent scholarship emphasises the neglect of the Qing authorities and the structural inequality between European expeditions and local custodians. The British Library regards its acquisition as lawful and has not received a formal restitution claim; instead, since 1994 the International Dunhuang Project, a collaboration of holding institutions including the Dunhuang Academy, has digitised and reunited the dispersed corpus virtually, raising the question of whether digital access can substitute for physical return.

maps.caption-2: Then: Orongo, Rapa Nui (Chile) - Now: London, UK

fun.short: This giant stone statue, made by the Rapa Nui people of Rapa Nui, is one of the famous Moai statues! British sailors took it back to England in the 1800s, and now it’s in the British Museum. Fun fact: The Moai were carved to represent important ancestors, and some weigh more than 80 tons!
fun.medium: The Moai statues of Rapa Nui, carved by the Rapa Nui people, are some of the most iconic stone figures in the world! Standing tall and proud, these statues were made to honor important ancestors, and some of them weigh as much as 80 tons! The Moai called Hoa Hakananai’a is one of the most famous—it was taken by British sailors in the 1800s and is now housed in the British Museum.  - Fun fact: Many Moai statues were placed to watch over the villages of the Rapa Nui people, facing inward toward the land as a symbol of protection and ancestral power. The Moai statues are not only symbols of artistic achievement but also deeply spiritual objects, representing the connection between the Rapa Nui and their ancestors. This statue’s removal to the UK is part of a larger story of cultural loss for the Rapa Nui people, who continue to fight for its return to Rapa Nui.
fun.long: The Moai statues of Rapa Nui, carved by the Rapa Nui people between 1000 and 1500 CE, are monumental symbols of the island’s rich spiritual and cultural heritage. Standing tall and majestic, these stone figures were sculpted from volcanic rock, with some reaching over 10 meters in height and weighing up to 80 tons. Each Moai was painstakingly created to represent the deified spirits of Rapa Nui ancestors, honoring their legacies and ensuring their protective presence over the living. They were not just statues; they embodied the island’s deep connection to its past, with many facing inward toward the land to oversee and safeguard their communities. Among the many Moai statues, the one known as Hoa Hakananai’a is particularly famous, both for its intricate carvings and for its controversial history. Hoa Hakananai’a was removed from the island in 1868 by British sailors aboard the HMS Topaze, during a period when European powers were increasingly interested in artifacts from indigenous cultures. The statue was transported to England, where it has been exhibited at the British Museum for over 150 years. Its name, meaning stolen or hidden friend in the Rapa Nui language, poignantly reflects its spiritual significance and the painful reality of its removal. While admired in London as a piece of remarkable artistry, for the Rapa Nui, the statue’s removal is a symbol of colonial-era exploitation and cultural erasure. Hoa Hakananai’a's removal stripped the Rapa Nui people of a vital part of their ancestral lineage. The Moai were carved to embody the spirits of revered ancestors, believed to watch over the island and ensure its fertility, prosperity, and peace. By taking the statue, British colonial forces not only displaced an artistic masterpiece but also severed a spiritual link between the Rapa Nui people and their ancestors. For the Rapa Nui, the statue was more than a representation of the past; it was a living connection to their forebears, their traditions, and their identity. Its absence has been felt deeply on Rapa Nui, where the other Moai remain as silent but enduring guardians of the Rapa Nui legacy. In recent decades, there has been a growing movement by the Rapa Nui people to reclaim Hoa Hakananai’a and return it to its rightful place on the island. The calls for repatriation have gained momentum, with increasing recognition of the importance of cultural restitution. The Rapa Nui believe that the statue’s return is essential for healing the wounds of colonialism and restoring the cultural equilibrium disrupted by its removal. International discussions about repatriation continue, with the British Museum facing pressure to acknowledge the deep spiritual and cultural significance of such artifacts beyond their aesthetic or historical value. For the Rapa Nui people, the return of Hoa Hakananai’a is not just about bringing home a stolen artifact—it is about reclaiming their identity, honoring their ancestors, and preserving their cultural legacy for future generations. The statue’s displacement raises broader questions about the impact of colonialism on indigenous communities and the ongoing struggles for cultural justice. Hoa Hakananai’a stands as a powerful symbol of the resilience of the Rapa Nui people, who continue to fight for the restitution of their heritage. Its return to Rapa Nui would represent a triumph not just for the Rapa Nui, but for all indigenous peoples who seek to reclaim the sacred objects taken from them during centuries of colonial exploitation. The Moai statues, including Hoa Hakananai’a, remind us that cultural heritage is more than just art; it is the heart and soul of a people’s history, beliefs, and identity.

basic.long: The Moai statue known as Hoa Hakananai’a, carved by the Rapa Nui people between 1000 and 1500 CE, is a remarkable example of the monumental stone figures that define Rapa Nui's cultural and spiritual landscape. These statues, carved from volcanic rock, were created to embody the spirits of deified ancestors, known as “ariki”, who were believed to watch over and protect the island’s communities. Standing tall, the Moai were a testament to the craftsmanship and spiritual devotion of the Rapa Nui, with each statue serving as a guardian of the people and a link to their ancestral past. Hoa Hakananai’a, which stands at a height of approximately 2.5 meters, is particularly notable for its detailed carvings and the distinctive symbols etched into its back, which are believed to represent motifs from the “birdman” cult, a later religious tradition on the island. In 1868, the statue was forcibly removed from its home by British sailors aboard the HMS “Topaze” and transported to England. This act of cultural theft occurred during a period of heightened European exploration and colonial expansion, when indigenous cultures around the world were being appropriated for their material wealth and cultural treasures. The sailors who took Hoa Hakananai’a saw the statue as a curiosity and an object of artistic value, oblivious to its deep spiritual significance for the Rapa Nui people. The statue was presented as a gift to Queen Victoria and has been housed in the British Museum ever since. There, it has been displayed as an example of the artistic ingenuity of a remote and mysterious civilization, removed from its sacred context and placed in a colonial museum setting where it became an artifact of Western curiosity rather than a living symbol of Rapa Nui heritage. The removal of Hoa Hakananai’a from Rapa Nui exemplifies the broader pattern of cultural loss and exploitation that indigenous communities faced during the colonial era. For the Rapa Nui people, the statue is not just a piece of art or a historical object; it is a sacred link to their ancestors, imbued with spiritual significance and tied to the island’s rituals and belief systems. The British sailors who took the statue could not have understood its meaning within the context of Rapa Nui spirituality, where the Moai were believed to hold “mana”, a spiritual force that protected the island and its people. The displacement of Hoa Hakananai’a therefore represented a profound disruption to the Rapa Nui’s connection with their ancestors and the land. In recent years, the Rapa Nui people have intensified their calls for the repatriation of Hoa Hakananai’a, arguing that the statue’s rightful place is on Rapa Nui, where it can be reunited with the landscape and culture from which it was taken. These calls for repatriation are part of a larger global movement advocating for the return of cultural objects taken during the colonial period, as many indigenous communities seek to reclaim the sacred and symbolic items that were taken from them. The Rapa Nui argue that the return of the Moai is essential not only for restoring their cultural heritage but also for healing the wounds of colonialism and reestablishing their connection to their ancestral spirits. The British Museum, like many institutions holding artifacts acquired during the colonial era, has faced growing pressure to reconsider the ethics of retaining such objects. While the museum has acknowledged the significance of Hoa Hakananai’a to the Rapa Nui people, it has yet to agree to return the statue, citing concerns about the preservation and global accessibility of the object. However, for the Rapa Nui, the statue’s cultural and spiritual value far outweighs its role as a museum piece. The ongoing debates over the repatriation of Hoa Hakananai’a highlight the complex intersections of cultural heritage, colonial history, and modern-day justice. The Rapa Nui’s struggle for the statue’s return is emblematic of the broader fight for indigenous peoples around the world to reclaim their heritage and assert their sovereignty over the cultural objects that represent their histories, identities, and spiritual beliefs.
