maps.caption-2: Then: Ganghwa Island (Joseon Korea), South Korea - Now: Seoul, South Korea (returned 2011 on renewable loan)

fun.short: The Uigwe are illustrated books recording the great ceremonies of Korea's kings: weddings, funerals and royal processions. French soldiers took almost 300 of them in 1866. Fun fact: a Korean librarian found them in Paris more than a hundred years later!
fun.medium: Korea's Joseon kings liked to do things properly. For every big royal event, like a wedding, a funeral or the building of a palace, officials wrote a detailed book called an uigwe, with lists, instructions and colourful paintings of long processions with hundreds of people, horses and banners. Special copies made for the king were kept in a royal library on Ganghwa Island, near the coast. In 1866 French warships attacked Ganghwa to punish Korea for killing French missionaries. The soldiers burned the library and took 297 volumes. Fun fact: in 1975 a Korean historian working at the National Library of France, Park Byeong-seon, discovered them in Paris, and after years of campaigning they came back to Korea in 2011!
fun.long:
The Joseon dynasty ruled Korea for more than 500 years, from 1392 to 1910, and it cared a lot about ceremonies done the right way. For every important royal event, such as a wedding, a coronation, a funeral or a big banquet, the court wrote a book called an uigwe, which means something like "rules for rituals". It recorded everything: who took part, what they wore, how much things cost and in what order people walked. Many uigwe also have beautiful painted pages showing processions stretching across several sheets, with the king's palanquin, soldiers, musicians and flag-bearers.

The finest copies, made for the king to read, were kept in a special library built in 1782 by King Jeongjo on Ganghwa Island, an island at the mouth of the Han River, close to the capital. It was called the Oegyujanggak, the "outer royal library".

In 1866 Korea arrested and executed several French Catholic missionaries, who were in the country illegally. In return, France sent warships to Ganghwa Island. The French troops occupied the island for several weeks, and before leaving they burned the library and took 297 volumes of uigwe, along with other treasures, to France.

For over a hundred years almost nobody knew where they were. Then, in 1975, Park Byeong-seon, a Korean historian working at the National Library of France, found them in the library's storerooms. She spent years studying them and telling Korea about them.

Fun fact: in 2011 the books finally came back to Korea, and they are now in the National Museum of Korea in Seoul. Legally they are on a loan that is renewed every five years, because French law makes it hard for museums and libraries to give things away.

basic.short: The Oegyujanggak Uigwe, illustrated records of Joseon royal ceremonies, were taken by French troops from Ganghwa Island in 1866. Rediscovered at the Bibliothèque nationale de France in 1975, they returned to Korea in 2011 on a renewable loan.
basic.medium: Uigwe are the official records of the state ceremonies of the Joseon dynasty (1392–1910): royal weddings, funerals, coronations, banquets and building projects. They include detailed texts and painted illustrations of processions and ritual objects. In 1782 King Jeongjo founded the Oegyujanggak on Ganghwa Island as an annex of the royal library, where the finest copies, those made for the king's own reading, were stored. In 1866, in retaliation for the execution of French Catholic missionaries, a French naval expedition under Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze occupied Ganghwa, burned the library and carried off 297 volumes of uigwe. In 1975 the historian Park Byeong-seon, a librarian at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, identified them. After decades of negotiation, the manuscripts returned to Korea in 2011 under a five-year renewable loan and are now held by the National Museum of Korea.
basic.long:
Uigwe are the court records of the Joseon dynasty's great ceremonies. For each royal wedding, funeral, investiture or major building project, a temporary office compiled a record of the preparations and proceedings: the officials involved, the materials used and their costs, the order of procession and the design of ritual objects. Many uigwe include painted illustrations, notably banchado, long painted processions showing the arrangement of participants. The genre was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.

Several copies of each uigwe were made and stored in different places. The copies for the king's personal use, known as eoram copies, were of the highest quality. In 1782 King Jeongjo established the Oegyujanggak, an annex of the royal library, on Ganghwa Island, near the mouth of the Han River, to keep important records safe from threats to the capital.

In 1866 the Korean government executed several French Catholic missionaries and many Korean converts. France responded with a naval expedition commanded by Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze, which occupied Ganghwa for several weeks. Before withdrawing, the French troops set fire to the Oegyujanggak and took 297 volumes of uigwe, together with other objects, to France.

The manuscripts entered the imperial library in Paris, the future Bibliothèque nationale de France, and were largely forgotten. In 1975 Park Byeong-seon, a Korean historian working there, identified them, and her research fuelled calls for their return. In 1993 President François Mitterrand returned one volume during a state visit.

In 2010 the presidents of France and South Korea agreed on a solution: the manuscripts would return under a five-year loan, renewable automatically, since French law made a transfer of ownership difficult. They arrived in Korea in four shipments in 2011 and are now at the National Museum of Korea.

expert.short: Taken by Admiral Roze's expedition to Ganghwa in 1866, the 297 royal Uigwe were identified at the BnF by Park Byeong-seon in 1975 and returned to Korea in 2011 under a renewable loan, a legal compromise reflecting the French principle of inalienability.
expert.medium: The Oegyujanggak collection consisted mainly of eoram uigwe, the royal-viewing copies of the protocol records compiled by temporary offices (dogam) for major state rites, which document Confucian ritual practice, court organisation and material culture of Joseon Korea, often uniquely. The French punitive expedition of 1866 (Byeongin yangyo), launched by the naval commander Pierre-Gustave Roze after the persecution of Catholics, occupied Ganghwa, burned the Oegyujanggak and removed 297 volumes. Identified in 1975 by Park Byeong-seon in the BnF, they became the object of sustained diplomatic efforts; a single volume was returned in 1993 in the context of the TGV contract negotiations. The 2010 agreement between Presidents Lee Myung-bak and Nicolas Sarkozy provided for return by a renewable five-year loan, circumventing the inalienability of French public collections. Korean scholars have criticised the arrangement for leaving ownership with France.
expert.long:
The uigwe are the protocol records of the Joseon court, compiled by temporary offices, or dogam, set up for each major state rite: royal weddings, funerals, investitures, ancestral rites and building projects. Combining prose records, inventories, accounts and illustrations, notably the long procession paintings known as banchado, they document with exceptional precision the ritual, administrative and material culture of Confucian kingship. Multiple copies were produced and distributed among repositories; the royal-viewing copies, or eoram, were made with the finest paper, binding and painting. The uigwe of the Joseon dynasty were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.

In 1782 King Jeongjo founded the Oegyujanggak on Ganghwa Island as an annex of the Kyujanggak royal library, a strategic location that had served as a refuge for the court in earlier invasions. By the nineteenth century it held many eoram uigwe, some of which survived nowhere else.

In 1866, following the execution of French missionaries and thousands of Korean Catholics, a French naval expedition under Rear Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze attacked Ganghwa. Known in Korea as the Byeongin yangyo, the 'Western disturbance of 1866', it ended in French withdrawal after defeats by Korean forces, but not before the troops had burned the Oegyujanggak and removed 297 volumes of uigwe, together with silver and other objects. The episode reinforced the Joseon court's policy of isolation.

The manuscripts entered the imperial library in Paris and remained largely unknown until 1975, when the historian Park Byeong-seon, a librarian at the Bibliothèque nationale de France, identified them. Her research, published in Korea, made their return a national cause. In 1993 President François Mitterrand returned a single volume during negotiations over the sale of TGV technology to Korea, promising further returns that met with resistance from BnF curators.

The issue was resolved at the G20 summit in Seoul in 2010, when Presidents Lee Myung-bak and Nicolas Sarkozy agreed that the manuscripts would return under a five-year loan, renewable automatically. The arrangement allowed France to circumvent the inalienability of its public collections without legislation. The manuscripts arrived in 2011 and are held by the National Museum of Korea. Korean scholars and civic groups have criticised the formula for leaving legal ownership in France, while French critics saw it as a precedent weakening inalienability. The case thus illustrates both the diplomatic creativity and the legal limits of restitution in a system that treats public collections as inalienable.

maps.caption-2: Then: Lahore (Sikh Empire), Pakistan - Now: London, UK (Crown Jewels)

fun.short: The Koh-i-Noor diamond is one of the biggest diamonds in the world! Weighing a whopping 105 carats, it was taken by the British in 1849. Now it’s part of the Crown Jewels in London, where it sparkles for visitors. Fun fact: Legends say this diamond brings bad luck to men who wear it!
fun.medium: The Koh-i-Noor diamond is one of the largest and most famous diamonds in the world! Weighing a massive 105 carats, this dazzling gemstone was originally found in India, where it became a prized possession of Indian rulers. However, it was taken by the British in 1849, after they annexed the region of Punjab. Since then, the diamond has been part of the British Crown Jewels, sparkling in royal crowns and tiaras in London. The diamond’s name, Koh-i-Noor, means Mountain of Light in Persian, a fitting title for such a magnificent gem.  - Fun fact: There’s a legend that the Koh-i-Noor brings bad luck to any man who wears it, which is why it has only been worn by women in the British royal family! Today, the Koh-i-Noor remains a symbol of British imperialism, with India, Pakistan, and even Afghanistan calling for its return.
fun.long: The Koh-i-Noor, one of the most infamous diamonds in history, is not only celebrated for its brilliance but also for the many legends, power struggles, and controversies surrounding it. Weighing 105 carats, this enormous diamond was mined in India’s Golconda region and is believed to have been in circulation since the early 5th century. It has passed through the hands of numerous rulers across empires, becoming a symbol of divine and earthly power. From Mughal emperors to Persian kings, and from Sikh rulers to British monarchs, the Koh-i-Noor has been both a gift and a prize in diplomatic exchanges and military conquests. In 1849, as part of the annexation of Punjab, the British East India Company obtained the diamond and presented it to Queen Victoria. Since then, it has become a glittering centerpiece in the British Crown Jewels, mounted in crowns worn by queens and consorts of the British royal family. But its dazzling beauty hides a painful history. India and Pakistan, among others, have been demanding its return for decades, viewing the diamond not just as a stolen gem but as a symbol of colonial exploitation. Even Afghanistan has claimed ownership, as the diamond was briefly in the possession of an Afghan ruler.Interestingly, despite its size and beauty, the Koh-i-Noor is said to carry a curse: bad luck for any man who wears it. Perhaps that's why, throughout its British history, only women of the royal family have donned it. But this “curse” is often overshadowed by the more significant political tensions surrounding its rightful ownership. India views the Koh-i-Noor as part of its heritage, a cultural treasure taken at the height of British imperialism. With ongoing debates about colonial restitution, the Koh-i-Noor’s fate remains uncertain, a glittering but contested relic of history. Fun fact: It’s said that in some cultures, possessing the Koh-i-Noor would bring so much power and fortune that kings waged wars for it, with each ruler hoping to keep it forever. But as history shows, the diamond’s path has never been steady, moving from one empire to another. Would returning it to India close this chapter, or would its legacy as a spoils of conquest continue to haunt future generations?

basic.short: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, one of the largest diamonds in the world, was taken by the British East India Company in 1849 after the annexation of Punjab. Now part of the British Crown Jewels, it has been the subject of on-going calls for its return, above all from India and Pakistan.
basic.medium: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, formed millions of years ago and weighing 105 carats, is one of the most famous and controversial diamonds in the world. Historically, it belonged to various Indian dynasties before being seized by the British East India Company in 1849 after the annexation of Punjab. The diamond was presented to Queen Victoria, and it has since become a centerpiece of the British Crown Jewels, where it remains to this day. The diamond’s storied history includes legends of it being passed down through the hands of many rulers, often as spoils of war. The diamond’s current placement in the British Crown Jewels has been the subject of numerous calls for restitution, with India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan each laying claim to it. The Koh-i-Noor is not just a jewel but a powerful symbol of colonialism and the material wealth extracted from India during British rule. Its continued presence in the British royal collection underscores the ongoing debates about the legacy of imperialism and the restitution of cultural treasures.
basic.long: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, one of the largest and most famous gems in the world, has a complex and deeply entangled history that stretches back over 1,500 years. Originally found in the Golconda mines of India, this 105-carat diamond has been a symbol of power, divinity, and sovereignty for centuries. Its early history is somewhat shrouded in legend, but it first rose to prominence in the hands of India’s Mughal emperors, where it adorned the famous Peacock Throne. The diamond’s name, Koh-i-Noor, means Mountain of Light in Persian, a fitting title for a jewel so large and radiant. From the Mughal Empire, it passed to the Persian and Afghan dynasties, each of which coveted its symbolic value as much as its monetary worth. However, its modern story began in 1849 when it was forcibly taken by the British during the annexation of Punjab, after the Second Anglo-Sikh War. The young Maharaja Duleep Singh, just a boy at the time, was coerced into surrendering his kingdom and, along with it, the priceless diamond. The British East India Company presented the Koh-i-Noor to Queen Victoria, marking the jewel’s transformation into a prized possession of the British monarchy. Its display during the Great Exhibition of 1851 in London attracted thousands of visitors, though some found its brilliance underwhelming. To address this, the diamond was later recut, further enhancing its brilliance but also reducing its weight. Today, the Koh-i-Noor is set in the Crown of the British Queen Mother, part of the Crown Jewels on display at the Tower of London. But its beauty is marred by its contested ownership. India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan have all laid claims to the diamond, each asserting that the gem was stolen from their people. India, in particular, views the Koh-i-Noor as a vivid reminder of British colonial exploitation. Requests for its return have been consistently denied by the British government, which argues that the diamond was legally acquired under the terms of the Treaty of Lahore. The removal of the Koh-i-Noor is emblematic of a broader pattern of cultural extraction that occurred under British imperial rule, with many artifacts and treasures taken from colonized nations and displayed in European museums. The debate over its restitution reflects wider global discussions about the ethics of such acquisitions and the responsibility of modern institutions to rectify historical wrongs. Yet, despite numerous requests, the Koh-i-Noor remains in London, glittering in the Crown Jewels but steeped in the painful history of conquest, loss, and imperial ambition.

expert.short: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, seized by the British after the 1849 conquest of Punjab, remains a potent symbol of British imperialism. Currently part of the Crown Jewels, it continues to spark debates about restitution, representing both the material and cultural exploitation of India under colonial rule.
expert.medium: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, weighing 105 carats, is one of the most iconic symbols of British colonial rule in India. Originally found in India and passed through the hands of various rulers, the diamond became a prized possession in the region for centuries. Its capture by the British in 1849, following their conquest of Punjab, marked a turning point in its history. Once part of the treasury of Indian rulers, it was forcibly transferred to the British monarchy, becoming part of the Crown Jewels. The diamond’s name, which means “Mountain of Light,” reflects its immense size and brilliance, but it also carries the weight of imperialism and cultural loss. The removal of the Koh-i-Noor from India has been a point of contention ever since it was taken. While the British monarchy considers it a symbol of the empire’s grandeur, it is seen by many in India and other former British colonies as a reminder of the exploitation and material extraction that characterized British colonial rule. The debate over the Koh-i-Noor’s ownership highlights broader questions of restitution and the responsibility of modern nations to return cultural objects acquired through colonialism. Its glittering beauty belies a complex and painful history of conquest and power struggles, making it one of the most potent symbols of the legacy of empire.
expert.long: The Koh-i-Noor diamond, renowned for its staggering 105-carat size and brilliance, stands as one of the most potent symbols of British colonial acquisition. Originating in India, the diamond has a long and complex history, having passed through the hands of numerous rulers over centuries, including the Mughals, Persians, and Sikhs. It was initially unearthed in India, likely in the Golconda mines, and became a treasure coveted by many regional dynasties. By the early 19th century, it had come into the possession of the Sikh Empire, under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Following the annexation of Punjab by the British East India Company in 1849, the diamond was taken as part of the spoils of war and subsequently presented to Queen Victoria. This act of seizure marked its transformation from a symbol of Indian royalty to a gem emblematic of British imperial dominance. The diamond, now part of the British Crown Jewels, has been displayed in numerous royal events, mounted into crowns and tiaras worn by British queens, including Queen Alexandra and Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother. Its aesthetic appeal—combined with the mastery involved in cutting and setting such a large diamond—exemplifies the craftsmanship of the period. However, beyond its beauty, the Koh-i-Noor’s political and cultural significance looms large. Made of carbon atoms crystallized millions of years ago, the stone is not merely a jewel but a historical artifact tied to narratives of power, conquest, and subjugation. The decision to cut it down to enhance its brilliance in the mid-19th century also symbolizes an attempt to reshape and control its legacy, paralleling the British Empire’s broader efforts to exert dominance over its colonies. The Koh-i-Noor has become the subject of several legal and diplomatic debates. India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, and even Iran have all laid claim to the diamond at various times, reflecting the deep-seated emotions surrounding its removal from the Indian subcontinent. The diamond’s journey from the hands of South Asian monarchs to the British Crown encapsulates the story of imperialism and its enduring consequences. The unresolved controversy over its rightful ownership continues to fuel discussions on the return of looted colonial artifacts. In modern times, the Koh-i-Noor remains a glittering yet contested symbol—its physical presence in the Tower of London serving as a reminder of the material wealth extracted from colonized lands, while its absence from its place of origin evokes a lingering sense of cultural and historical displacement.

fun.short: These treasures came from the Old Summer Palace in Beijing. British and French soldiers looted them during the Second Opium War in 1860. Fun fact: The Old Summer Palace was so huge, it had over 1,000 buildings filled with art and treasures!
fun.medium: The treasures of the Old Summer Palace in Beijing are some of the most valuable artefacts in Chinese history. These treasures were looted by British and French soldiers during the Second Opium War in 1860, when the palace was destroyed. The palace, also known as Yuanmingyuan, was a sprawling complex with over 1,000 buildings, all filled with priceless art, jewellery, and historical items.  - Fun fact: The Old Summer Palace was so vast and beautiful that it was often called the Versailles of the East! Imagine a place with lakes, gardens, and palaces stretching over hundreds of hectares! The looting and destruction of the Old Summer Palace remains a painful memory in China’s history, as many of its treasures were taken to European museums, where they are still displayed today.
fun.long: The Old Summer Palace, known as Yuanmingyuan, is a remarkable testament to Chinese imperial grandeur and artistic achievement. This expansive complex, constructed over several decades in the 18th century, included more than 1,000 exquisite buildings and an intricate system of gardens, lakes, and waterways. It was designed to reflect both traditional Chinese aesthetics and European architectural influences, making it a unique fusion of cultures. Each area of the palace was meticulously crafted, featuring stunning landscapes that combined nature and artistry, embodying the philosophical principles of harmony and balance deeply rooted in Chinese culture. Among its countless treasures, the Old Summer Palace housed a vast collection of artworks, including delicate ceramics, intricate carvings, and lavish textiles, all celebrating the rich cultural heritage of China. It was not only a royal residence but also a center of intellectual and artistic pursuits, where scholars and artists thrived, contributing to the rich tapestry of Chinese history. The palace's serene environment was meant to inspire contemplation and creativity, serving as a retreat for emperors seeking peace and inspiration from nature. Tragically, in 1860, during the Second Opium War, British and French troops attacked Yuanmingyuan as an act of reprisal, resulting in its systematic looting and destruction. The forces pillaged its magnificent artifacts and set fire to the buildings, reducing much of this cultural marvel to ashes. The looting left a profound scar on the cultural landscape of China, symbolizing the broader impact of colonial aggression and exploitation. The artifacts taken from the palace, including bronze sculptures, jade objects, and gold regalia, were transported to Europe and distributed among various museums, where they remain to this day. The Old Summer Palace's treasures are more than mere art objects; they are vital elements of Chinese identity and history, encapsulating centuries of imperial rule, artistry, and cultural significance. The loss of these artifacts continues to resonate deeply within the Chinese collective memory, evoking a sense of cultural dispossession and a longing for restitution. In recent years, there has been a resurgence of efforts by China to reclaim these stolen treasures, highlighting the ongoing struggles of nations to recover their cultural heritage from the clutches of colonial powers. The legacy of Yuanmingyuan serves as a poignant reminder of the fragility of cultural heritage in the face of imperial ambitions, emphasizing the need for dialogue and reconciliation in addressing historical injustices.

basic.short: The Old Summer Palace, also known as Yuanmingyuan, was a vast complex of gardens and palaces in Beijing. British and French forces looted its artefacts in 1860 during the Second Opium War, and many of these treasures now reside in European museums.
basic.medium: The Old Summer Palace, also known as Yuanmingyuan, was a vast and magnificent imperial garden and palace complex located outside Beijing. Built in the 18th century, it was famed for its artistic and architectural splendour, with over 1,000 buildings housing a vast collection of Chinese art, ceramics, and historical treasures. In 1860, during the Second Opium War, British and French forces looted the palace’s artefacts and burned it to the ground as retaliation for the capture of European prisoners. Many of the artefacts from the palace were dispersed to European museums, where they remain to this day. The looting of the Old Summer Palace represents one of the most dramatic acts of cultural destruction in modern Chinese history, and the loss of these artefacts has become a symbol of the exploitation China faced during its “century of humiliation.” Despite efforts to reclaim some of these treasures, many remain abroad, sparking debates about cultural restitution and the legacy of colonial violence.
basic.long: The Old Summer Palace, or Yuanmingyuan, was a sprawling imperial garden and palace complex located outside of Beijing, built in the 18th century during the Qing Dynasty. Spanning over 860 acres, it was a masterpiece of architecture and landscape design, blending traditional Chinese styles with Western influences to create a symbol of imperial grandeur. The palace was home to priceless collections of art, jade, porcelain, and cultural relics spanning centuries of Chinese history. Yuanmingyuan was not only a royal residence but also a cultural hub, representing the peak of Qing artistic achievement and serving as a repository of the nation’s cultural heritage. In 1860, during the Second Opium War, British and French forces launched a punitive expedition against China after the capture and mistreatment of European envoys. As part of this retaliation, the forces targeted Yuanmingyuan, looting the palace of its treasures and systematically burning it to the ground. The scale of destruction was immense, with soldiers pillaging gold, silver, silk, sculptures, and paintings before setting fire to the palace’s wooden structures. The once-great complex was reduced to ruins, its magnificent gardens and buildings obliterated. The looted items, which included sculptures, ceramics, and rare books, were dispersed across Europe, where they became prized possessions in museums and private collections. The sacking of the Old Summer Palace is often regarded as one of the most egregious acts of cultural vandalism in modern history. For China, the destruction of Yuanmingyuan was more than just the loss of physical treasures; it marked a devastating cultural and psychological blow. The event has come to symbolize the broader humiliation and exploitation that China endured during the 19th century, as Western powers exerted military and economic dominance over the Qing Dynasty. The looting of Yuanmingyuan became a lasting reminder of China’s vulnerability during its “century of humiliation,” a period marked by foreign interventions, unequal treaties, and the extraction of Chinese wealth and heritage by imperial powers. Efforts to recover the looted artefacts have been ongoing, with China making repeated diplomatic appeals for the return of treasures taken from the palace. Some items have been returned in recent years, often through private donations or as part of efforts to improve cultural diplomacy. However, many artefacts remain in European museums, where their presence continues to spark debates about the legacy of colonialism and the ethics of displaying looted cultural heritage. These artefacts, often displayed without acknowledging their violent acquisition, raise questions about the role of museums in perpetuating colonial narratives and the importance of repatriating culturally significant objects to their countries of origin. The looting of the Old Summer Palace also serves as a broader case study in the history of cultural restitution. As global awareness of the colonial origins of many museum collections grows, institutions are increasingly being pressured to reconsider the ethical implications of holding objects obtained through violence and exploitation. Yuanmingyuan’s treasures, which include some of the finest examples of Qing Dynasty art and craftsmanship, are at the heart of these debates. For China, reclaiming these artefacts is not only about restoring its material heritage but also about addressing the historical wrongs inflicted during an era of foreign domination. The ruins of the Old Summer Palace, which remain a national monument in China today, serve as a reminder of the country’s cultural losses during the 19th century. The site is visited by thousands of Chinese citizens each year, who come to reflect on this painful chapter in their history. The continued presence of Yuanmingyuan’s treasures in European institutions, however, remains a source of tension, as China’s efforts to recover its looted heritage are emblematic of its broader quest to assert its cultural sovereignty and redress the injustices of the past.

expert.long: The looting and destruction of the Old Summer Palace (Yuanmingyuan) during the Second Opium War in 1860 stands as one of the most egregious examples of cultural devastation perpetrated by colonial powers in the 19th century. Built as a grand imperial retreat for the Qing Dynasty, the Old Summer Palace was renowned for its architectural beauty and artistic significance, embodying a harmonious blend of traditional Chinese aesthetics and Western influences. Its vast landscape was designed to reflect philosophical ideals, featuring exquisite gardens, lakes, and buildings that showcased the artistry of the period. This complex served as more than just a royal residence; it was a symbol of cultural sophistication and a center for intellectual exchange. The British and French forces, motivated by revenge for the imprisonment of their envoys, launched a punitive expedition against the palace. In an act that signified the intersection of military might and cultural exploitation, they looted an extensive collection of priceless artifacts, including intricate bronzes, delicate ceramics, and historical manuscripts. The soldiers not only stripped the palace of its treasures but also set fire to its buildings, annihilating centuries of artistic and historical achievement. The destruction of Yuanmingyuan, accompanied by the theft of its artifacts, marked a significant moment in China’s history, resonating deeply within its national consciousness as a symbol of humiliation and loss. The dispersal of the Old Summer Palace's treasures to European museums and private collections has fueled ongoing debates about cultural restitution and the moral obligations of institutions that house these artefacts. Many of these items are not simply relics of art; they hold profound cultural and spiritual significance for the Chinese people, representing a tangible connection to their past and a reflection of their identity. The continued presence of these artefacts abroad raises critical questions about the legacy of colonialism and the ethics of cultural ownership.  In recent years, calls for the repatriation of the Old Summer Palace artefacts have intensified, fueled by a growing awareness of the historical injustices inflicted upon non-Western nations. Chinese officials and cultural advocates argue that the return of these treasures is essential for healing the wounds of colonialism and restoring cultural integrity. International dialogues surrounding the restitution of such artefacts have become more prominent, as countries grapple with their colonial histories and the implications of cultural theft. The legacy of the Old Summer Palace serves as a powerful reminder of the need for cultural sensitivity and accountability in the context of global heritage preservation. The treasures taken from Yuanmingyuan symbolize the broader patterns of exploitation faced by indigenous cultures during colonial times. For China, the ongoing quest to reclaim its lost heritage represents not only a fight for restitution but also a reaffirmation of its cultural identity and a commitment to honoring its historical legacy. The conversation surrounding the Old Summer Palace and its artefacts invites reflection on the intricate relationships between art, history, and the enduring impact of colonialism, emphasizing the importance of understanding and respecting cultural narratives across the globe.

maps.caption-2: Then: Kamay (Botany Bay), Gweagal country, Australia - Now: London, UK

fun.short: In April 1770 Captain James Cook's ship landed at Kamay (Botany Bay) in Australia. Two Gweagal men told them to go away, the sailors fired, and one man dropped his bark shield. Fun fact: nobody is completely sure the shield in the British Museum is that same shield!
fun.medium: On 29 April 1770 the British ship Endeavour, led by James Cook, sailed into a wide bay on the east coast of Australia. The Gweagal people, who had lived there for thousands of years, called it Kamay. When the sailors rowed to the beach, two Gweagal men stood up to stop them, throwing stones and spears. Cook fired his musket, and one man was hit by small shot in the legs. He ran away, leaving behind a shield made from the bark of a tree. The sailors took the shield and dozens of spears. Fun fact: for years people believed the bark shield in the British Museum was that very shield, but recent research suggests it may come from somewhere else!
fun.long:
Aboriginal people have lived in Australia for more than 60,000 years, making theirs the oldest living cultures in the world. On the coast where the city of Sydney now stands lived the Gweagal, a clan of the Dharawal people, around a bay called Kamay.

On 29 April 1770 a strange ship appeared: the Endeavour, commanded by the British naval officer James Cook, on a voyage of exploration in the Pacific. Cook, the botanist Joseph Banks and some sailors rowed towards the beach. Two Gweagal men came forward, shouting and waving their spears, clearly telling the strangers to leave.

Cook fired his musket, first over their heads and then with small shot. One man was hit in the legs. He ran to fetch a shield made from tree bark, and the men threw spears before retreating. When the sailors landed, they found the Gweagal houses empty, and they took away about forty spears and a shield.

Because of all the plants Banks collected there, Cook named the place Botany Bay. Eighteen years later, in 1788, the British returned to set up a colony nearby, which changed life for Aboriginal people forever.

The British Museum has a bark shield with a hole in it, long said to be the shield from Kamay. In 2018 historians who studied it closely reported that the wood may come from further north, and that the hole might not come from a musket ball. Fun fact: four spears from the same landing were kept at the University of Cambridge, and in 2024 Trinity College gave them back to the Aboriginal community of La Perouse, on the shores of Kamay.

basic.short: The Gweagal Shield in the British Museum has long been identified as the bark shield taken at Kamay (Botany Bay) in April 1770, during the first encounter between James Cook's crew and Aboriginal people. The identification is debated; the Gweagal descendant Rodney Kelly has asked for its return.
basic.medium: On 29 April 1770 James Cook's Endeavour anchored in Kamay (Botany Bay). As a landing party approached, two Gweagal men opposed them; Cook fired shots, wounding one, and the crew took a bark shield and some forty spears from the camp. The British Museum holds a bark shield with a small hole, catalogued since the nineteenth century as the one taken at that landing, and displayed in Australia in 2015–2016. Research published in 2018 by Nicholas Thomas, Maria Nugent and others questioned this identification, arguing that the wood came from a red mangrove found further north and that the hole was not made by shot. Rodney Kelly, who identifies as a descendant of the Gweagal warrior Cooman, has campaigned since 2016 for its return. Four spears taken at the same landing, held at Cambridge, were returned to the La Perouse community in 2024.
basic.long:
Kamay, now Botany Bay, lies on the southern edge of modern Sydney. Its shores were the country of the Gweagal, a clan of the Dharawal people. On 29 April 1770 the Endeavour, commanded by James Cook, anchored in the bay during a British naval and scientific voyage. It was the first recorded encounter between Europeans and Aboriginal people on the east coast of Australia.

When a landing party approached the beach, two Gweagal men opposed them. Cook fired several musket shots, the second with small shot that wounded one of the men, who retreated and returned with a bark shield. After an exchange of stones and spears, the men withdrew. The landing party found a few bark huts, left beads and cloth as gifts and took about forty spears. The shield was also taken on board.

The landing at Kamay became a founding moment in the British narrative of Australia's colonisation, which began with the arrival of the First Fleet at Botany Bay in 1788 and continued with the dispossession of Aboriginal peoples across the continent.

The British Museum holds a bark shield with a small hole near its centre, catalogued as the shield taken at Kamay. It was lent to the National Museum of Australia for the exhibition 'Encounters' in 2015–2016. Research by Nicholas Thomas, Maria Nugent and their colleagues, published in 2018, argued that it was probably not the same shield, because its wood appears to be red mangrove, not found at Botany Bay, and the hole does not match musket shot.

Rodney Kelly, a Gweagal descendant, has campaigned since 2016 for its return. The British Museum holds that it cannot give it up under the British Museum Act 1963. Four spears from the same landing, held by Trinity College, Cambridge, were returned to the La Perouse Aboriginal community in April 2024, after Trinity College agreed in 2023.

expert.short: Catalogued as the shield dropped by a Gweagal man at Kamay in April 1770, the British Museum's bark shield condenses the colonial symbolism of the first landing, though its provenance was challenged in 2018. Its contested identity has not settled the claims of Gweagal descendants.
expert.medium: The encounter at Kamay on 29 April 1770, recorded in the journals of Cook and Banks, occupies a foundational place in Australian settler narrative and in Aboriginal accounts of invasion. The removal of a shield and some forty spears was minor in scale but symbolically charged. The British Museum's bark shield was associated with the landing on the basis of nineteenth-century documentation and gained iconic status during its loan to the National Museum of Australia in 2015–2016. Research led by Nicholas Thomas and Maria Nugent (2018) argued, on the basis of wood identification and the character of the hole, that the attribution is unlikely. The claim by Rodney Kelly, representing descendants of the Gweagal warrior, rests less on precise provenance than on the shield's standing as a symbol of first resistance. Trinity College, Cambridge's return of four spears in 2024 shows the difference that institutional frameworks make.
expert.long:
The encounter at Kamay on 29 April 1770 is documented in the journals of James Cook, Joseph Banks and other members of the Endeavour's company. As the landing party approached, two Gweagal men opposed them. Cook fired warning shots and then small shot, wounding one, who fetched a bark shield; spears and stones were thrown before the men withdrew. The landing party entered the camp, left beads and cloth and removed some forty spears. The episode, which Cook recorded with some self-justification, has been read in Aboriginal historiography as the first act of armed resistance to the British and in settler narrative as the prelude to the colonisation that began at Botany Bay with the First Fleet in 1788.

The British Museum's bark shield has been associated with the landing on the basis of documentation linking it to Cook's voyage, and its hole was interpreted as the mark of the shot. The shield acquired iconic status when it was lent to the National Museum of Australia for the exhibition 'Encounters' in 2015–2016, which also highlighted Aboriginal perspectives on colonial collecting.

In 2018 Nicholas Thomas, Maria Nugent and colleagues published research arguing that the attribution is unlikely. Wood analysis suggested red mangrove, a species not found at Botany Bay but common further north, and the hole appeared to be a deliberate feature rather than a projectile wound. The British Museum has acknowledged the uncertainty while maintaining the shield's association with the Endeavour voyage.

The Gweagal claim, advanced most prominently by Rodney Kelly since 2016, has continued regardless. Kelly, who identifies as a descendant of the Gweagal warrior Cooman, has argued that the shield symbolises the resistance of his ancestors and the violence of the encounter, and that uncertainties of provenance, themselves a consequence of colonial collecting practices, should not defeat the claim. The British Museum has declined to return it, citing the British Museum Act 1963.

The contrast with the Cambridge spears is instructive. Four spears from the landing, held by the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology on behalf of Trinity College, were returned to the La Perouse Aboriginal community in April 2024, following a decision of 2023 and a decade of dialogue. Unlike the British Museum, Trinity College was not bound by statute, a difference that underlines how the fate of objects from the same event can diverge according to institutional law. The case also illustrates how the meaning of an object in restitution debates can rest as much on its symbolic role as on the precision of its provenance.

maps.caption-2: Then: Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi (USA) - Now: Honolulu, Hawaiʻi (returned 2016, permanently 2020)

fun.short: This bright red and yellow feather cloak and helmet belonged to Kalaniʻōpuʻu, the high chief of Hawaiʻi Island. He gave them to Captain Cook in 1779. Fun fact: after more than 200 years abroad, they came home to Hawaiʻi in 2016!
fun.medium: In January 1779 the British ships of Captain James Cook sailed into Kealakekua Bay, on the island of Hawaiʻi. The high chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu came out to meet Cook and, as a sign of honour, placed his own feather cloak, the ʻahu ʻula, on Cook's shoulders and his feather helmet, the mahiole, on his head. The cloak shines red and yellow because it is covered in tiny feathers from forest birds, tied one bunch at a time onto a net of plant fibre. A few weeks later, things went badly wrong: Cook was killed at the same bay in February 1779. The cloak and helmet travelled to England, and in 1912 they were given to a museum in New Zealand. Fun fact: in 2016 they flew back to Hawaiʻi, and in 2020 their return became permanent!
fun.long:
For Native Hawaiians, feathers were one of the most precious materials in the world. Red and yellow feathers came from small forest birds, such as the red ʻiʻiwi and the black and yellow ʻōʻō, caught by expert bird catchers. The feathers were tied in tiny bunches onto a fine net made from the fibres of the olonā plant, row after row, to make cloaks and helmets. Only the highest chiefs, the aliʻi, could wear them, and they were believed to carry the chief's mana, their spiritual power.

In January 1779 two British ships commanded by James Cook arrived at Kealakekua Bay, on the west coast of the island of Hawaiʻi. It was the season of the Makahiki, a festival for the god Lono. Kalaniʻōpuʻu, the aliʻi nui, the supreme chief of the island, came to meet Cook in a grand procession of canoes. He took off his own feather cloak and helmet and placed them on Cook, a great honour and a sign of an alliance.

But the relationship soured. After the ships left and came back for repairs, there were quarrels over stolen boats, and on 14 February 1779 Cook was killed in a fight on the shore of the same bay.

The cloak and helmet sailed to England with the rest of the expedition. They passed through several collections until, in 1912, Lord St Oswald gave them to the Dominion Museum in New Zealand, today Te Papa Tongarewa in Wellington.

Fun fact: in 2016, after 237 years, they returned to Hawaiʻi on a long-term loan, welcomed with chants and ceremonies, and in 2020 Te Papa made the return permanent. They are now cared for by Bishop Museum in Honolulu.

basic.short: The feather cloak (ʻahu ʻula) and helmet (mahiole) of Kalaniʻōpuʻu were given to James Cook at Kealakekua Bay in 1779. Held in New Zealand from 1912, they returned to Hawaiʻi in 2016 and permanently in 2020, and are cared for by Bishop Museum.
basic.medium: The ʻahu ʻula and mahiole of Kalaniʻōpuʻu are masterpieces of Hawaiian featherwork. The cloak is made of red and yellow feathers from forest birds tied onto a netting of olonā fibre; the helmet has a woven frame of ʻieʻie aerial roots covered with feathers. Such regalia were reserved for the aliʻi, the chiefly class, and embodied their mana and genealogy. In January 1779 Kalaniʻōpuʻu, aliʻi nui of Hawaiʻi Island, presented them to James Cook at Kealakekua Bay. After Cook's death there in February 1779, the pieces were taken to England and later passed into private hands. In 1912 Lord St Oswald gave them to the Dominion Museum in Wellington. In 2016 Te Papa, Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs agreed to return them to Hawaiʻi on a long-term loan, and in 2020 their return was made permanent.
basic.long:
Hawaiian featherwork was among the most valued arts of Polynesia. Feathers of the red ʻiʻiwi, the yellow-tufted ʻōʻō and other forest birds were collected by specialist bird catchers and tied in small bundles onto a net of olonā fibre, producing cloaks of brilliant colour. Helmets, or mahiole, were built on a frame of woven ʻieʻie aerial roots. Feather cloaks were worn only by high-ranking aliʻi and were associated with their mana and their descent from the gods.

In January 1779, during the Makahiki season dedicated to the god Lono, James Cook's ships Resolution and Discovery anchored in Kealakekua Bay. The aliʻi nui of Hawaiʻi Island, Kalaniʻōpuʻu, welcomed Cook with ceremony and placed his own ʻahu ʻula and mahiole on him, a gesture that established a relationship of honour and alliance between the chief and the foreign captain.

Relations deteriorated when the ships returned for repairs in February. On 14 February 1779, during an attempt to take Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage after the theft of a boat, Cook and several of his men were killed.

The cloak and helmet travelled to England with the expedition. They passed through the hands of collectors and were shown in William Bullock's museum in London; when Bullock sold his collection in 1819, they were bought by Charles Winn, grandfather of Lord St Oswald. In 1912 Lord St Oswald gave them to the Dominion Museum, now Te Papa Tongarewa, in Wellington.

In 2016, following discussions between Te Papa, Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, the cloak and helmet returned to Hawaiʻi on a long-term loan and were welcomed in ceremonies at Honolulu. In 2020 the arrangement became permanent. They are now held at Bishop Museum on behalf of the people of Hawaiʻi.

expert.short: Presented by Kalaniʻōpuʻu to James Cook in 1779, the ʻahu ʻula and mahiole were a diplomatic gift rather than loot, yet their subsequent trajectory through British collections to Wellington exemplifies the dislocation of sacred regalia. Their return in 2016, made permanent in 2020, resulted from inter-Indigenous and institutional cooperation.
expert.medium: The ʻahu ʻula and mahiole of Kalaniʻōpuʻu are among the finest surviving examples of Hawaiian featherwork, whose production involved specialised bird catchers (kia manu) and the enormous labour of tying feather bundles onto olonā netting. As regalia of the aliʻi, they embodied genealogical rank and mana, and their bestowal on Cook at Kealakekua in January 1779 enacted a ritualised relationship whose meaning is debated, notably in the controversy between Marshall Sahlins and Gananath Obeyesekere over Cook's reception as Lono. After Cook's death, the regalia entered the circuits of British curiosity collecting, including William Bullock's London museum, whose sale in 1819 brought them to Charles Winn, before his grandson Lord St Oswald donated them to the Dominion Museum in 1912. Their return in 2016 on long-term loan, made permanent in 2020, was negotiated between Te Papa, Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, and framed by Māori and Hawaiian protocols of kinship, offering a model of restitution outside the framework of the former colonial power.
expert.long:
The ʻahu ʻula and mahiole of Kalaniʻōpuʻu belong to the most prestigious category of Hawaiian material culture. Featherwork required specialised bird catchers, the kia manu, who captured forest birds such as the ʻiʻiwi, ʻōʻō and mamo, and the labour of skilled makers who tied tens of thousands of small feather bundles onto netting of olonā fibre. Cloaks and helmets were worn by aliʻi in battle and ceremony, and embodied their genealogical rank, their mana and their relationship with the gods. Their colours, red and yellow, were sacred.

Kalaniʻōpuʻu, aliʻi nui of Hawaiʻi Island, bestowed his regalia on James Cook at Kealakekua Bay in January 1779, during the Makahiki season associated with Lono. The meaning of this reception has been the subject of a famous controversy. Marshall Sahlins argued that Cook was received as a manifestation of Lono, while Gananath Obeyesekere criticised this view as a European myth projected onto Hawaiians. Whatever the interpretation, the gift was an act of chiefly diplomacy, establishing a relationship that Hawaiians understood in their own terms.

Cook's death on 14 February 1779, during an attempt to take Kalaniʻōpuʻu hostage, transformed the context of the gift. The regalia were taken to England with the expedition's collections and entered the circuits of curiosity collecting. They were exhibited in William Bullock's museum in London and, at the sale of his collection in 1819, bought by Charles Winn, whose grandson Lord St Oswald in 1912 donated them to the Dominion Museum in Wellington, the predecessor of Te Papa Tongarewa.

The case differs from those of looted objects: the regalia were given, not seized. Yet the gift was made to Cook as a person within a Hawaiian relationship, and its passage into British commerce and then to a New Zealand museum detached it from that relationship. Their return was negotiated not with Britain but between Te Papa, Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs. In 2016 they returned on a ten-year loan, received with ceremonies that emphasised the kinship between Māori and Hawaiians as Polynesian peoples, and in 2020 Te Papa agreed to make the return permanent.

The case thus offers a model of restitution between institutions of settler states, grounded in Indigenous protocols rather than in a reckoning with the former imperial power. It also shows that the return of gifted objects can be justified by the recognition that their meaning belongs to the community that made them, not to the circuits through which they later passed.

The tiger’s fierce stance and the soldier’s helpless position highlight the bravery and resistance of the Indian people. Today, Tipu Sultan’s Tiger is displayed in a British museum, where it continues to amaze visitors with its lifelike sounds and movements. maps.caption-2: Then: Kumbo (Nso' kingdom), Cameroon - Now: Berlin, Germany (return agreed 2022, pending)

fun.short: Ngonnso' is a carved figure of the woman who founded the Nso' kingdom in Cameroon, and the Nso' people call her their mother. A German officer took her to Berlin in 1902. Fun fact: in 2022 Berlin finally agreed to send her home.
fun.medium: A long time ago, a princess called Ngonnso' left her home and founded a new kingdom in the green hills of what is now Cameroon. Her people, the Nso', still honour her as their mother, and a carved wooden figure of her was kept by the royal family as a sacred object. In 1902, when Germany ruled Cameroon as a colony, German troops fought the Nso', and an officer called Kurt von Pavel took the figure. In 1903 he gave it to the ethnological museum in Berlin. For more than a hundred years the Nso' asked for her back. Fun fact: a young Nso' woman, Sylvie Njobati, started an online campaign with the hashtag #BringBackNgonnso, and in 2022 the German museums agreed to return her!
fun.long:
The Nso' kingdom lies in the grassy highlands of north-western Cameroon. Its story begins with a woman. According to Nso' history, Ngonnso', a princess, left her homeland with her followers, perhaps in the 1300s or 1400s, and founded a new kingdom. The Nso' see her not as a legend but as their ancestor and mother, and she is at the heart of their identity.

The kingdom kept a carved wooden figure representing Ngonnso'. For the Nso' she is not a work of art to look at, but a sacred being, part of the family of the Fon, their king.

In the late 1800s Germany made Cameroon a colony. German troops pushed into the highlands to force the kingdoms there to accept German rule. In 1902 they fought the Nso', and the German officer Kurt von Pavel took the figure of Ngonnso'. The next year he gave her to the Royal Museum of Ethnology in Berlin, where she was stored with thousands of other objects from Africa.

The Nso' never forgot her. They say that many of their troubles began when she was taken. In the 2010s a young Nso' woman, Sylvie Njobati, started a campaign called #BringBackNgonnso, using social media, letters and visits to Berlin.

In June 2022 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which runs the Berlin museums, agreed to return Ngonnso'. But her journey home has been delayed, because the region where the Nso' live is affected by a violent conflict. Fun fact: in Berlin, Nso' visitors have been able to meet her and perform ceremonies for her, as if visiting a relative.

basic.short: Ngonnso', a figure representing the founding mother of the Nso' kingdom in Cameroon, was taken by the German officer Kurt von Pavel in 1902 and given to Berlin in 1903. The Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation agreed to return her in 2022.

For the Nso' she is a sacred ancestor, whose figure was kept within the royal compound of the Fon at Kumbo. During the German colonial conquest of the Cameroon Grassfields, the officer Kurt von Pavel led a military campaign against the Nso' in 1902 and took the figure; in 1903 he donated it to the Royal Museum of Ethnology in Berlin. The Nso' asked for her return for decades, and from 2019 the activist Sylvie Njobati led the campaign #BringBackNgonnso. In June 2022 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation authorised her return, but insecurity in Cameroon's Anglophone regions has so far delayed the transfer.
basic.long:
The kingdom of Nso' is one of the largest of the Bamenda Grassfields, a region of high plateaus and volcanic hills in the North-West Region of Cameroon. Its capital is Kumbo, seat of the Fon, the kingdom's ruler. According to Nso' tradition, the kingdom was founded by Ngonnso', a princess who left the kingdom of Rifum with a group of followers; her name, meaning 'mother of Nso'', gave the kingdom its name.

A wooden figure of Ngonnso' was kept in the royal compound. For the Nso' she is not simply a sculpture but an embodiment of their founder, a sacred being tied to the well-being of the community.

Germany claimed Cameroon as a colony in 1884 and in the following decades extended its control into the interior. In the Grassfields, military expeditions forced local kingdoms to submit. In 1902 the officer Kurt von Pavel led a campaign against the Nso', during which the figure was taken. In 1903 he gave it to the Royal Museum of Ethnology in Berlin.

In Berlin, Ngonnso' became one of thousands of objects from Cameroon, much of it acquired through colonial violence. The Nso' continued to ask for her return, and in the 2010s the Nso' activist Sylvie Njobati launched the campaign #BringBackNgonnso, working with the Fon and with German partners.

In June 2022 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation's board authorised the return of Ngonnso' to Cameroon. By 2025, however, she was still in Berlin, because the conflict in Cameroon's Anglophone regions, including the area around Kumbo, made the transfer unsafe. Nso' delegations have visited her in Berlin in the meantime.

expert.short: Seized during Kurt von Pavel's punitive campaign against Nso' in 1902 and donated to Berlin in 1903, Ngonnso' is a sacred founding ancestor rather than an artwork for the Nso'. Her return, authorised by the SPK in 2022, has been delayed by the Anglophone crisis in Cameroon.
expert.medium: Ngonnso' is a wooden figure embodying the eponymous founder of the Nso' kingdom in the Bamenda Grassfields of Cameroon, whose oral history traces its origins to her migration from Rifum. Kept within the royal compound at Kumbo, she was an ancestral presence linked to the legitimacy of the Fon and the welfare of the kingdom. Her removal in 1902 occurred during the German military conquest of the Grassfields, in a campaign led by Kurt von Pavel, and her donation to the Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde in 1903 placed her within the vast Cameroon collections of Berlin, among the largest outside Africa. The campaign #BringBackNgonnso, led by Sylvie Njobati in cooperation with the Nso' palace, mobilised digital activism and diplomatic engagement. In June 2022 the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz authorised her return; the transfer has been postponed because of the armed conflict in Cameroon's Anglophone North-West and South-West regions.
expert.long:
Ngonnso' is a carved wooden figure representing the founder of the kingdom of Nso', the largest polity of the Bamenda Grassfields in the North-West Region of Cameroon. According to Nso' oral history, Ngonnso', a princess of the Tikar-related dynasty of Rifum, migrated with her followers and founded the kingdom, which bears her name. The figure was kept within the palace at Kumbo, where it functioned as an ancestral presence connected to the legitimacy of the Fon and to the fertility and welfare of the kingdom. For the Nso', she is therefore not an ethnographic specimen but a relative, a point emphasised in their claims.

Germany declared a protectorate over the Cameroon coast in 1884 and extended its control into the interior through a series of military campaigns. In the Grassfields, where powerful kingdoms resisted, the colonial army conducted punitive expeditions that combined violence with the seizure of prestige objects. In 1902 the officer Kurt von Pavel led a campaign against Nso', in the course of which the figure was taken. In 1903 he donated it to the Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde in Berlin, contributing to a Cameroon collection that, largely assembled during the colonial period by officers, traders and missionaries, is among the largest in the world.

The Nso' continued to ask for her return, attributing misfortunes suffered by the community to her absence. From 2019 the activist Sylvie Njobati, founder of the organisation Sysy House of Fame, led the campaign #BringBackNgonnso, which used social media, petitions and meetings with German institutions, in cooperation with the Nso' palace and Cameroonian authorities. The campaign coincided with Germany's broader reassessment of its colonial collections after the debates over the Humboldt Forum and the return of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria.

In June 2022 the board of the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz authorised the return of Ngonnso' to Cameroon. Her transfer, however, was postponed because of the armed conflict in Cameroon's Anglophone regions, which has affected the area around Kumbo since 2017. Nso' delegations have visited her in Berlin to perform rites, and the delay has highlighted the practical and political complexities of restitution: agreement in principle does not guarantee return when the conditions for safe reception are contested. Her case also underlines the distinction between return to a state and return to a community, since the Nso' palace, not only the Cameroonian government, is a key party to the process.

This royal throne was taken by French soldiers after the French-Dahomey wars of the 1890s and spent more than a century in Paris, until France gave it back to Benin in 2021. fun.long: The Achaemenid Reliefs are breathtaking stone carvings from the Persian Empire, crafted over 2,500 years ago! These intricate artworks not only showcase the remarkable talent of ancient Persian artisans but also narrate compelling stories about kings, warriors, and the grandeur of one of history’s most influential empires. Originally adorning the ceremonial capital of Persepolis, these reliefs depicted scenes of royal ceremonies, military victories, and tributes from conquered nations, illustrating the immense power and cultural diversity of the Achaemenid dynasty. The Achaemenid Empire, which flourished from the 6th to the 4th century BCE, was a beacon of cultural exchange, uniting a vast expanse of territory that included modern-day Iran, Iraq, parts of Turkey, Egypt, and beyond. The reliefs were not merely decorative; they were meant to convey the glory of the king and the divine right of the Achaemenids to rule over such a diverse populace. These carvings reflect the sophisticated artistry and engineering of their time, with intricate details showcasing the clothing, hairstyles, and weapons of various peoples, thus providing a window into the ancient world. However, during the 19th century, many of these priceless works were taken by European explorers and archaeologists who sought to uncover and collect the remnants of the ancient world. These reliefs are now displayed in various museums across Europe, far removed from their original context and significance. Fun fact: The Persian Empire was so vast that it stretched across three continents, encompassing diverse cultures and traditions, making it one of the largest empires in history! The journey of the Achaemenid Reliefs highlights the lasting impact of colonial looting on cultural heritage, reminding us that even great civilizations can fall victim to the whims of exploration and extraction. The removal of these artworks not only severed a critical link to Persia's historical narrative but also serves as a stark reminder of the broader patterns of cultural appropriation and imperial exploitation. Today, these reliefs symbolize not only the artistry of the Achaemenid period but also the ongoing struggles for the restitution of cultural heritage to its rightful home. Many scholars and cultural activists are advocating for the return of such artifacts, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and honoring the histories they represent. The discourse surrounding these reliefs has evolved to include questions about national identity, cultural ownership, and the ethical responsibilities of modern institutions in addressing historical injustices.

maps.caption-2: Then: Beijing Ancient Observatory (Qing China), China - Now: Beijing, China (returned 1902 and 1921)

fun.short: In 1900, eight foreign armies marched into Beijing and took many treasures, including the emperor's giant bronze star-measuring machines! Fun fact: they came back after a peace treaty told Germany to return them.
fun.medium: In 1900 people in northern China rose up against foreign powers in what is called the Boxer Rebellion. To stop it, eight countries sent their armies into Beijing. When they won, their soldiers looted the city, grabbing treasures from palaces and temples. French and German soldiers even took the enormous bronze instruments that the emperor's astronomers used to watch the stars! Some went to the French embassy, others all the way to a garden in Potsdam, Germany. France returned its instruments in 1902, and Germany sent the rest back in 1921. Fun fact: taking them back to Beijing cost Germany a lot of money, because the treaty said Germany had to pay for everything!
fun.long:
At the end of the 1800s, powerful countries like Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Japan were competing for control over China. They forced China to open its ports, give up land and pay money. Many Chinese people were angry, and in 1899 and 1900 a movement known as the Boxers attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians in the north of the country.

In the summer of 1900 the Boxers besieged the foreign embassies in Beijing. Eight countries sent an army together, called the Eight-Nation Alliance, to break the siege. When the soldiers entered Beijing, they did not only rescue the embassies: they also looted the city, taking silk, porcelain, gold and works of art from palaces and temples.

One of the places they visited was the imperial observatory on the city wall. There stood giant bronze instruments, some made in 1673 under a Belgian priest called Ferdinand Verbiest, decorated with dragons and used to follow the stars for the emperor's calendar. French and German soldiers decided to take them as trophies. Some went to the French embassy, and the Germans shipped theirs all the way to Potsdam and put them in a palace garden.

Not everyone in Europe thought this was right, and France gave its instruments back in 1902. Germany kept its share until it lost the First World War. The peace treaty signed in 1919 said that Germany had to return all the astronomical instruments its troops had taken from China, and pay for the trip. So in 1921 they came back to Beijing.

Fun fact: China refused to sign that same peace treaty, because it gave another part of China, Shandong, to Japan. So the treaty that brought the instruments home also took something else away!

basic.short: When the Eight-Nation Alliance occupied Beijing in 1900 to crush the Boxer Rebellion, French and German troops seized the bronze instruments of the imperial observatory. France returned them in 1902, and Germany in 1921 under the Treaty of Versailles.
basic.medium: By 1900 China had been forced by a series of wars and 'unequal treaties' to open its ports and grant privileges to foreign powers. The Boxer movement, which attacked foreigners and Chinese Christians, besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in the summer of that year. An international force of eight nations relieved the siege and occupied the capital, where looting by soldiers and civilians was widespread. French and German troops took the bronze instruments of the imperial observatory, several of them cast in 1673 under the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest, as trophies. The French share was returned in 1902 after criticism of the seizure. The German share, displayed at Potsdam, came back in 1921 because Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles obliged defeated Germany to return all the astronomical instruments its troops had carried away from China and to pay the costs.
basic.long:
The looting of the Beijing observatory belongs to the history of foreign intervention in China. After the Opium Wars of the nineteenth century, China had been compelled to sign 'unequal treaties' that opened ports, granted foreigners legal privileges and ceded territory. At the end of the century the European powers and Japan were competing for spheres of influence, and resentment against them grew.

In 1899–1900 the Boxer movement attacked missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreign interests in northern China, and in June 1900 laid siege to the foreign legations in Beijing. An expedition of eight nations, Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Japan, the United States, Italy and Austria-Hungary, relieved the siege in August and occupied the capital. The occupation was followed by extensive looting of the imperial palaces, temples and government buildings.

The observatory on the city wall held some of the most remarkable objects of the Qing court: bronze instruments cast in 1673 under the direction of the Flemish Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest, and later eighteenth-century additions. French and German troops divided them between them. The French took their share to the legation in Beijing, while the Germans shipped theirs to Potsdam, where they were displayed in the grounds of the royal palaces as a trophy of the campaign.

The seizure was criticised even in Europe, and France returned its instruments in 1902. Germany's share was restored only after its defeat in the First World War. Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles required Germany to return, within twelve months, all the astronomical instruments that its troops had carried away in 1900–1901, and to pay for dismantling, transport and reinstallation in Peking. The instruments arrived back in 1921.

The episode is one of the first cases in which the return of looted objects was written into an international treaty. Yet the same treaty handed German rights in Shandong to Japan, and China refused to sign it. The return of the instruments was a by-product of great-power politics, not a recognition of Chinese sovereignty over its heritage.

expert.short: Seized by French and German troops during the Allied occupation of Beijing in 1900, the Qing observatory's instruments exemplify the looting that accompanied intervention in China. Their return, in 1902 and under Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles in 1921, reflected shifts in power rather than recognition of Chinese claims.
expert.medium: The removal of the observatory instruments must be read within the semi-colonial order imposed on Qing China after the Opium Wars, in which treaty ports, extraterritoriality and indemnities subordinated Chinese sovereignty to the interests of foreign powers. The Allied occupation of Beijing in August 1900, following the siege of the legations, was marked by systematic looting that contemporaries described as a scramble for spoils, and French and German contingents appropriated the bronze instruments cast under Ferdinand Verbiest in 1673 and their eighteenth-century successors. France returned its share in 1902 under diplomatic and public pressure. The German share, displayed at Potsdam as a trophy of the China expedition, was restored under Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles, one of the earliest restitution clauses in a peace treaty. Its inclusion served Allied interests in penalising Germany; the same treaty transferred German concessions in Shandong to Japan, prompting China's refusal to sign.
expert.long:
The fate of the Beijing observatory instruments illustrates the entanglement of looting, imperial rivalry and diplomacy in late Qing China. Although China was never formally colonised, the treaty system imposed after the Opium Wars, with its treaty ports, extraterritorial jurisdiction, foreign-controlled customs and indemnities, created a semi-colonial condition in which multiple powers competed for concessions and spheres of influence.

The Boxer uprising of 1899–1900 was a violent response to this order. When the Boxers and allied Qing forces besieged the foreign legations in Beijing in June 1900, the powers assembled an expeditionary force that relieved the siege on 14 August and occupied the capital. The occupation was accompanied by looting on a massive scale, in which soldiers, diplomats, missionaries and traders took part; contemporary observers described auctions of loot held within the legations.

The observatory's instruments were among the most conspicuous trophies. Cast in 1673 under the direction of the Jesuit Ferdinand Verbiest, who had secured control of the Bureau of Astronomy for European methods, and supplemented under Qianlong, they embodied the Qing court's appropriation of European science. French and German forces divided them: the French share was moved to the legation, the German share shipped to Potsdam and displayed in the palace grounds as a monument to the East Asian expedition. International criticism led France to return its instruments in 1902.

Germany's retention of its share became part of the post-war settlement. Article 131 of the Treaty of Versailles obliged Germany to restore to China, within twelve months, all astronomical instruments removed by its troops in 1900–1901, and to bear the costs of their dismantling, packing, transport, insurance and reinstallation. Together with provisions on other seized cultural property, it represents an early codification of restitution in international law. The clause, however, served the Allies' punitive agenda towards Germany rather than any principle of Chinese cultural sovereignty. The same treaty transferred Germany's Shandong concessions to Japan, provoking the May Fourth Movement and China's refusal to sign.

The instruments returned to Beijing in 1921 and remain on the observatory platform, now a museum. Their history complicates narratives of restitution as moral progress: return was contingent on the defeat of the holding power and bundled with decisions that violated the claims of the country to which the objects were returned. It thus anticipates a recurring feature of later restitution debates, in which the fate of objects depends on the shifting balance of power between states.
