maps.caption-2: Then: Prague Castle (Kingdom of Bohemia), Czechia - Now: Stockholm, Sweden

fun.short: The Codex Gigas was not taken from a colony but from a European city, Prague, by the Swedish army at the end of a terrible war. Fun fact: Sweden took so many books from other countries in the 1600s that some libraries in Stockholm are still full of them!
fun.medium: Between 1618 and 1648, Central Europe was torn apart by the Thirty Years' War, a war between Catholic and Protestant states and powerful families. Sweden, a Protestant kingdom, became one of the strongest armies in Europe. Its soldiers and officers took rich war booty from the cities they captured, including libraries, paintings and treasures. In July 1648 Swedish troops made a surprise attack on Prague and captured the castle, where the emperor's famous collections were kept. They shipped them to Stockholm for Queen Christina, who loved books and art. Fun fact: the peace treaty signed a few months later did not ask anyone to give back what they had taken, so the Codex Gigas stayed in Sweden!
fun.long:
Not all looting in history happened in far-off colonies. In Europe itself, wars often ended with the winners taking treasures from the losers.

The Thirty Years' War, from 1618 to 1648, began in Prague, when Protestant nobles in Bohemia rebelled against the Catholic Habsburg emperor. It grew into a huge war involving the Holy Roman Empire, Spain, France, Denmark and Sweden. Armies marched back and forth across Central Europe, and millions of people died from fighting, hunger and disease.

Sweden, led by King Gustavus Adolphus and later by Queen Christina's government, joined the war in 1630 and became one of Europe's great powers. Swedish armies captured many cities, and they often took libraries and treasures as booty. Christina, who became queen as a child, wanted Stockholm to be a great centre of learning, like Paris or Rome.

In July 1648, while diplomats were already negotiating peace, a Swedish army under General Königsmarck made a surprise attack on Prague. They captured Prague Castle, where Emperor Rudolf II's collection of paintings, sculptures, clocks, scientific instruments and books was kept. Everything was packed up and shipped to Sweden, including the Codex Gigas.

In October 1648 the Peace of Westphalia ended the war, but it did not say that looted art had to be returned.

Fun fact: in 2007 the Codex Gigas went back to Prague, but only on loan for a few months. More than 100,000 people came to see it, and then it went home to Stockholm again.

basic.short: The Codex Gigas was taken as war booty by Sweden during the Thirty Years' War, part of a policy of cultural appropriation that enriched Stockholm with collections from Central Europe and Poland. Such early modern spoils have rarely been returned.
basic.medium: The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) made cultural plunder a routine part of warfare in Central Europe. Sweden, which entered the war in 1630 and emerged as a major power, systematically removed libraries and collections from captured cities, encouraged by Queen Christina's ambition to make Stockholm a centre of European culture. The seizure of Rudolf II's collections at Prague Castle in July 1648, including the Codex Gigas, was one of the largest acts of cultural plunder of the war. The Peace of Westphalia did not require the return of booty. In the following decade, during the Swedish invasion of Poland-Lithuania known as the Deluge, Sweden removed further collections, some of which were later returned to Poland under twentieth-century agreements. The Codex Gigas remains in Stockholm, and its loan to Prague in 2007–2008 was presented as an act of cultural cooperation rather than restitution.
basic.long:
The Codex Gigas belongs to a history of cultural plunder within Europe that preceded the colonial looting of later centuries and shaped attitudes towards the spoils of war.

In the Thirty Years' War, armies of all sides seized goods, and libraries and art collections were valuable prizes. Sweden, which entered the war in 1630 under King Gustavus Adolphus, removed libraries from the cities it captured, including Würzburg, Mainz and Olomouc. After the king's death in 1632, the government of the young Queen Christina continued the practice. Christina, who was deeply interested in learning and art, wanted to turn Stockholm into a cultural capital.

The most spectacular seizure came at the end of the war. In July 1648 a Swedish army under Hans Christoph von Königsmarck captured the Lesser Town and Prague Castle by surprise. The collections of Emperor Rudolf II, one of the most famous in Europe, were packed and sent to Sweden. They included paintings by Titian and Arcimboldo, sculptures, scientific instruments and manuscripts, among them the Codex Gigas.

The Peace of Westphalia, signed a few months later, did not require the return of looted art. Christina took many of the paintings with her when she left Sweden and moved to Rome, and they were later dispersed across Europe.

In the 1650s Sweden invaded Poland-Lithuania, an episode known as the Deluge, and removed large quantities of books, archives and artworks. Some of these were returned to Poland in the twentieth century under agreements such as the Treaty of Riga of 1921, but most Swedish war booty remains in Sweden.

The Codex Gigas was lent to Prague in 2007–2008, and the loan was celebrated as a sign of friendship between Sweden and the Czech Republic. It then returned to Stockholm.

expert.short: The Codex Gigas exemplifies the early modern 'right of booty', under which cultural plunder was an accepted prerogative of victors. Its case marks the chronological limit of modern restitution norms, which have not been applied retroactively to pre-modern European spoils.
expert.medium: Early modern law of war, as articulated by Grotius in De iure belli ac pacis (1625), recognised the victor's right to seize enemy property, including movable cultural goods, although Grotius urged moderation towards sacred and artistic objects. Swedish practice in the Thirty Years' War, shaped by Gustavus Adolphus and continued under Christina, transformed this right into a policy of cultural accumulation aimed at elevating Sweden's status within the European republic of letters. The seizure of Rudolf II's Kunstkammer in 1648 was its culmination. Modern restitution norms, from the settlement of 1815 to the Hague Conventions and the 1970 UNESCO Convention, are not retroactive, and the Codex's status as Swedish state property is uncontested in law. Its loan to Prague and the digitisation by the National Library of Sweden represent the modes of engagement available for pre-modern spoils. Comparing it with colonial cases raises the question of where the temporal limit of restitution should lie, and why.
expert.long:
The Codex Gigas illustrates the legal and political status of early modern war booty. In the seventeenth century, the law of war recognised the victor's right to seize enemy property. Hugo Grotius, in De iure belli ac pacis (1625), acknowledged this right while urging restraint towards sacred objects and works of art whose destruction served no military purpose. In practice, cultural plunder was widespread in the Thirty Years' War, and libraries and collections were valued prizes.

Sweden made such seizures a matter of policy. Gustavus Adolphus had libraries removed from captured cities and sent to Uppsala University and Stockholm, and after his death the regency and then Queen Christina continued the practice, seeking to elevate Sweden's standing in the European republic of letters. The capture of Prague Castle in July 1648 by Hans Christoph von Königsmarck, in the final months of the war, allowed the removal of Rudolf II's Kunstkammer, one of the most celebrated collections in Europe. Its paintings, sculptures, instruments and manuscripts, including the Codex Gigas, were shipped to Stockholm. The Peace of Westphalia did not address the return of booty.

The fate of these collections varied. Christina took many paintings with her after her abdication and conversion, and they were dispersed across Europe after her death in Rome in 1689. Manuscripts and books largely remained in Swedish libraries. Swedish removals from Poland-Lithuania in the 1650s were partly reversed by the Treaty of Riga of 1921 and later arrangements, reflecting the specific politics of Polish claims after independence.

Modern restitution norms, beginning with the Allied settlement of 1815 and codified in the Hague Conventions and the 1970 UNESCO Convention, are not retroactive. The Codex Gigas is therefore uncontested Swedish state property, and Czech engagement has taken the form of loans and cooperation, most notably the exhibition at the Clementinum in 2007–2008, and of digital access through the National Library of Sweden's online edition.

Comparison with colonial cases is instructive. Many objects in this collection were removed under rules that the holders regarded as lawful at the time, and their claimants argue that later moral and legal standards should apply. The Codex Gigas marks the point at which such arguments have so far stopped: early modern spoils within Europe are treated as settled history. The case thus raises the question of where the temporal limit of restitution should lie, and whether the distinction between European and colonial spoils rests on principle or on the power of those who make the rules.

maps.caption-2: Then: Temple of Hathor, Dendera, Egypt - Now: Paris, France

fun.short: In 1820 a French collector paid for a team to cut the zodiac out of an Egyptian temple ceiling, using gunpowder! Egypt's ruler at the time allowed it. Fun fact: today Egyptians say that permission was not really theirs to give.
fun.medium: After Napoleon's army left Egypt, Europeans were crazy about Egyptian antiquities. Collectors and consuls competed to ship statues, obelisks and mummies back home. Egypt was ruled by Muhammad Ali, a governor for the Ottoman Empire who wanted friendship and help from European countries, and he often let foreigners take ancient monuments. In 1820 a French collector sent Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain to Dendera. With saws, chisels and gunpowder, he cut the round zodiac out of a temple ceiling and shipped it to France, where the king bought it. Fun fact: in 2022 the Egyptian archaeologist Zahi Hawass started a petition asking for the zodiac, the Rosetta Stone and the bust of Nefertiti to come home.
fun.long:
In the early 1800s, Egypt became a treasure hunt for Europeans. After Napoleon's expedition, books full of drawings of temples made people in Paris and London dream of ancient Egypt, and museums and rich collectors wanted real pieces. French and British consuls paid agents to dig and ship statues, coffins and even whole walls.

Egypt at that time was governed by Muhammad Ali, who ruled for the Ottoman sultan but wanted to modernise the country with European help. Giving antiquities to Europeans was one way to win friends, and he gave out many permits.

One of the most famous objects in Egypt was the round zodiac on a ceiling in the Temple of Hathor at Dendera. In 1820 a French collector, Sébastien Saulnier, sent Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain to fetch it. Lelorrain worked quickly, because he was afraid British agents would stop him. He sawed through the stone and used gunpowder, and in a few weeks the ceiling was out of the temple and on its way down the Nile. In France, King Louis XVIII bought it for a huge sum, 150,000 francs.

Today the zodiac is in the Louvre in Paris, and a plaster copy fills the hole in Dendera. Many Egyptians feel that it was taken unfairly, because the permission came from a ruler who was trying to please foreign powers, not from the Egyptian people. Fun fact: in 2022, 200 years after Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs, the archaeologist Zahi Hawass started a petition asking for the zodiac to come back.

basic.short: The Dendera Zodiac was removed in 1820 by an agent of a French collector, with a permit from Muhammad Ali's government, during the European scramble for Egyptian antiquities. Egypt asks for its return.
basic.medium: In the decades after Napoleon's expedition, European consuls, collectors and dealers competed to acquire Egyptian antiquities for museums in Paris, London and Turin. Egypt was governed by Muhammad Ali, an Ottoman viceroy who sought European support for his reforms and often granted permits to export antiquities. In 1820 the Parisian collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier sent Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain to remove the zodiac from the ceiling of a chapel at Dendera; Lelorrain used saws, chisels and gunpowder and shipped it to France. Louis XVIII bought it in 1821, and it has been in the Louvre since 1922. Egyptian archaeologists, led by Zahi Hawass, argue that a permit issued to please foreign powers does not make the removal legitimate, and in 2022 they included the zodiac in a petition for the return of major antiquities.
basic.long:
The removal of the Dendera Zodiac took place during what historians have called the scramble for Egyptian antiquities. After Napoleon's expedition and the publication of the Description de l'Égypte, ancient Egypt became fashionable in Europe. The French and British consuls in Egypt, Bernardino Drovetti and Henry Salt, employed agents to excavate and export antiquities, which they sold to the Louvre, the British Museum and the museum in Turin.

Egypt was then governed by Muhammad Ali, nominally a viceroy of the Ottoman sultan, who was building a modern army and economy with European experts. Permits to remove antiquities were a way to win the goodwill of European powers, and the local population had no say in them.

The zodiac at Dendera, already famous from Denon's drawings, attracted the Parisian collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier. In 1820 he sent the engineer Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain, who obtained a permit and removed the ceiling with saws, chisels and gunpowder, working quickly to avoid British competition. The relief was taken down the Nile, shipped to Marseille and bought by Louis XVIII for 150,000 francs.

Later in the century, Egypt created an antiquities service under the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette, partly to stop such removals, although it remained under European control until the twentieth century.

Today the zodiac is in the Louvre, and a cast fills its place at Dendera. Egyptian archaeologists, led by Zahi Hawass, have asked for its return, arguing that permits granted by a ruler seeking foreign favour cannot justify the removal of a temple ceiling. The Louvre is bound by the rule that French public collections cannot be given away. A framework law to make restitutions easier passed the French Senate in January 2026, but its effect on objects like the zodiac is still uncertain.

expert.short: The zodiac's removal in 1820 exemplifies the extraction of monuments under Muhammad Ali's permit regime, in which antiquities served as diplomatic currency. Egyptian claims challenge both the legitimacy of that regime and the French principle of inalienability.
expert.medium: The Dendera Zodiac was removed in a period when Egyptian antiquities circulated as diplomatic and commercial currency. Muhammad Ali, pursuing state-building with European expertise, granted firmans to consuls and collectors, while the rivalry of agents such as Drovetti and Salt shaped the formation of the Egyptian collections of the Louvre, the British Museum and Turin. The zodiac's removal by Lelorrain for Saulnier in 1820, with the use of explosives, illustrates the commercial character of this extraction. The Egyptian Antiquities Service, founded in 1858, was itself directed by French scholars until 1952, so that the regulation of antiquities long remained in foreign hands. Contemporary Egyptian claims question the legitimacy of permits granted within this asymmetrical relationship, while France's doctrine of inalienability has so far limited restitution to cases authorised by specific legislation; the framework bill approved by the Senate in January 2026 may change the procedural landscape.
expert.long:
The removal of the Dendera Zodiac must be situated within the political economy of antiquities in early nineteenth-century Egypt. Muhammad Ali, who governed Egypt from 1805 as a nominal viceroy of the Ottoman sultan, pursued an ambitious programme of military and economic modernisation dependent on European expertise and goodwill. Antiquities, which he valued little in themselves, became a form of diplomatic currency: firmans authorising excavation and export were granted to European consuls and their agents, and major monuments were offered as gifts to foreign rulers.

The rivalry between the French consul Bernardino Drovetti and the British consul Henry Salt, each employing agents such as Giovanni Belzoni, turned Egypt into a field of competitive extraction. Their collections, sold to the Louvre, the British Museum and the Museo Egizio in Turin, formed the core of the great European Egyptian collections. Within this market, the zodiac was an exceptional prize. Its removal in 1820 by Jean-Baptiste Lelorrain, commissioned by the Parisian collector Sébastien Louis Saulnier, involved saws, chisels and gunpowder and was conducted with haste to forestall British interference. Its purchase by Louis XVIII for 150,000 francs turned a speculative enterprise into national property.

The institutional response came late and remained in European hands. The Egyptian Antiquities Service, established in 1858 under Auguste Mariette, restricted exports but was directed by French scholars until 1952, and the division of finds between Egypt and foreign excavators continued well into the twentieth century.

Contemporary Egyptian claims therefore question more than the circumstances of a single removal. Zahi Hawass and others argue that permits granted within a relationship of dependency on European powers, without regard for the wishes of the Egyptian population, cannot be treated as a source of legitimate title, and in 2022 included the zodiac in a petition for the return of emblematic objects. On the French side, the principle of the inalienability of public collections has meant that restitutions have required specific laws, such as those for Benin in 2020 and for other objects since. A framework law intended to create a general procedure was passed unanimously by the Senate in January 2026 and was pending before the National Assembly in spring 2026. Whether such a framework would extend to an object removed from a sovereign, if dependent, Ottoman province rather than a French colony remains an open question.

maps.caption-2: Then: Mogao Caves, Dunhuang (Qing China), China - Now: London, UK

fun.short: The Diamond Sutra was not taken by soldiers. An explorer working for British India bought it, together with thousands of manuscripts, from the monk who guarded the caves. Fun fact: he paid only a small donation for one of the greatest libraries ever found.
fun.medium: In the early 1900s explorers from Britain, France, Germany, Russia and Japan raced through Central Asia, along the old Silk Road, looking for ancient ruins and treasures. Some of them worked for governments that wanted to control the region. Aurel Stein was an archaeologist working for British India. When he heard about a hidden library at Dunhuang, he went there in 1907 and met the monk Wang Yuanlu, who was trying to raise money to repair the caves. Stein offered a donation and took away thousands of manuscripts, including the Diamond Sutra, in boxes carried by camels and horses. Fun fact: Stein was knighted in Britain for his expeditions, but in China many people remember him as a thief.
fun.long:
About a hundred years ago, Central Asia was the scene of a "Great Game": Britain, which ruled India, and Russia, which was expanding into Central Asia, competed for influence. At the same time, explorers from many countries travelled along the ancient Silk Road, the network of trade routes that once linked China to the Mediterranean, searching for buried cities and lost manuscripts.

China's last imperial dynasty, the Qing, was weak and had lost wars against foreign powers. It could not easily protect its distant western regions, and foreign expeditions travelled there with little control.

In 1907 Aurel Stein, an archaeologist working for the government of British India, reached Dunhuang. He had heard that a monk, Wang Yuanlu, had found a hidden cave full of manuscripts. Wang was cautious at first, but Stein told him he admired the famous Chinese monk Xuanzang, who had travelled to India, and offered money for the restoration of the caves. In the end Wang let him take thousands of manuscripts and paintings. They were packed in boxes and carried by camels and horses across the desert to India and then shipped to London.

The next year the Frenchman Paul Pelliot, who could read Chinese, came and took many more. Japanese and Russian explorers followed.

Fun fact: today Dunhuang manuscripts are spread around the world, in London, Paris, St Petersburg, Kyoto and Beijing. Many Chinese people see this as a painful loss, while the museums say the manuscripts were bought legally and are now shared with everyone online.

basic.short: Aurel Stein acquired the Diamond Sutra in 1907 during an expedition for British India, part of the competition among foreign powers for Central Asian antiquities. China remembers the dispersal of the Dunhuang manuscripts as a national loss.
basic.medium: The Diamond Sutra left China during a period when foreign expeditions explored the Silk Road regions of western China with little restraint. The weakened Qing state, defeated in the Opium Wars and the Boxer War, exercised limited control over its western frontier, while Britain and Russia competed for influence in Central Asia. Aurel Stein, an archaeologist in the service of British India, acquired thousands of Dunhuang manuscripts from the monk Wang Yuanlu in 1907 in exchange for donations to his restoration work. Paul Pelliot followed in 1908, and Japanese and Russian expeditions later. The British Library considers its collection legally acquired. In China, the episode is remembered as part of the 'century of humiliation'. Instead of restitution, the holding institutions cooperate through the International Dunhuang Project, which has placed the manuscripts online.
basic.long:
The acquisition of the Diamond Sutra was part of a wider scramble for the antiquities of Central Asia in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. As Britain and Russia competed for influence in the region, in what was called the Great Game, archaeological and geographical expeditions also served as instruments of imperial knowledge. Explorers from Britain, France, Germany, Russia, Sweden and Japan crossed the deserts of the Tarim Basin and Gansu, excavating ruined cities and removing manuscripts, murals and sculptures.

China's Qing dynasty, weakened by defeats in the Opium Wars, the Sino-Japanese War and the Boxer War of 1900, exercised limited control over these regions and had no effective laws protecting antiquities.

Aurel Stein, a Hungarian-born scholar working for the government of British India, reached Dunhuang in 1907. Using an interpreter and appealing to the monk's devotion to the pilgrim Xuanzang, he persuaded Wang Yuanlu to part with thousands of manuscripts and paintings in exchange for donations to his restoration of the caves. Stein later wrote openly about the secrecy of the transaction. The collection was shipped to London and divided between the British Museum and the government of India.

Paul Pelliot acquired thousands more in 1908 for France, and further material went to Japan and Russia before the Qing government ordered the rest to be transferred to Beijing in 1910.

In China, the loss of the Dunhuang manuscripts is remembered as part of the 'century of humiliation' by foreign powers, and Stein is widely seen as a plunderer. The British Library maintains that the acquisition was lawful. Since 1994, the International Dunhuang Project has brought together holding institutions, including the Dunhuang Academy in China, to digitise and share the dispersed collections.

expert.short: Stein's acquisition of the Diamond Sutra in 1907 exemplifies the entanglement of archaeology and imperial rivalry in Central Asia. The case turns on consent under asymmetrical conditions, and has been addressed through digital reunification rather than restitution.
expert.medium: The Dunhuang acquisitions belong to the era of competing expeditions in Chinese Central Asia, in which scholarship was entwined with the strategic interests of British India, Russia and Japan and with the weakness of late Qing sovereignty in its western frontier. Stein's 1907 transaction with Wang Yuanlu, framed as a donation to temple restoration, obtained material of immense scholarly value for minimal payment under conditions of secrecy and unequal knowledge, which Stein himself recounted with some candour in Ruins of Desert Cathay. Unlike wartime looting, the case raises the question of whether a sale by a local custodian, in the absence of effective state protection, confers valid title. The British Library maintains that it does. Chinese discourse situates the episode within the 'century of humiliation'. The International Dunhuang Project, launched in 1994, represents a model of digital repatriation that has broadened access while leaving questions of ownership untouched.
expert.long:
The acquisition of the Dunhuang Diamond Sutra must be understood within the imperial geography of Central Asia at the turn of the twentieth century. As the British and Russian empires competed for influence in the region, exploratory missions combined surveying, intelligence and archaeology. Expeditions from Britain, Russia, Germany, France, Sweden and Japan crossed the Tarim Basin and the Hexi Corridor, removing manuscripts, murals and sculptures from sites that had been abandoned for centuries. The late Qing state, weakened by military defeats and indemnities, exercised limited authority in the region and had no legal framework for protecting antiquities until the Republican period.

Aurel Stein's second expedition, undertaken for the government of British India, reached Dunhuang in 1907. His account in Ruins of Desert Cathay describes how, through his secretary Jiang Xiaowan and by invoking the pilgrim Xuanzang, he overcame Wang Yuanlu's hesitation and removed thousands of manuscripts and paintings in exchange for donations towards Wang's restoration of the caves. The transaction was conducted secretly, and the sums involved were minimal in relation to the scholarly value of the material. Paul Pelliot, a sinologist able to select the most important texts, followed in 1908; Ōtani Kōzui's Japanese expeditions and Sergei Oldenburg's Russian expedition acquired more. The Qing authorities ordered the transfer of the remaining manuscripts to Beijing only in 1910, and losses continued during that transfer.

The case differs from wartime looting in that it involved an apparent sale by a local custodian. The question is whether consent obtained under conditions of asymmetrical knowledge, economic need and absent state protection can confer valid title. The British Library, which holds the Stein collection including the Diamond Sutra (Or.8210/P.2), regards the acquisition as lawful. In Chinese discourse, by contrast, the dispersal belongs to the 'century of humiliation', and the historian Chen Yinke's phrase describing Dunhuang as a 'history of sorrow' for Chinese scholarship has become emblematic.

Instead of restitution, the holding institutions have pursued digital reunification. The International Dunhuang Project, founded in 1994 at the British Library, brings together partners in China, France, Russia, Japan, Germany and elsewhere to digitise and catalogue the dispersed corpus. It has transformed scholarly access, but critics note that digital repatriation leaves the physical objects, and the authority to interpret them, in the institutions that acquired them.

maps.caption-2: Then: Ghent, Belgium - Now: Ghent, Belgium (returned 1945)

fun.short: The Ghent Altarpiece shows that European armies looted each other too. The French took it in 1794, and the Nazis in 1942. Fun fact: after the Second World War, special soldiers called the Monuments Men searched for looted art all over Europe!
fun.medium: Looting was not only something that European empires did in faraway colonies. In Europe, too, armies took art from the people they defeated. In 1794 the French Revolutionary army conquered Belgium and took the central panels of the Ghent Altarpiece to Paris. During the Second World War, Nazi Germany looted art on a huge scale from the countries it occupied and from Jewish families it persecuted. Hitler dreamed of building a giant museum in the Austrian city of Linz, and the Ghent Altarpiece was one of the treasures his officials took. Fun fact: at the end of the war, about 350 experts, soldiers and art historians from 13 countries, called the Monuments Men, found and returned hundreds of thousands of looted objects!
fun.long:
When we think about looting, we often think of European empires taking treasures from Africa, Asia or the Americas. But Europeans also looted each other, and the Ghent Altarpiece was a victim several times.

In 1794 the armies of the French Revolution conquered what is now Belgium. French officials selected the finest paintings from churches and palaces and sent them to Paris, saying that masterpieces belonged in the capital of liberty. The central panels of the Ghent Altarpiece went to the Louvre. They came back in 1815, after Napoleon lost at Waterloo.

In the Second World War, Nazi Germany carried out one of the largest art thefts in history. It took artworks from museums and churches in the countries it occupied, and it stole huge numbers of paintings, books and objects from Jewish families, who were persecuted and murdered in the Holocaust. Hitler planned to build a huge museum, the Führermuseum, in Linz, the Austrian city where he grew up.

In 1942 Nazi officials seized the Ghent Altarpiece in France, where it had been sent for safety. As the war turned against Germany, looted art was hidden in castles and mines, including the salt mine at Altaussee.

In 1945 the Monuments Men, a team of museum experts and soldiers from the Allied countries, found it. They also found Michelangelo's Madonna of Bruges and thousands of other works, and returned them to their countries.

Fun fact: the search for Nazi-looted art is still going on today. Many museums check the history of their paintings to find out whether they were taken from Jewish families, and give them back to their descendants.

basic.short: The Ghent Altarpiece was a target of revolutionary France in 1794 and of Nazi Germany in 1942. Its recovery in 1945 was part of the Allied effort to return art looted in Europe, which shaped modern restitution principles.
basic.medium: The Ghent Altarpiece shows that appropriation of cultural heritage also took place within Europe. The French Revolution and Napoleon turned art confiscation into state policy in the territories they occupied, and the altarpiece's central panels were taken to Paris in 1794. During the Second World War, Nazi Germany looted art systematically from occupied countries and from Jewish owners, through confiscation, forced sales and theft. The altarpiece, seized in 1942, was stored with thousands of other works in the salt mine at Altaussee, intended in part for Hitler's planned museum in Linz. After the war, the Allied Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives programme recovered and returned hundreds of thousands of objects. This experience led to the Hague Convention of 1954 on the protection of cultural property in armed conflict and, later, to the Washington Principles of 1998 on Nazi-looted art.
basic.long:
The history of the Ghent Altarpiece shows that the looting of cultural heritage was not limited to colonial contexts. Europe's wars repeatedly moved art from one country to another.

The French Revolution made the confiscation of art a policy. From 1794, commissioners following the armies selected works of art in Belgium, the Netherlands, the Rhineland and Italy and sent them to Paris. The central panels of the Ghent Altarpiece were among them. In 1815 the victorious Allies required their return, establishing the idea that works of art should not be taken as spoils of war.

In the twentieth century, Nazi Germany carried out looting on an unprecedented scale. Organisations such as the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg confiscated art from museums, churches and libraries in occupied countries, while Jewish collectors were robbed through confiscation, forced sales and theft as part of their persecution. Hitler planned a great museum in Linz, and his agents acquired works for it across Europe.

The Ghent Altarpiece had been sent from Belgium to the Vatican for safety in 1940, but it was stranded at Pau, in southern France. In 1942 German authorities took it to Germany. As Allied bombing increased, looted works were moved to underground stores, including the salt mine at Altaussee, which held thousands of artworks.

In 1945 the Monuments Men secured the mine and returned the altarpiece to Belgium. Their work led to the Hague Convention of 1954 for the protection of cultural property in armed conflict. In 1998 the Washington Principles committed governments to identifying Nazi-looted art and finding just solutions with the heirs of victims. Some campaigners argue that similar principles should apply to objects taken in colonial conquests.

expert.short: The altarpiece's seizures by revolutionary France and Nazi Germany frame the European genealogy of restitution norms, from the 1815 settlement to the Hague Convention of 1954 and the Washington Principles, now invoked as models for colonial restitution.
expert.medium: The Ghent Altarpiece situates the colonial cases of this collection within a European genealogy of restitution. The revolutionary confiscations of the 1790s, legitimised by a discourse of universal patrimony, were reversed in 1815 by an Allied settlement that articulated the attachment of art to its place of origin. Nazi spoliation combined state-organised confiscation in occupied territories, carried out by agencies such as the ERR, with the racially motivated dispossession of Jewish owners, and the Altaussee repository, destined in part for the Führermuseum, epitomised its scale. Allied restitution after 1945, through the MFAA and the principle of return to the country of origin, informed the 1954 Hague Convention and its First Protocol. The Washington Principles of 1998 extended restitution to private claims for Nazi-confiscated art, emphasising 'just and fair solutions' irrespective of limitation periods. Advocates of colonial restitution, including the Sarr–Savoy report of 2018, have invoked these precedents, while critics note the different treatment of European and colonial losses.
expert.long:
The Ghent Altarpiece allows the colonial cases in this collection to be read against a European genealogy of restitution.

The revolutionary confiscations of the 1790s were justified by a discourse of universal patrimony: masterpieces, liberated from the despotism of princes and clergy, were to be gathered in Paris for the benefit of humanity. The panels of the Ghent Altarpiece, removed in 1794, belonged to this project. Their return in 1815, imposed by the Allied powers against French protests, articulated a contrary principle, that works of art are attached to the places and communities for which they were made.

The restoration of the altarpiece's wings under the Treaty of Versailles introduced another logic: restitution as reparation. Article 247 required Germany to deliver the wings, legally acquired by Prussia in 1821, as compensation for the burning of the Louvain University Library in 1914. Restitution here was not the return of looted property but a transfer justified by wartime destruction.

Nazi spoliation combined two forms of appropriation. In occupied territories, agencies such as the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg confiscated public and ecclesiastical collections, while the racial persecution of Jews involved confiscation, forced sales and theft of private property. The Altaussee salt mine, which held thousands of works, some destined for the planned Führermuseum in Linz, epitomised the scale of this system. The altarpiece, seized at Pau in 1942, was among its most prominent treasures.

After 1945, the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives programme and national restitution commissions returned works to their countries of origin, which then undertook restitution to owners. This experience informed the Hague Convention of 1954 and its First Protocol, which prohibited the export of cultural property from occupied territory. In 1998 the Washington Principles committed signatory states to identifying Nazi-confiscated art and seeking just and fair solutions with the heirs of victims, regardless of limitation periods.

Advocates of colonial restitution, notably Felwine Sarr and Bénédicte Savoy in their 2018 report to the French president, have invoked these precedents to argue that objects taken through colonial violence deserve comparable treatment. Critics of the double standard observe that European states developed robust restitution mechanisms for losses suffered in Europe while resisting similar claims from former colonies. The Ghent Altarpiece, repeatedly returned, thus stands as a reference point for asking why restitution has been available to some losses and not others.

maps.caption-2: Then: Kamay (Botany Bay), Gweagal country, Australia - Now: London, UK

fun.short: The shield comes from the very first meeting between Captain Cook's crew and Aboriginal people on Australia's east coast, when two Gweagal men bravely stood up to them. Eighteen years later, Britain started a colony there. Fun fact: many Aboriginal people see the two men as the first defenders of their country.
fun.medium: When Captain Cook sailed along the east coast of Australia in 1770, he claimed the whole coast for Britain, even though hundreds of Aboriginal nations already lived there. At Kamay, two Gweagal men tried to stop his sailors from landing, and one of them was shot and dropped his shield. In 1788 Britain sent the First Fleet, ships full of convicts and soldiers, to start a colony at Sydney. The British treated the land as if it belonged to nobody, and Aboriginal people lost their land, and many their lives, through violence and disease. Fun fact: for Aboriginal people, 26 January, the day the First Fleet raised the British flag at Sydney, is remembered as "Invasion Day" or "Survival Day".
fun.long:
When the British arrived in Australia, they said the land was "terra nullius", a Latin phrase meaning land belonging to no one. But Australia was home to hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations, each with its own language, laws and deep connection to its country.

In 1770 James Cook sailed along the east coast. At Kamay, now Botany Bay, two Gweagal men bravely tried to stop his crew from landing. Cook shot one of them, and the sailors took a shield and spears from their camp. A few months later, on an island in the north, Cook claimed the whole east coast for King George III, without asking anyone who lived there.

In 1788 the First Fleet arrived with about 1,500 people, many of them convicts, to set up a prison colony at Sydney Cove, close to Kamay. The colony spread, and over the next century Aboriginal people across Australia were pushed off their lands, killed in massacres or struck by diseases like smallpox. Many children were later taken from their families.

The objects collected by Cook's voyages were sent to Britain, where they ended up in museums. For Aboriginal communities today, getting back such objects, and the remains of their ancestors, is part of healing and justice.

Fun fact: in 1992 Australia's High Court, in the Mabo case, finally rejected the idea of terra nullius and recognised that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had rights to their land before the British came.

basic.short: Taken at the first encounter between Cook's crew and Aboriginal people on the east coast, the shield symbolises the beginning of the British colonisation of Australia. Its return is sought as part of Aboriginal efforts to recover their heritage.
basic.medium: The landing at Kamay in 1770 was the prelude to colonisation. In August of that year Cook claimed the east coast of Australia for the British Crown, and in 1788 the First Fleet established a penal colony at Sydney Cove. British law treated Australia as terra nullius, land without owners, ignoring the sovereignty of Aboriginal peoples, who suffered dispossession, frontier violence and epidemics. The objects collected on Cook's voyages became part of British museum collections and of a narrative celebrating exploration. For Aboriginal communities, their return, together with that of ancestral remains, is linked to recognition and healing. Australia has supported the repatriation of ancestral remains from overseas for decades, and in 2024 Trinity College, Cambridge, returned four spears from Kamay. The British Museum has declined to return the shield, citing the law that governs its collections.
basic.long:
The encounter at Kamay was followed by one of the most far-reaching colonial projects of the eighteenth century. After leaving Botany Bay, Cook continued north along the coast and, on 22 August 1770, on Possession Island in the Torres Strait, claimed the entire east coast for the British Crown. In 1788 the First Fleet, carrying convicts, marines and officials, established a penal colony at Sydney Cove, a short distance from Kamay.

British authorities treated the continent as terra nullius, a territory without recognised owners, disregarding the sovereignty and laws of Aboriginal peoples. The expansion of the colony brought dispossession, frontier violence, including massacres, and epidemics such as the smallpox outbreak of 1789 around Sydney. In later periods, policies of removing Aboriginal children from their families, the Stolen Generations, caused lasting harm.

The collecting of Aboriginal objects and, later, human remains was part of this history. Objects from Cook's voyages entered British collections as souvenirs of exploration, while nineteenth-century scientists collected remains to support racial theories.

Since the late twentieth century, Aboriginal communities have sought the return of their heritage. The Australian government has supported the repatriation of ancestral remains from overseas institutions, and museums in Britain, Germany and elsewhere have returned remains. Returns of cultural objects have been slower. In 2024 Trinity College, Cambridge, returned four spears taken at Kamay to the La Perouse community.

The British Museum has declined to return the Gweagal shield, citing the British Museum Act 1963. The High Court of Australia's Mabo decision of 1992, which rejected terra nullius, provides a legal context in which Aboriginal claims to their heritage are increasingly recognised in Australia, if not yet abroad.

expert.short: The shield marks the threshold of a settler-colonial project founded on the doctrine of terra nullius. Its contested repatriation illustrates how Aboriginal claims operate within, and against, the legal frameworks of both Australia and Britain.
expert.medium: The landing at Kamay initiated a settler-colonial trajectory distinct from extractive colonialism: the objective was territorial occupation, legitimised by the doctrine of terra nullius, which denied Aboriginal sovereignty and land title. The collection of objects on Cook's voyages, and later the extensive collecting of ancestral remains for race science, belonged to this project of possession. Since the 1970s Aboriginal activism has linked land rights, recognition and repatriation. The Mabo decision (1992) repudiated terra nullius in Australian law, and Australian governments have supported international repatriation of ancestral remains through programmes such as the Indigenous Repatriation Program. Cultural objects held abroad, however, remain subject to the laws of holding states. The British Museum Act 1963 limits deaccession, whereas institutions such as Trinity College, Cambridge, have discretion, as shown by the return of the Kamay spears in 2024. The shield thus exemplifies a jurisdictional asymmetry in which Indigenous claims recognised at home remain constrained abroad.
expert.long:
The landing at Kamay stands at the threshold of a settler-colonial project whose aims differed from those of extractive empires. Where the British in India or West Africa sought revenue and trade, in Australia they sought land for settlement, legitimised by the doctrine of terra nullius, which held that the continent was not subject to recognisable sovereignty or property. Cook's instructions directed him to take possession 'with the consent of the natives'; his proclamation on Possession Island in August 1770 was made without it.

The First Fleet's arrival in 1788 inaugurated a century of expansion marked by dispossession, frontier warfare, massacres and epidemic disease. Collecting was integral to the colonial knowledge of Aboriginal peoples: objects from the Cook voyages entered British collections as curiosities of exploration, while in the nineteenth century the collection of ancestral remains for comparative anatomy and race science became systematic, with remains shipped to museums and universities in Britain and Europe.

From the 1970s Aboriginal activism linked land rights, recognition and the return of heritage. In Australian law, the High Court's Mabo decision of 1992 repudiated terra nullius and recognised native title. Australian governments have supported international repatriation of ancestral remains, and many institutions in Britain have returned remains under the Human Tissue Act 2004, which enabled national museums to deaccession them.

Cultural objects are treated differently. The British Museum Act 1963 prevents the Trustees from disposing of objects except in narrow circumstances, and the museum has cited it in declining the Gweagal claim, while offering loans and collaboration. Institutions not bound by comparable statutes have greater latitude: in 2024 Trinity College, Cambridge, returned four spears taken at Kamay to the La Perouse Aboriginal community, after consultation and with the support of its Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology.

The shield therefore exemplifies a jurisdictional asymmetry. Aboriginal claims recognised within Australian law and policy remain subject abroad to the legal frameworks of former colonial powers. The disputed provenance of the British Museum's shield adds a further dimension: the uncertainty itself results from colonial collecting practices, and Gweagal claimants have argued that it should not be used against them. The case thus raises the question of whether restitution should depend on the precise provenance of an object or on its role as a symbol of a history that is not in doubt.

maps.caption-2: Then: Constantinople (Byzantine Empire), Türkiye - Now: Venice, Italy (returned from Paris 1815)

fun.short: The horses were war trophies twice over: first for Venice, then for Napoleon's France. After Napoleon lost, European countries decided that art taken in war should go back. Fun fact: this was one of the first big returns of stolen art in history!
fun.medium: Looting was not only something empires did far away: European armies also plundered each other. In 1204 Venice took the horses from Constantinople as a prize of the Fourth Crusade and showed them off on its most important church. In 1797 Napoleon's France took them from Venice, along with hundreds of paintings and statues from all over Italy, to fill the Louvre. When Napoleon was defeated in 1815, the countries that beat him said that the works of art must be sent back home. British, Austrian and Prussian officials organised the return of thousands of works, and the horses went back to Venice. Fun fact: when the horses left Paris, crowds of angry Parisians gathered to watch soldiers take them down from the arch!
fun.long:
In the Middle Ages, Venice was a rich and powerful republic that controlled trade routes across the Mediterranean. In 1204 it supplied the ships for the Fourth Crusade, and when the crusaders attacked Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, the Venetians took a large share of the treasures. The four bronze horses became a symbol of Venice's victory and power, displayed on the front of St Mark's Basilica for almost 600 years.

In 1796 and 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte led French armies into Italy. He forced the Italian states to hand over paintings, sculptures and manuscripts as part of peace treaties. When he conquered Venice in 1797, he took the horses too. In Paris, the works of art were paraded through the streets in a grand festival, with banners saying they had come to France, the land of liberty. Many were displayed in the Louvre, then called the Musée Napoléon.

When Napoleon was finally defeated at Waterloo in 1815, the victorious countries insisted that the looted art be returned. The Duke of Wellington argued that keeping it would be unfair. Workers took down the horses from the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel under the protection of Austrian soldiers, and they travelled back to Venice.

This return became famous as an early example of the idea that art should not be taken as a prize of war.

Fun fact: but nobody gave the horses back to Constantinople! Venice kept its own loot from 1204, which shows that the rules about returning art have not always been applied to everyone in the same way.

basic.short: Taken by Venice in 1204 and by Napoleon in 1797, the horses were returned to Venice in 1815 as part of the first large-scale restitution of looted art in Europe. The earlier looting of Constantinople was never undone.
basic.medium: The horses illustrate looting within Europe and its borderlands. The Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople in 1204 enriched Venice, which displayed the horses as trophies. Six centuries later, the French Revolution and Napoleon turned art confiscation into state policy. Treaties imposed on the Papal States, Venice and other Italian states required the surrender of artworks, which were brought to Paris to fill the Musée Napoléon, justified by the idea that France was the home of liberty and of the arts. After Napoleon's defeat in 1815, the Allies, led by Britain, Austria and Prussia, demanded the return of these works, and thousands were sent back to their countries. The horses returned to Venice in December 1815. This restitution is often seen as a turning point in the idea that cultural property should be protected in war. But Venice's own spoils from Constantinople were never returned.
basic.long:
The history of the horses shows that looting was not only a colonial phenomenon but also part of wars between Europeans and their neighbours.

In 1204 the Fourth Crusade, whose ships had been supplied by Venice, sacked Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire. Its treasures were distributed among the crusaders, and Venice took a large share. The horses, installed on the façade of St Mark's, became symbols of Venice's triumph and its claim to be the heir of Byzantium.

The French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars made art confiscation a systematic policy. From 1794 French armies removed works from Belgium, the Netherlands, the German states and above all Italy. Treaties such as the Treaty of Tolentino (1797) with the Pope required the surrender of hundreds of works of art. Revolutionary leaders argued that masterpieces belonged in Paris, the capital of liberty, where they would be available to all citizens. The Louvre, renamed the Musée Napoléon, became the greatest museum in Europe.

When Venice fell to Napoleon in 1797, the horses were taken to Paris, where they were placed on the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel in 1808.

After Napoleon's final defeat in 1815, the Allies insisted on the restitution of looted works. Despite French resistance, including from the Louvre's director Vivant Denon, thousands of works were returned. The horses left Paris in the autumn of 1815 and reached Venice on 13 December.

The restitutions of 1815 are often cited as a precedent for the protection of cultural property in war, later written into international treaties. Yet they were selective: many works stayed in France, and Venice kept the treasures it had taken from Constantinople six centuries earlier.

expert.short: The horses' double displacement links medieval spoliation to the revolutionary confiscations that shaped the modern museum. Their return in 1815 inaugurated a European norm of restitution whose limits were defined by the victors.
expert.medium: The horses connect two paradigms of appropriation. The spoliation of Constantinople in 1204 belonged to a medieval economy of relics and trophies in which the translation of objects conveyed legitimacy and sacred power. Revolutionary and Napoleonic confiscation, by contrast, was theorised as the liberation of art for a universal public, and it shaped the modern encyclopaedic museum embodied in the Musée Napoléon. The restitutions of 1815, advocated by Wellington and Castlereagh and implemented by Allied commissioners such as Antonio Canova for the Papal States, articulated the principle that works of art were attached to their places of origin and not legitimate objects of conquest. This principle, later formalised in the Lieber Code and the Hague Conventions, emerged from a victors' settlement and applied only to works taken by France. Venice, restored under Austria, retained its Byzantine spoils, and non-European claims were not considered, anticipating the selective application of restitution norms in the colonial era.
expert.long:
The Horses of Saint Mark link two moments in the history of appropriation that shaped European attitudes to cultural property.

The spoliation of Constantinople in 1204 belonged to a medieval economy in which the translation of relics, liturgical objects and monuments conveyed sacred power and political legitimacy. Venice, having secured a large share of the spoils, built a civic identity around them: the façade of San Marco, incorporating Byzantine columns, reliefs and the horses, proclaimed the Republic as heir to Rome and Constantinople. The horses were thus not simply loot but part of a programme of translatio imperii.

The revolutionary and Napoleonic confiscations of the 1790s and 1800s were theorised differently. Revolutionary discourse presented the removal of masterpieces from Belgium, Italy and Germany as their liberation from the tyranny of princes and churches and their dedication to a universal public in Paris. Treaties, such as those of Tolentino and Campo Formio, gave legal form to these removals. The Musée Napoléon became the prototype of the encyclopaedic museum, and the horses, set on the Arc du Carrousel, crowned its triumphal topography.

The restitutions of 1815 reversed this project. The Allied powers, with Wellington and Castlereagh playing leading roles, rejected French arguments that treaties had legitimised the transfers, and commissioners such as Antonio Canova for the Papal States supervised the recovery of works. Wellington's letter to Castlereagh argued that works of art belonged to the countries from which they had been taken. The principle that cultural property is attached to its place of origin and is not a legitimate object of conquest, later formalised in the Lieber Code of 1863 and the Hague Conventions, took shape in this moment.

The principle's origins, however, reveal its limits. It emerged from a victors' settlement and applied to works taken by France. Venice, restored under Austrian rule, retained its Byzantine spoils, and British collectors, who had acquired works during the same wars, faced no comparable claims. At the same time, Britain was acquiring antiquities from the Ottoman Empire, including the Parthenon sculptures, and European powers continued to remove objects from their colonies throughout the nineteenth century. The horses thus embody both the emergence of a European norm of restitution and its selective application, a tension that runs through the colonial cases in this collection.

maps.caption-2: Then: Babylon, Iraq - Now: Berlin, Germany

fun.short: German archaeologists dug up the Ishtar Gate when Iraq was part of the Ottoman Empire. After the First World War, Iraq was ruled by Britain, and the gate's bricks went to Berlin. Fun fact: Iraqis had little say in any of it!
fun.medium: About 120 years ago, Germany wanted more influence in the Middle East, and it was building a railway from Berlin to Baghdad. German archaeologists also came to dig ancient cities, which made Germany look powerful and cultured. At Babylon they found the pieces of the Ishtar Gate. At that time the land belonged to the Ottoman Empire, which had laws about keeping antiquities. After the First World War, the Ottoman Empire collapsed and Britain took control of Iraq. The new antiquities service, run by British officials, agreed to let Germany take most of the gate's bricks to Berlin. Fun fact: in those days, foreign archaeologists usually kept a big share of what they found, a system called "partage", which means sharing.
fun.long:
Around 1900, European empires competed not only for land and trade, but also for the treasures of ancient civilisations. Museums in London, Paris and Berlin filled their halls with statues and monuments from Egypt, Greece and Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

Germany had come late to this competition. Its emperor, Wilhelm II, wanted German museums to rival the British Museum and the Louvre. He supported a new society, the German Oriental Society, which sent archaeologists to dig in the Ottoman Empire, Germany's ally. At the same time, German companies were building a railway to Baghdad.

In 1899 Robert Koldewey started digging at Babylon, and in 1902 he found the Ishtar Gate. The Ottoman Empire had laws saying that antiquities belonged to it, so most of the broken glazed bricks stayed in boxes in Babylon for years.

Then came the First World War. The Ottoman Empire was defeated and broke apart, and Britain took control of Iraq under a "mandate" from the League of Nations. The new Iraqi antiquities department was run by British officials. In 1926 they agreed to divide the finds from Babylon, and Germany received most of the gate's bricks. They were shipped to Berlin in 1927.

Today the gate is one of the most famous sights in Berlin. Fun fact: in Iraq, some people say that the gate was taken when their country was not truly free to decide, and Iraqi officials have called for it to come back to Babylon.

basic.short: The Ishtar Gate was excavated as part of Germany's imperial projects in the Ottoman Empire and removed to Berlin under a division of finds agreed in 1926, when Iraq was under British mandate. Iraqi officials have called for its return.
basic.medium: The excavation of Babylon was part of Germany's ambition, under Wilhelm II, to compete with Britain and France in the Middle East, both economically, through the Baghdad Railway, and culturally, through archaeology and museums. The German Oriental Society's work at Babylon from 1899 was carried out with Ottoman permission, and Ottoman law restricted the export of antiquities. After the First World War, the Ottoman provinces of Mesopotamia became the British Mandate of Iraq. In 1926 the Iraqi Department of Antiquities, directed by British officials, agreed to a division of the Babylon finds that sent most of the Ishtar Gate's glazed bricks to Berlin. The system of partage, dividing finds between the host country and foreign excavators, was common at the time. Iraqi officials have since called for the gate's return, arguing that the division was made when Iraq lacked full sovereignty.
basic.long:
The Ishtar Gate reached Berlin through a combination of imperial rivalry, archaeology and colonial administration. In the late nineteenth century, Germany under Wilhelm II sought influence in the Ottoman Empire. German banks financed the Baghdad Railway, and German archaeologists, supported by the German Oriental Society founded in 1898, began excavations in Mesopotamia to build collections that could rival those of the British Museum and the Louvre.

The excavation of Babylon under Robert Koldewey was carried out with Ottoman authorisation. The Ottoman antiquities law of 1884 declared antiquities state property and restricted their export, although exceptions were made through diplomatic agreements. Most of the fragments of the Ishtar Gate remained in Babylon while negotiations continued.

After the First World War, the Ottoman Empire was dismembered, and the League of Nations entrusted Iraq to Britain as a mandate. A new antiquities law, drafted with the involvement of the British official Gertrude Bell, allowed foreign expeditions to take a share of their finds. In 1926 the Iraqi Department of Antiquities, headed by British staff, agreed to divide the material from Babylon, and most of the gate's glazed bricks were shipped to Berlin in 1927. A share remained in Iraq.

This system, known as partage, was presented as a fair exchange: foreign expeditions funded excavations, and in return received part of the finds. Critics point out that it was designed by colonial officials and favoured Western museums.

Iraqi officials have called for the return of the Ishtar Gate. German museums consider the division legal. The case raises the question of whether agreements made under colonial mandates should be judged by the law of the time or by today's understanding of sovereignty.

expert.short: The Ishtar Gate's removal was enabled by German imperial archaeology in the Ottoman Empire and completed through partage under the British Mandate, raising the question of whether mandate-era divisions express consent by the Iraqi state.
expert.medium: The German excavation of Babylon exemplifies the entanglement of archaeology with Wilhelmine Weltpolitik in the Ottoman Empire, where cultural prestige accompanied economic projects such as the Baghdad Railway. Ottoman antiquities legislation, notably Osman Hamdi Bey's law of 1884, sought to retain finds, and the export of the Babylon fragments stalled until after 1918. The British Mandate for Mesopotamia reconfigured the legal framework: the Antiquities Law of 1924, shaped by Gertrude Bell, institutionalised partage, and in 1926 the British-directed Department of Antiquities agreed to the division that sent most of the Ishtar Gate fragments to Berlin. The legitimacy of such divisions is contested. Holders emphasise their legality and reciprocity; critics argue that mandate administrations represented imperial interests rather than Iraqi sovereignty, a view reinforced by Iraq's later nationalisation of antiquities under Sati' al-Husri in 1936.
expert.long:
The excavation and removal of the Ishtar Gate illustrate the relationship between archaeology and empire in the late Ottoman and mandate periods. Under Wilhelm II, Germany pursued a Weltpolitik in which the Ottoman Empire played a central role, through military cooperation, investment and the Baghdad Railway. Archaeology served this policy by projecting German cultural prestige and by building collections to rival those of London and Paris. The Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft, founded in 1898 with imperial patronage, financed excavations at Babylon and later Assur, directed by Robert Koldewey and Walter Andrae.

Ottoman law sought to limit such removals. The antiquities law of 1884, associated with Osman Hamdi Bey, director of the Imperial Museum in Istanbul, declared antiquities state property and prohibited their export, although diplomatic pressure produced exceptions. The Babylon fragments remained largely in situ until the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.

The British Mandate for Mesopotamia reconfigured the legal context. The Iraqi Antiquities Law of 1924, drafted with the involvement of Gertrude Bell, who served as honorary director of antiquities, institutionalised partage, allowing foreign expeditions to take a share of their finds in exchange for funding excavations. In 1926 the Department of Antiquities agreed to a division of the Babylon material that sent the majority of the Ishtar Gate's glazed brick fragments to Berlin, where they arrived in 1927.

The legitimacy of such divisions is debated. Holding institutions argue that they were lawful under the law in force, negotiated with the competent authority and reciprocal, since a share remained in Iraq and excavations produced knowledge. Critics argue that mandate authorities represented imperial interests rather than those of an Iraqi state, whose sovereignty was constrained until independence in 1932. Iraq's subsequent revision of its antiquities law in 1936, under Sati' al-Husri, which sharply restricted partage and asserted national ownership, has been read as a repudiation of the mandate system.

Iraqi officials have called for the Ishtar Gate's return, framing it within broader efforts to recover heritage lost through colonial-era removals and through looting after 2003. German institutions have not agreed, pointing to the legality of the division and to the gate's fragility. The case exemplifies the reassessment of partage as a colonial institution rather than a neutral legal arrangement.

maps.caption-2: Then: Kealakekua Bay, Hawaiʻi (USA) - Now: Honolulu, Hawaiʻi (returned 2016, permanently 2020)

fun.short: The cloak and helmet were not stolen: the Hawaiian chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu gave them to Captain Cook as a gift. But Cook's arrival was the beginning of huge changes for Hawaiʻi. Fun fact: they were brought home by museums in New Zealand and Hawaiʻi working together.
fun.medium: When Captain Cook reached Hawaiʻi in 1778 and 1779, he was the first European known to visit the islands. The chief Kalaniʻōpuʻu welcomed him with a gift of his own feather cloak and helmet. But Cook's visit opened Hawaiʻi to the outside world. Ships brought traders, missionaries and diseases that killed many Hawaiians. In the 1800s Hawaiʻi became a kingdom recognised by other countries, but American businessmen grew powerful there. In 1893 they overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, and in 1898 the United States annexed Hawaiʻi. Fun fact: when the cloak and helmet came home in 2016, Māori from New Zealand travelled with them to Hawaiʻi, because Māori and Hawaiians are Polynesian cousins!
fun.long:
When James Cook arrived in Hawaiʻi in 1778, the islands were ruled by powerful chiefs, and about 300,000 or more people lived there, perhaps many more. Hawaiians had sailed to the islands centuries earlier across thousands of kilometres of ocean, and they had built a rich society with its own religion, laws and arts, including the famous featherwork.

The feather cloak and helmet of Kalaniʻōpuʻu were not looted. The chief gave them to Cook as a gift, to honour him and create a bond. But after Cook's death in 1779, the gift became something else: a trophy of a famous explorer, bought and sold in England as a curiosity.

Cook's voyages also opened Hawaiʻi to the world. Traders came for sandalwood, whalers stopped to rest, and missionaries arrived from America in 1820. New diseases, against which Hawaiians had no protection, caused the population to fall dramatically. Hawaiʻi became a united kingdom under Kamehameha I, but foreign businessmen, especially Americans who ran sugar plantations, gained more and more power.

In 1893 a group of American businessmen, supported by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani, the last Hawaiian monarch. In 1898 the United States annexed Hawaiʻi, and in 1959 it became a US state. Many Native Hawaiians still campaign for their rights and their sovereignty.

Fun fact: the return of the cloak and helmet in 2016 was not arranged with Britain. It was agreed between Te Papa, the national museum of New Zealand, and Hawaiian institutions, and Māori elders travelled with the treasures to hand them over.

basic.short: Given as a gift in 1779, Kalaniʻōpuʻu's regalia became a colonial curiosity after Cook's death. Their return in 2016 was negotiated between Pacific institutions, within the wider Hawaiian movement for cultural and political recognition.
basic.medium: Unlike many objects in this collection, the cloak and helmet were a gift: Kalaniʻōpuʻu bestowed them on Cook in an act of chiefly diplomacy. After Cook's death, however, they entered British collections as souvenirs of the famous navigator, separated from the relationship that gave them meaning. Cook's voyages opened Hawaiʻi to traders, whalers and missionaries, and introduced diseases that caused a catastrophic population decline. In the nineteenth century the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi became an internationally recognised state, but in 1893 American businessmen overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani with the support of US troops, and in 1898 the United States annexed the islands. The Hawaiian Renaissance of the 1970s revived language, navigation and arts, and led to the creation of the Office of Hawaiian Affairs in 1978, which took part in negotiating the return of the regalia in 2016.
basic.long:
The regalia of Kalaniʻōpuʻu occupy an unusual place among contested objects. They were not seized but given, in a gesture of chiefly diplomacy. Yet their subsequent history reflects the colonial transformation of the Pacific. After Cook's death, objects from his voyages became prized curiosities in Britain, detached from the relationships in which they had been exchanged, and circulated through private collections and sales.

Cook's arrival opened Hawaiʻi to the outside world. Traders came for sandalwood, whaling ships used Hawaiian ports, and American Protestant missionaries arrived in 1820. Introduced diseases caused a catastrophic decline of the Native Hawaiian population in the nineteenth century. At the same time, Kamehameha I united the islands, and the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi became a sovereign state with treaties with the United States, Britain and France.

Foreign influence grew with the sugar industry, dominated by American planters. In 1887 they forced King Kalākaua to accept a constitution limiting royal power, and in 1893 a group of businessmen, supported by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani. The United States annexed Hawaiʻi in 1898, and it became a state in 1959. In 1993 the US Congress formally apologised for the overthrow.

From the 1970s, the Hawaiian Renaissance revived the Hawaiian language, hula, voyaging and traditional arts. The Office of Hawaiian Affairs was created in 1978 to serve Native Hawaiians, and Hawaiian organisations have worked to recover ancestral remains and sacred objects from museums.

The return of the regalia in 2016 was negotiated between Te Papa, Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, not with Britain. It was celebrated as an encounter between Polynesian peoples, and its permanence, agreed in 2020, was seen as recognition that the regalia belong with the people of Hawaiʻi.

expert.short: The regalia's history spans chiefly diplomacy, the curiosity economy of the Cook voyages and the colonisation of Hawaiʻi. Their return through a Te Papa–Hawaiian agreement illustrates restitution within Indigenous and settler-state networks rather than imperial ones.
expert.medium: The bestowal of the regalia in 1779 was embedded in Hawaiian chiefly politics, and their conversion into curiosities after Cook's death illustrates how Pacific gifts were recontextualised in the metropolitan culture of collecting, where association with Cook conferred value. Hawaiʻi's subsequent history, from depopulation and missionary influence to the overthrow of the kingdom in 1893 and annexation in 1898, positioned Native Hawaiians as an Indigenous people within a settler state, a status reflected in the establishment of the Office of Hawaiian Affairs (1978) and in the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act (1990), which applies to Native Hawaiian organisations. The return of the regalia from Te Papa, itself a bicultural institution shaped by Māori claims under the Treaty of Waitangi, operated within this landscape of Indigenous policy. It demonstrates a form of restitution between Pacific institutions, framed by Polynesian kinship and cultural protocols, that bypasses the metropolitan centres through which the objects originally travelled.
expert.long:
The regalia of Kalaniʻōpuʻu embody three successive regimes of value. In 1779 they were instruments of chiefly politics: their bestowal on Cook integrated the foreign captain into a Hawaiian system of rank and alliance. After Cook's death, they entered the metropolitan curiosity economy, where objects from the Pacific acquired value through their association with the famous navigator. William Bullock's commercial museum in London, where they were displayed, and its sale in 1819, exemplify how gifts were converted into commodities and relics of exploration.

The third regime is that of colonial and post-colonial heritage. Hawaiʻi's nineteenth-century history, marked by depopulation, the influence of American missionaries and planters, the Bayonet Constitution of 1887, the overthrow of Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893 and annexation by the United States in 1898, transformed Native Hawaiians from citizens of a sovereign kingdom into an Indigenous minority within a settler state. The US Apology Resolution of 1993 acknowledged the illegality of the overthrow.

From the 1970s, the Hawaiian Renaissance and the sovereignty movement reasserted Native Hawaiian identity. Institutional recognition followed: the Office of Hawaiian Affairs was established by the state constitution in 1978, and the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act of 1990 extended repatriation rights to Native Hawaiian organisations, enabling the return of ancestral remains and sacred objects from US institutions.

The return of the regalia took place outside this US framework, as the objects were in New Zealand. Te Papa, founded in 1998 as a bicultural national museum shaped by Māori claims under the Treaty of Waitangi, negotiated with Bishop Museum and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs. The return in 2016 on a ten-year loan was framed by Māori and Hawaiian protocols, with ceremonies emphasising Polynesian kinship, and in 2020 Te Papa agreed to make it permanent.

The case thus illustrates a form of restitution between institutions of settler states in the Pacific, grounded in Indigenous cultural authority, which bypasses the metropolitan centres through which the objects had passed. It also shows that restitution claims can extend to gifts when their subsequent history has severed them from the community to whose relationships they belonged.

fun.short: The Koh-i-Noor is one of the biggest and most famous diamonds in the world! It once belonged to Indian rulers, but the British took it after they conquered the Punjab. Fun fact: The Koh-i-Noor has had many owners—kings, queens, and even conquerors!

The British colonial forces, following the annexation of the Sikh Empire, claimed the Koh-i-Noor as a “gift” to Queen Victoria, masking the act of theft with a veneer of diplomacy. This appropriation was emblematic of a broader pattern of colonial exploitation, where the British systematically extracted wealth and resources from colonized territories. The Koh-i-Noor diamond, once a symbol of sovereignty and regal authority for Indian rulers, became a trophy in the Crown Jewels of the British monarchy, signifying not just the acquisition of a gem but the erasure of an essential part of India’s heritage and identity. Fun fact: The Koh-i-Noor has passed through the hands of numerous kings and conquerors, each asserting their power through its possession. From the Mughal emperors who adorned themselves with it to the Sikh Maharajas who revered it, the diamond was imbued with cultural and political significance. Yet, its transition into British hands marks a pivotal moment of loss for India. The British crown’s ownership of the diamond exemplifies how colonial powers appropriated not only natural resources but also cultural symbols, reinforcing their dominance while diminishing the pride of colonized nations. The extraction of the Koh-i-Noor is part of a larger narrative of colonial exploitation that stripped nations of their resources and cultural pride. The diamond's removal from India serves as a potent reminder of how colonialism sought to dominate and control by appropriating the very symbols that defined the identities of the conquered peoples. The loss of the Koh-i-Noor diamond represents a deep cultural wound, as the people of India grapple with the implications of this theft on their national identity and historical narrative. Today, the Koh-i-Noor diamond remains a subject of contention, as debates surrounding its rightful ownership continue. Many in India see the diamond not only as a symbol of artistic achievement but also as a reminder of the injustices wrought by colonialism. The calls for its return echo a broader movement advocating for the restitution of cultural artifacts and treasures looted during the colonial era. This ongoing struggle for reclamation speaks to the desire for healing and acknowledgment of historical grievances, highlighting the enduring impact of colonialism on post-colonial societies. In summary, the Koh-i-Noor diamond encapsulates the complexities of colonial history and the lasting consequences of cultural appropriation. Its journey from a revered symbol of Indian royalty to an emblem of British imperialism reflects the broader themes of loss, identity, and the quest for justice that resonate throughout the former colonies. As discussions regarding the diamond’s fate continue, it stands as a powerful reminder of the legacies of colonialism, the importance of cultural heritage, and the ongoing pursuit of restitution and recognition in the face of historical injustices. This diamond, like many other colonial trophies, illustrates the need for a deeper understanding of how imperial conquests not only redefined boundaries but also reconfigured the cultural landscapes of nations. The Koh-i-Noor’s legacy invites us to reflect on the significance of returning such treasures to their countries of origin, recognizing the intrinsic value of cultural heritage in fostering identity, pride, and dignity among peoples whose histories have been marred by colonial domination.
