maps.caption-2: Then: Machu Picchu, Cusco region, Peru - Now: Cusco, Peru (returned 2011–2012)

fun.short: Machu Picchu was not a lost city: Quechua families were farming there when an American expedition arrived in 1911. Yale University borrowed thousands of objects from Peru and kept them for a hundred years. Fun fact: Peru had to go to court to get them back in 2011–2012!
fun.medium: When the American Hiram Bingham reached Machu Picchu in 1911, he told the world he had found a "lost city". But local farmers had guided him there, and Quechua families were living on its terraces! In the early 1900s, the United States had huge influence in Latin America, and American universities and museums wanted collections from the region. Bingham's Yale expeditions dug up thousands of objects: pots, tools and even the bones of people buried in caves. Peru agreed to let Yale borrow them for study, as long as they would come back when Peru asked. Peru asked many times, but Yale kept most of them. Fun fact: in 2008 Peru took Yale to court, and the objects finally went home to Cusco in 2011 and 2012!
fun.long:
In the early 1900s, Peru was an independent country, but powerful nations still shaped what happened there. The United States had growing influence across Latin America, and American museums and universities were eager to build collections of ancient objects from the region.

In 1911 Hiram Bingham, a lecturer at Yale University, travelled through the Urubamba valley looking for Inca ruins. A local farmer, Melchor Arteaga, guided him up the mountain to Machu Picchu, and a boy from a family living there showed him around. Bingham told the world he had discovered a "lost city", but the people living nearby had always known it. That story made him famous and hid the knowledge of the local people.

Bingham came back with more expeditions in 1912 and 1914–1915. His team excavated thousands of objects, including pottery, bronze tools, jewellery and the bones of people buried in caves around the site. The Peruvian government allowed Yale to take them for study, on one condition: Peru could ask for them back.

Peru asked for them back, but most of the objects stayed at Yale's Peabody Museum for almost a hundred years. Some people at Yale even argued that the university now owned them.

In 2008 Peru took Yale to court in the United States. Thousands of people in Cusco marched in the streets to demand the return. In 2010 Yale and Peru made an agreement, and between 2011 and 2012 the objects travelled home.

Fun fact: today they are in a museum in Cusco called the Casa Concha, run by the local university with Yale. Peru's success shows that the words of an old agreement can help bring heritage home.

basic.short: Hiram Bingham's Yale expeditions took thousands of objects from Machu Picchu in 1911–1915, at a time of growing US influence in Latin America, under Peruvian decrees that treated them as a loan. Yale kept them until Peru's lawsuit led to their return in 2011–2012.
basic.medium: The Machu Picchu collections left Peru during a period of growing North American influence in Latin America, when US universities and museums built collections through expeditions in the region. Hiram Bingham, guided in 1911 by the farmer Melchor Arteaga to a site that Quechua families were still farming, presented Machu Picchu to the world as a 'lost city', erasing the local knowledge he relied on. His Yale expeditions of 1912 and 1914–1915 excavated ceramics, metal objects and human remains, exported under Peruvian decrees of 1912 and 1916 that allowed Peru to request their return. Peru did so, but Yale returned only a small part in the 1920s and later claimed ownership of the rest. Peru sued Yale in 2008, public protests grew in Cusco, and after an agreement in 2010 the collections came home in 2011–2012.
basic.long:
The removal of the Machu Picchu collections belongs to a period in which the United States exercised growing economic and political influence in Latin America. Alongside companies and diplomats, American universities and museums sent expeditions to the region and built large collections of its archaeological heritage.

Hiram Bingham, a lecturer at Yale, led the Yale Peruvian Expeditions from 1911. In July 1911 he was guided to Machu Picchu by the local farmer Melchor Arteaga and a Peruvian police sergeant, and a boy from the families farming the site showed him the ruins. Bingham presented the site as a 'lost city' that he had discovered, a narrative that made him famous and ignored the Quechua people who had always known it.

The expeditions of 1912 and 1914–1915 excavated thousands of objects: ceramics, bronze and silver objects, jewellery and the skeletal remains of more than a hundred people. The Peruvian government, which was beginning to protect its archaeological heritage, allowed their export through decrees of 1912 and 1916, on condition that Peru could ask for them to be returned.

Peru made such requests from the 1920s, but only part of the material was sent back. Over the decades Yale came to treat the collections as its property. In the early 2000s the dispute became public, and in 2008 Peru sued Yale in a US federal court. The Peruvian government and people in Cusco campaigned for the return, with public marches and appeals to the US government.

In 2010 Yale and Peru, through the National University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco, reached an agreement. The collections returned between 2011 and 2012 and are kept at the Museo Machu Picchu in the Casa Concha in Cusco. The case shows how the terms of an original agreement, and sustained public pressure, can lead to restitution.

expert.short: The Machu Picchu collections exemplify scientific extraction under US hegemony in Latin America and the 'discovery' narrative that erased Quechua presence. Their return in 2011–2012 enforced the loan conditions of Peru's export decrees after the 2008 lawsuit.
expert.medium: The Yale Peruvian Expeditions (1911–1915) operated within the informal empire of the United States in Latin America, where universities, learned societies such as the National Geographic Society and corporate patrons converged in the production of knowledge about the region. Bingham's construction of Machu Picchu as a 'lost city' erased the Quechua families farming the site and the local guides on whom he relied, framing Indigenous Peru as a landscape of ruins awaiting foreign revelation. The export of excavated material, including human remains, took place under decrees of 1912 and 1916 by which the Peruvian state, still consolidating its heritage legislation, reserved the right to recall the objects. Yale's later assertion of title transformed a loan into a claim of ownership. Peru's 2008 lawsuit and the 2010 memorandum with the National University of San Antonio Abad produced the return of 2011–2012, a settlement that joined restitution with continued scientific collaboration.
expert.long:
The Machu Picchu case illustrates scientific extraction under conditions of informal empire. In the early twentieth century, the United States exercised growing economic and political influence in Latin America, and US universities, learned societies and corporate patrons organised expeditions that produced collections, maps and images of the region. The Yale Peruvian Expeditions, led by Hiram Bingham from 1911 with the support of Yale and the National Geographic Society, belonged to this configuration.

Bingham's representation of Machu Picchu as a 'lost city' was central to its effect. The site was known to Quechua farmers, and in 1911 families were living on and cultivating its terraces; Bingham was guided there by the farmer Melchor Arteaga, and earlier visitors had left inscriptions. The discourse of discovery, amplified by National Geographic, reframed Indigenous Peru as a landscape of ruins awaiting revelation by foreign science, and turned local knowledge into anonymous assistance.

The expeditions of 1912 and 1914–1915 excavated thousands of objects, including ceramics, metalwork and the skeletal remains of more than a hundred individuals. The Peruvian state, which was then consolidating its heritage legislation, authorised their export through decrees of 1912 and 1916 that reserved its right to request their return. The legal form was thus a loan for study. Peru's requests in the 1920s led to a partial return, while Yale retained the bulk of the material at the Peabody Museum and, over time, asserted title to it.

The dispute re-emerged in the early 2000s, when negotiations on a joint arrangement failed, and in 2008 Peru filed suit in a US federal court. Political mobilisation in Peru, including presidential appeals and demonstrations in Cusco, framed the return as a matter of national dignity. In 2010 Yale and Peru, through the National University of San Antonio Abad of Cusco, concluded a memorandum establishing a joint museum and research centre in the Casa Concha, and the collections returned in 2011–2012.

The settlement combined restitution with continued scientific collaboration, a model that some commentators have praised for moving beyond binary disputes and others have questioned for preserving a role for the former holder. The case also shows the importance of the original terms of transfer: because the objects had left Peru as a loan, restitution could be framed as the fulfilment of an agreement rather than as a concession.

fun.short: The Mask of Queen Idia is a beautiful ivory mask from Nigeria, made to honour a powerful queen. But when the British attacked, they took the mask, and now it’s far from home.  Fun fact: Queen Idia was so important to her people that this mask was made to protect her spirit forever!
fun.medium: The Mask of Queen Idia is an exquisite ivory mask made in the Kingdom of Benin to honor Queen Idia, a powerful and revered leader. This beautiful mask was crafted to protect her spirit and ensure her legacy lived on. However, when British forces attacked Benin in 1897, they looted this and many other treasures, taking them to Europe, where they are now kept in museums. Fun fact: Queen Idia was such an important figure that she is considered the mother of the first Oba (king) to unite the kingdom! The looting of the mask represents the larger cultural devastation caused by colonial invasions, as entire societies lost their heritage, identity, and symbols of power, leaving a lasting impact on future generations.
fun.long: The Mask of Queen Idia, a masterful piece of Benin artistry, stands as an emblem of strength, wisdom, and legacy. Queen Idia, revered as the “mother of the kingdom,” played a pivotal role in shaping the political and military landscape of the Kingdom of Benin. Her influence was so profound that the mask, carved in her honor, symbolizes her guidance and protection of her son, Oba Esigie, and the kingdom’s unity. The mask is carved from ivory, a material reserved for the most esteemed figures, representing not only the queen’s power but also the artistic achievements of Benin's society. However, this powerful cultural symbol was violently removed from its homeland during the British Punitive Expedition of 1897. As British forces invaded Benin, they ransacked the royal palace, seizing treasures, sacred artifacts, and objects of deep spiritual significance. The mask of Queen Idia was one of the thousands of objects looted and transported to Europe, where it now resides in foreign museums, far from its origins. Fun fact: Queen Idia was so influential that her mask became the symbol for the Festival of Black Arts and Culture in 1977, representing not just Benin but the artistic achievements of African civilizations. The looting of Queen Idia’s mask is not merely the theft of a beautiful artifact; it reflects a broader tragedy that unfolded in colonized regions across the world. Colonial powers, driven by the desire to dominate and extract wealth, tore apart the cultural fabric of societies, depriving them of their symbols of authority, pride, and identity. The removal of Queen Idia’s mask left a cultural void, stripping the Benin people of a link to their past, their leaders, and their spiritual beliefs. The consequences of this looting resonate to this day, as the descendants of the Benin Kingdom and other colonized peoples seek restitution and the return of their stolen heritage.This history is not just about the physical removal of objects—it’s about the erasure of stories, legacies, and the disconnection from ancestral heritage. For the people of Benin, the loss of Queen Idia’s mask and similar treasures represents the larger narrative of cultural devastation under colonial rule. The mask was more than just an object; it was a source of pride, a reminder of a great leader, and a link to a shared history. Its absence signifies not only the theft of a cultural icon but also the symbolic domination of a society. The humanitarian toll of such acts is immeasurable, as they stripped communities of the means to preserve and celebrate their heritage.  Today, the mask remains in foreign museums, and its presence there is a constant reminder of the unfinished business of colonialism. While calls for repatriation grow louder, the story of Queen Idia’s mask stands as a powerful example of how colonial looting continues to impact societies, depriving them of their cultural continuity and historical integrity. The ongoing struggle for its return symbolizes a broader quest for justice, one that seeks to heal the wounds of colonialism by restoring the cultural legacies that were so violently taken.

maps.caption-2: Then: Tenochtitlan (Aztec Empire), Mexico - Now: Vienna, Austria

fun.short: After Spanish conquerors took the Aztec capital in 1521, many Aztec treasures were shipped to the rulers of Europe. The feather headdress ended up with the Austrian Habsburg family. Fun fact: the Habsburgs ruled both Spain and Austria, which is how Aztec objects reached Vienna!
fun.medium: In 1519 the Spanish conqueror Hernán Cortés landed in Mexico with a few hundred soldiers. With the help of thousands of Indigenous allies who were enemies of the Aztecs, and of diseases like smallpox that killed huge numbers of people, he conquered Tenochtitlan in 1521. The Spaniards melted most of the Aztec gold into bars, but they sent some objects to Europe as gifts for King Charles V, who belonged to the Habsburg family. The Habsburgs also ruled Austria, and Aztec treasures passed between their palaces. That is how the feather headdress reached an Austrian castle. Fun fact: when the German artist Albrecht Dürer saw Aztec treasures in Brussels in 1520, he wrote that he had never seen anything so wonderful!
fun.long:
In 1519 Hernán Cortés sailed from Cuba to Mexico with about 500 soldiers. The Aztec Empire ruled much of central Mexico from its capital Tenochtitlan, and many peoples it had conquered hated paying it tribute. Cortés made allies of them, especially the Tlaxcalans, and marched to Tenochtitlan.

The emperor Moctezuma II welcomed the Spaniards and sent them gifts, including gold and feather objects. But Cortés took Moctezuma prisoner, and fighting broke out. Moctezuma died in 1520. In 1521, after a long siege and a terrible epidemic of smallpox, the city fell. The Spaniards built Mexico City on its ruins.

The conquerors wanted gold above all, and they melted down many beautiful objects. Some treasures, however, were sent to Europe as gifts to the Spanish king, Charles V. Charles belonged to the Habsburg family, which ruled Spain, Austria and many other lands. Aztec objects travelled from court to court and became curiosities in the collections of princes. The feather headdress was in the Austrian castle of Ambras by 1596.

For the people of Mexico, the conquest was the beginning of three centuries of Spanish colonial rule. Mexico became independent in 1821, and today it proudly remembers its Indigenous past.

Fun fact: in 2021, for the 500th anniversary of the fall of Tenochtitlan, Mexico asked Austria to lend the headdress for an exhibition. Austria said no, explaining that the journey would damage it. Many Mexicans were disappointed, but the debate helped more people learn about the treasure.

basic.short: The penacho reached Europe in the aftermath of the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (1519–1521) and passed into the collections of the Habsburgs, who ruled both Spain and Austria. Mexico sees it as a symbol of its conquered heritage.
basic.medium: The Spanish conquest of Mexico, led by Hernán Cortés with the support of tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, ended with the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521, after a siege worsened by a smallpox epidemic. The conquerors seized the treasures of the Mexica state, melting most gold objects into bullion, but sent a selection of objects, including featherwork, to Charles V. Charles was a Habsburg, ruler of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor, and Mexican objects circulated among the dynasty's courts as marvels of the New World. The penacho appears in the Austrian branch's collection at Ambras in 1596. For Mexico, independent since 1821, the headdress symbolises both the splendour of the pre-Hispanic past and the losses of the conquest. Its requests for return, and the Austrian refusal on conservation grounds, have made it a symbol of unequal custody of colonial-era heritage.
basic.long:
The Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire was one of the most dramatic events of early colonialism. Hernán Cortés landed on the Gulf coast in 1519 with a small force, allied with the Totonacs and the Tlaxcalans and other enemies of the Mexica, and reached Tenochtitlan in November. Moctezuma II received him with gifts, but was taken hostage and died in 1520 during an uprising. The Spaniards were driven out, but returned in 1521 with Indigenous allies and laid siege to the city, which fell in August after months of fighting and a devastating smallpox epidemic.

The conquest was followed by the seizure of treasures. Most gold was melted into bars, a fifth of which, the quinto real, was reserved for the Crown. Some objects were sent to Europe intact as gifts to Charles V, among them feather shields, headdresses and mosaics. Charles, a Habsburg, was king of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor, and objects from the Americas circulated among the dynasty's courts in Spain, the Netherlands and Austria. The artist Albrecht Dürer saw a shipment in Brussels in 1520 and marvelled at its artistry.

The penacho entered the collection of the Austrian Habsburgs and was recorded at Ambras Castle in 1596. Like other American objects in European Kunstkammern, it was displayed as an exotic marvel, detached from its meaning in Mexica society.

For Mexico, which became independent in 1821, the pre-Hispanic past became central to national identity after the Revolution of 1910–1920, and museums and archaeology celebrated Indigenous civilisations. The penacho, as one of the few surviving examples of Aztec featherwork, became a powerful symbol. Mexico's requests for its return or loan, including in 2020 for the 500th anniversary of the fall of Tenochtitlan, have been declined by Austria on grounds of fragility.

expert.short: The penacho's passage from Mexica ritual to Habsburg Kunstkammer exemplifies the conversion of conquest spoils into dynastic curiosities. Its role in Mexican nationalism and Austria's conservation-based refusals frame a debate over who may define the conditions of an object's care.
expert.medium: The removal of Mexica objects to Europe after 1519 occurred through gift, tribute and plunder, often indistinguishable in the conditions of conquest. Objects sent to Charles V entered a Habsburg circuit of courtly exchange and display, in which American featherwork, mosaics and codices became emblems of dynastic reach and of the wonders of the New World. The penacho's presence at Ambras by 1596 reflects this circulation. After independence, and particularly after the Revolution, Mexico's indigenista nationalism made the pre-Hispanic past central to state ideology, embodied in the Museo Nacional de Antropología (1964). The penacho became a focal point of this nationalism and of Mexico's diplomatic heritage agenda. Austria's refusals, grounded in conservation science rather than legal title, have shifted the terms of debate: the question is less whether the penacho was acquired legitimately than who holds authority to determine the conditions under which it can be cared for and seen.
expert.long:
The removal of Mexica objects to Europe after 1519 took place through a spectrum of transactions, from diplomatic gifts exchanged between Moctezuma and Cortés to tribute exacted from the defeated and outright plunder. In the conditions of conquest these categories were often indistinguishable. Objects sent to Charles V, such as the shipment exhibited in Brussels in 1520 and admired by Dürer, entered a Habsburg circuit of courtly exchange. Featherwork, turquoise mosaics and codices were distributed among members of the dynasty and displayed in Kunstkammern as emblems of dynastic reach over the New World and as marvels of nature and art.

The penacho's presence in Ferdinand II of Tyrol's collection at Ambras by 1596 reflects this circulation. In the Kunstkammer, it was classified among exotic curiosities, its identity as Mexica featherwork obscured by its description as a 'Moorish hat'. Its rediscovery as Mexican in the nineteenth century coincided with the rise of Americanist scholarship in Europe.

In Mexico, the pre-Hispanic past acquired new significance after independence and above all after the Revolution of 1910–1920. The indigenista ideology of the post-revolutionary state celebrated Indigenous civilisations as the foundation of the nation, while often marginalising living Indigenous peoples. The Museo Nacional de Antropología, opened in 1964, embodied this vision, and the penacho replica displayed there asserted a national claim to the original.

The penacho has since become a recurring subject of Mexican cultural diplomacy. Presidents and officials have requested its return or loan, most prominently in 2020, when Mexico sought it for the commemoration of the five-hundredth anniversary of the fall of Tenochtitlan. Austria has declined, relying on the findings of the binational conservation study of 2010–2012, which concluded that transport would endanger the object.

The case thus illustrates a shift in the terms of restitution debates. The legal question of title, difficult to resolve given the undocumented route of the object, has been displaced by a scientific argument about fragility. Critics note that this argument places the authority to decide in the hands of the holding institution, and that proposals for new transport technologies or for joint custodianship have not altered the outcome. The penacho thus poses the question of whether heritage that cannot move should remain where colonial history placed it.

maps.caption-2: Then: Kumbo (Nso' kingdom), Cameroon - Now: Berlin, Germany (return agreed 2022, pending)

fun.short: Germany once ruled Cameroon as a colony, and German soldiers took many treasures from kingdoms there. Ngonnso', the Nso' people's founding mother, was carried off in 1902. Fun fact: Germany agreed to give her back in 2022.
fun.medium: In 1884 Germany decided that Cameroon, in Central Africa, was its colony. The people living there had not agreed! German soldiers marched inland to force the kingdoms of the highlands to obey. When they fought the Nso' kingdom in 1902, an officer called Kurt von Pavel took the carved figure of Ngonnso', the kingdom's founder. She was sent to a museum in Berlin, along with thousands of other objects taken from Cameroon. After the First World War Germany lost its colonies, but it kept the objects. Fun fact: today Berlin museums hold one of the biggest collections of Cameroonian objects in the world, and the return of Ngonnso' is one of the first steps to share them back.
fun.long:
At the end of the 1800s, European countries divided Africa among themselves, often without asking the people who lived there. In 1884 Germany signed treaties with a few chiefs on the coast of Cameroon and declared the whole region its colony.

The kingdoms of the interior did not accept this easily. In the grassy highlands of the north-west lived powerful kingdoms like Nso', Bamum and Bali, each with its own king, called a Fon. German soldiers, many of them African recruits commanded by German officers, marched into the region to force them to obey and pay taxes.

When the Germans fought the Nso' in 1902, their commander Kurt von Pavel took the sacred figure of Ngonnso', the kingdom's founding mother. For the soldiers it was a trophy and a rare object for museums back home. For the Nso' it was like losing a family member. In 1903 von Pavel gave her to the ethnological museum in Berlin.

German officers, traders and missionaries sent many thousands of objects from Cameroon to Germany. After Germany lost the First World War, Cameroon was divided between Britain and France, but the objects stayed in German museums.

For a long time these collections were rarely discussed. In recent years activists from Africa and Germany have asked hard questions about how they were obtained. In 2022 the Berlin museums agreed to give Ngonnso' back. Fun fact: the Nso' say that when she comes home, they will welcome her with a great ceremony, like the return of a queen.

basic.short: Ngonnso' was taken during Germany's military conquest of the Cameroon Grassfields in 1902. Her case is part of a wider reckoning with the tens of thousands of objects from colonial Cameroon in German museums.
basic.medium: Germany claimed Cameroon in 1884 and spent the next two decades conquering its interior. In the Bamenda Grassfields, military expeditions, led by German officers commanding African soldiers, forced kingdoms to submit, burned villages and seized royal objects. The capture of Ngonnso' by Kurt von Pavel's campaign against Nso' in 1902 was part of this conquest. German museums received tens of thousands of objects from Cameroon during the colonial period, and a 2023 study, 'Atlas of Absence', estimated that at least 40,000 are held in German public collections. After the First World War Cameroon passed to British and French administration, but the objects remained in Germany. Ngonnso's return, agreed in 2022, is part of Germany's recent policy of reviewing and returning colonial collections, which also led to the return of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria.
basic.long:
Germany's colony of Kamerun was created in 1884, when the explorer Gustav Nachtigal signed treaties with Duala chiefs on the coast. Over the following decades the colonial state pushed inland, establishing plantations on the slopes of Mount Cameroon and military stations in the interior. The conquest of the interior was violent: kingdoms and communities that resisted were attacked, their settlements burned and their leaders deposed or killed.

The Bamenda Grassfields, a region of densely populated highland kingdoms, were subdued in the early 1900s. Military expeditions, often called punitive expeditions, targeted kingdoms that refused to accept German authority. Royal objects, such as thrones, masks and figures, were among the spoils, and many officers collected them for museums in Germany, which actively requested such material.

The seizure of Ngonnso' during Kurt von Pavel's campaign against Nso' in 1902 fits this pattern. Given to the Royal Museum of Ethnology in Berlin in 1903, she joined one of the largest collections of Cameroonian objects in the world. A 2023 research project, 'Atlas of Absence', estimated that German public museums hold at least 40,000 objects from Cameroon, most acquired in the colonial period.

After the First World War, Cameroon was divided between British and French mandates, and the Nso' kingdom came under British administration. The objects taken to Germany stayed there.

From the 2010s, debates about the Humboldt Forum and the Benin Bronzes pushed German institutions to confront their colonial collections. Germany adopted principles for returning objects taken in colonial contexts, and in 2022 the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation agreed to return Ngonnso'. For many, her return is a test of whether these principles will lead to real change for communities in Cameroon.

expert.short: Ngonnso's seizure in 1902 exemplifies the systematic acquisition of Grassfields regalia during German military conquest, facilitated by museum demand. Her return, agreed in 2022, tests German restitution policy's capacity to deliver objects to communities as well as states.
expert.medium: German colonial rule in Kamerun (1884–1916) was consolidated through military campaigns into the interior, in which the Schutztruppe's punitive expeditions against Grassfields kingdoms routinely involved the seizure of regalia. Berlin's Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde, under Felix von Luschan, actively solicited collections from officers, generating a close relationship between conquest and museum acquisition. Ngonnso's removal by Kurt von Pavel's campaign in 1902 belongs to this nexus. Research by the 'Atlas of Absence' project (Bénédicte Savoy, Albert Gouaffo and colleagues, 2023) estimated that German public collections hold at least 40,000 objects from Cameroon. The 2019 guidelines of Germany's culture ministers and the SPK's subsequent decisions, including the Benin Bronzes and Ngonnso' in 2022, signalled a policy shift. Yet the delay in her transfer, amid the Anglophone crisis, shows how restitution depends on political conditions in receiving states and on negotiations with communities and sub-national authorities.
expert.long:
German colonial rule in Kamerun, established in 1884 and ended by Allied occupation in 1916, was constructed through a sequence of military campaigns into the interior. The Schutztruppe, composed largely of African soldiers under German officers, conducted punitive expeditions against polities that resisted colonial authority. In the Bamenda Grassfields, where centralised kingdoms such as Nso', Bafut and Mankon possessed elaborate regalia, these campaigns routinely involved the seizure of thrones, figures, masks and other royal objects.

The acquisition of such objects was not incidental. Felix von Luschan, director of the African and Oceanic departments of Berlin's Königliches Museum für Völkerkunde, issued instructions to colonial officers on collecting and actively solicited donations, rewarding contributors with recognition. Museum demand and military violence thus reinforced each other, producing collections whose provenance is inseparable from conquest.

Ngonnso's removal by Kurt von Pavel's campaign in 1902 and her donation in 1903 exemplify this nexus. She joined a Cameroon collection that is among the largest in the world. The research project 'Atlas of Absence', directed by Bénédicte Savoy and Albert Gouaffo and published in 2023, estimated that German public collections hold at least 40,000 objects from Cameroon, the majority acquired in the colonial period, and documented the gap between this abundance and the absence of such heritage in Cameroon itself.

From the late 2010s, debates over the Humboldt Forum and the Benin Bronzes prompted a shift in German policy. In 2019 the culture ministers of the federal government and the Länder adopted principles for dealing with collections from colonial contexts, including openness to return. In 2022 the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz agreed to transfer ownership of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria and authorised the return of Ngonnso', following the campaign led by Sylvie Njobati and the Nso' palace.

The delay in her transfer, caused by the armed conflict in the Anglophone regions since 2017, raises structural questions. Restitution is usually negotiated between states, yet the Nso' palace is the community with which Ngonnso' is identified, and the Anglophone crisis itself stems from contested relations between these regions and the Cameroonian state. Her case thus shows that restitution is not only a matter of legal title and institutional will, but also of the political conditions and relationships in the receiving country.

maps.caption-2: Then: Nok culture sites, Kaduna State, Nigeria - Now: Various museums and private collections

fun.short: The Nok clay figures were not taken by colonial armies: most were dug up by looters from the 1990s and sold to collectors in rich countries. Fun fact: Nigeria's law says ancient objects belong to the nation and must not leave the country!
fun.medium: When we think of stolen treasures, we often imagine soldiers or explorers. But the Nok figures from central Nigeria tell a different story. The first one was found by tin miners in 1943, when Nigeria was a British colony, and most early finds stayed in Nigerian museums. The big problem started after Nigeria became independent in 1960. From the 1990s, art collectors in Europe and North America wanted Nok figures and paid a lot of money for them. People dug up ancient sites at night and smuggled the figures out of the country. Fun fact: museums around the world now use a "Red List" to check that they are not buying stolen Nok figures!
fun.long:
Not every loss of heritage happened in a colonial war. The story of the Nok terracottas shows how the art market can do just as much damage.

The Nok people lived in central Nigeria more than 2,000 years ago and made beautiful clay figures. Nobody knew about them until 1943, when tin miners found a head near the village of Nok. At that time Nigeria was ruled by Britain. A British archaeologist working for the colonial antiquities service, Bernard Fagg, collected finds, and many of them stayed in Nigeria, in the new museum at Jos.

Nigeria became independent in 1960. Its laws say that ancient objects belong to the nation and cannot be exported. But in the 1990s collectors in Europe and North America became very interested in "African art", and Nok figures began selling for large sums. Looters dug up hundreds of sites, often at night, and smugglers carried the figures across borders to dealers abroad.

Some museums bought them too. In 1998 France bought three Nok figures for the Louvre that had left Nigeria illegally. After people protested, France and Nigeria signed an agreement in 2002: France recognised that the figures belong to Nigeria, and Nigeria lent them to France.

Fun fact: to stop the trade, the International Council of Museums made a "Red List" in 2000 showing the kinds of objects most at risk, including Nok terracottas. Customs officers use it to spot and seize stolen figures and send them home.

basic.short: The Nok terracottas were lost mainly through illegal digging and smuggling from the 1990s, fed by collectors in Europe and North America, rather than by colonial conquest. Nigeria bans their export and has recovered some.
basic.medium: The Nok terracottas complicate the idea that looted African heritage was taken only by colonial armies. The first figure was found in 1943, under British rule, and early finds were mostly kept in Nigeria. The large-scale looting began after independence, in the 1990s, when the international market for 'African art', a category shaped by colonial collecting, made Nok figures valuable. Hundreds of sites were dug up and the figures smuggled to Europe and North America, despite Nigerian law. Western institutions were involved too: France bought three looted figures for the Louvre in 1998, and only in 2002 recognised Nigeria's ownership, keeping them on loan. The case shows that ending the demand for looted objects is as important as returning those already taken.
basic.long:
The history of the Nok terracottas shows that the loss of African heritage continued long after colonial rule, through the international art market.

Nigeria was a British colony when the first Nok head was found by tin miners in 1943. The colonial antiquities service, through the archaeologist Bernard Fagg, collected and studied the finds, and many were placed in Nigerian museums, above all the Jos Museum, opened in 1952. In this sense, the early history of Nok is not a history of removal.

The situation changed after independence in 1960. Nigeria's laws declared antiquities the property of the state and banned their export, but enforcement was difficult. From the 1990s demand from collectors in Europe and North America for 'authentic' African antiquities grew rapidly. The idea of 'African art' as a collectable category had itself been shaped in the colonial period, when objects taken from Africa were first displayed in European museums and galleries.

Looters dug up hundreds of Nok sites, and the figures were smuggled through neighbouring countries to dealers abroad. Some reached major institutions. In 1998 France acquired three looted Nok figures for the new African art gallery of the Louvre. After criticism in France and Nigeria, a 2002 agreement recognised Nigeria's ownership while leaving the figures in Paris on a long-term loan.

To fight the trade, the International Council of Museums included Nok terracottas in its Red List for Africa in 2000, and customs authorities in several countries have seized figures and returned them. The case shows that restitution also means controlling the demand that encourages looting today.

expert.short: The Nok case shifts the focus from colonial seizure to the post-colonial antiquities market, whose demand, shaped by the colonial construction of 'African art', drove the looting of hundreds of sites from the 1990s.
expert.medium: The Nok terracottas illustrate a post-colonial regime of loss. Their archaeology began under British rule, when Bernard Fagg's Antiquities Service assembled collections that largely stayed in Nigeria. The large-scale looting that destroyed the Nok record from the 1990s responded to demand in Europe and North America for African antiquities, a market whose aesthetic categories, notably that of 'African art', had been shaped by colonial collecting and modernist primitivism. Nigerian patrimonial law and international instruments, such as the 1970 UNESCO Convention and ICOM's Red List for Africa (2000), proved insufficient against this demand. The French acquisition of looted figures for the Louvre in 1998 and their regularisation in 2002, through an agreement recognising Nigerian title while keeping them in Paris, exemplifies the accommodation of illicitly exported heritage by Western institutions. Restitution debates centred on colonial loot risk overlooking this continuing circulation.
expert.long:
The Nok terracottas require a different analytic frame from the objects seized in colonial wars. Their archaeology began in 1943 under British colonial rule, when tin miners at Nok found a terracotta head and Bernard Fagg, of the Antiquities Service, began systematic collection. The resulting collections were largely retained in Nigeria, and the Jos Museum, founded in 1952, became their principal home. The colonial moment here produced knowledge and national collections rather than removal.

The destruction of the Nok record occurred after independence and was driven by the international antiquities market. From the 1990s demand in Europe and North America for African antiquities surged, and Nok terracottas, with their antiquity and formal sophistication, commanded high prices. The market's categories were a colonial legacy: the notion of 'African art' as a collectable aesthetic category was formed through the display of objects taken in colonial campaigns and through the modernist fascination with so-called primitivism. Looting organised through local labour and regional networks spread across hundreds of sites, destroying the stratigraphic contexts essential to interpretation.

Legal instruments proved insufficient. Nigerian law vests antiquities in the state and prohibits their export, and Nigeria is party to the 1970 UNESCO Convention. ICOM's Red List for Africa (2000) specifically warned against Nok terracottas. Yet Western institutions participated in the market. In 1998 France acquired three looted figures for the new gallery of African art at the Louvre, part of the project that led to the Musée du quai Branly. After public criticism, an agreement of 2002 recognised Nigeria's ownership while allowing the figures to remain in Paris on a renewable loan, a solution that preserved the display while conceding title.

Seizures by customs authorities in the United States and Europe have since repatriated some figures, and research projects have documented the extent of the looting. The case shows that the restitution debate, centred on colonial loot held in major museums, must also address the continuing circulation of illicitly excavated objects and the demand that sustains it. In the Nok case, the post-colonial market rather than the colonial state produced the greater loss.

maps.caption-2: Then: Ganghwa Island (Joseon Korea), South Korea - Now: Seoul, South Korea (returned 2011 on renewable loan)

fun.short: In 1866 France sent warships to Korea to punish it for killing French missionaries. French soldiers burned a royal library and took nearly 300 books. Fun fact: Korea got them back in 2011, but only as a "loan"!
fun.medium: In the 1800s Korea tried to keep foreign powers out, because it had seen how China was forced to open up after the Opium Wars. Christian missionaries were forbidden, but some French priests entered secretly. In 1866 the Korean government arrested and executed nine French missionaries and many Korean Christians. France answered by sending warships to Ganghwa Island, near Seoul. The French soldiers took over the island, but Korean troops fought back and forced them to leave. Before sailing away, the French burned the royal library and took 297 precious books. Fun fact: when France agreed to send them back in 2010, it called the return a "renewable loan", so that, on paper, the books still belong to France!
fun.long:
In the 1800s the countries of East Asia faced a dangerous new world. European powers, with their steamships and cannons, forced China and Japan to open their ports to trade. Korea's rulers watched and decided to keep their country closed. Foreigners were not welcome, and Christianity, which seemed to challenge Korea's Confucian traditions, was banned.

French Catholic priests nevertheless entered Korea secretly and converted thousands of people. In 1866 the Korean regent, the Heungseon Daewongun, ordered a harsh persecution: nine French missionaries and thousands of Korean Christians were killed.

France decided to punish Korea. Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze sailed with warships and soldiers to Ganghwa Island, which guards the river route to Seoul. The French captured the town and its royal library, but when they tried to advance further, Korean soldiers defeated them. After several weeks, the French gave up and sailed away. Before leaving, they set fire to the library and took 297 books of royal uigwe, as well as silver and other treasures.

In Korea the attack made the government even more determined to keep foreigners out. The books were kept in Paris and forgotten.

After they were rediscovered in 1975, Koreans campaigned for decades to get them back. In 2011 they finally returned home, but as a loan, renewed every five years, because French law says that objects in national collections cannot be given away. Fun fact: many Koreans were unhappy about the word "loan", saying you cannot borrow something that was yours in the first place!

basic.short: The Uigwe were taken during France's punitive expedition of 1866 against Korea, launched after the execution of French missionaries. Their return as a 'renewable loan' in 2011 shows how the law of the holder shapes restitution.
basic.medium: In the mid-nineteenth century Joseon Korea, under the regent Heungseon Daewongun, pursued a policy of closure to Western powers and persecuted Catholicism as a threat to the Confucian order. In 1866 nine French missionaries and thousands of Korean Catholics were executed. France, which claimed a role as protector of Catholic missions in Asia, sent a naval expedition under Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze. It occupied Ganghwa Island, but was repulsed by Korean forces and withdrew after a few weeks, burning the royal library and carrying off 297 volumes of uigwe. Korea's victory strengthened its isolationist policy until Japan forced it open in 1876. When the manuscripts returned in 2011, France structured the return as a renewable loan to avoid breaking the principle that public collections cannot be alienated. Many Koreans objected that this left ownership of their heritage in French hands.
basic.long:
The French expedition to Korea in 1866 was one of several Western attempts to open East Asia by force. After the Opium Wars in China and the arrival of American warships in Japan in 1853, the Joseon court, led by the regent Heungseon Daewongun, resolved to keep Korea closed. Christianity was seen as a Western ideology that threatened the Confucian social order, and it was repeatedly persecuted.

French missionaries of the Paris Foreign Missions Society had entered Korea secretly since the 1830s. In 1866 a wave of persecution led to the execution of nine French priests and thousands of Korean Catholics. France, which presented itself as the protector of Catholic missions in Asia, sent a squadron under Rear Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze from its base in China.

The French troops occupied Ganghwa Island in October 1866, but were defeated by Korean soldiers and hunters at the fortress of Jeongjoksan. They withdrew in November, burning the town's royal buildings, including the Oegyujanggak library, and taking 297 volumes of uigwe and other objects to France. In Korea the retreat was celebrated as a victory, and the regent erected stelae denouncing Western barbarians.

The manuscripts were deposited in the imperial library in Paris. After their rediscovery in 1975, South Korea asked for their return, and the case became a sensitive diplomatic issue.

The solution adopted in 2010, a five-year loan renewed automatically, reflected the French principle that objects in public collections are inalienable. It allowed the manuscripts to return in 2011 without a change of ownership. For many Koreans, this compromise preserved the logic of the original seizure, leaving France as the owner of Korean royal records.

expert.short: The 1866 Ganghwa expedition exemplifies gunboat diplomacy in defence of missionary interests. The 2011 loan formula shows how the holder's legal doctrine of inalienability structured the terms of return, preserving a formal asymmetry of ownership.
expert.medium: The Byeongin yangyo of 1866 belongs to the broader pattern of Western gunboat diplomacy in East Asia, in which the protection of missionaries served as a justification for coercion. France's self-appointed protectorate over Catholic missions, formalised in its treaties with China, framed the expedition as retaliation for the execution of French priests, but its failure reinforced the Daewongun's policy of seclusion until the Japan–Korea Treaty of Ganghwa (1876) opened the country. The removal of the uigwe was thus a by-product of punitive violence rather than a systematic acquisition. Their return in 2011 illustrates how restitution was shaped by French public law: the inalienability of public collections, affirmed in the Code du patrimoine, led to the adoption of a renewable loan. Korean critics argued that this formula perpetuated the asymmetry of the original seizure, while in France it was criticised as a precedent eroding inalienability.
expert.long:
The French expedition to Korea in 1866, remembered in Korea as the Byeongin yangyo, belongs to a pattern of Western gunboat diplomacy in East Asia in which the protection of missionaries and traders justified the use of force. France, which had obtained in its treaties with China the right to protect Catholic missions, framed the expedition as retaliation for the execution of nine priests of the Paris Foreign Missions Society and thousands of Korean Catholics in the persecution of that year.

The expedition, led by Rear Admiral Pierre-Gustave Roze from the French naval station in China, was limited in scale and outcome. It occupied Ganghwa Island, the strategic gateway to the Han River and Seoul, but was defeated at Jeongjoksan and withdrew after a few weeks. The burning of the Oegyujanggak and the removal of 297 uigwe were acts of punitive destruction and opportunistic seizure rather than systematic collecting. For the Joseon court, the retreat seemed to vindicate the regent Heungseon Daewongun's policy of seclusion, reinforced after the American expedition of 1871, until Japan imposed the unequal Treaty of Ganghwa in 1876.

The manuscripts' subsequent history reflects the institutional logic of French heritage law. Deposited in the imperial library, they became part of the national collections, which under French law are inalienable. When South Korea requested their return after Park Byeong-seon's identification in 1975, this principle limited the options. The return of a single volume by Mitterrand in 1993, linked to the TGV contract, provoked resistance among BnF staff, who opposed any alienation.

The agreement reached at the G20 summit in Seoul in 2010 resolved the issue through a five-year loan renewable automatically, which allowed physical return without a transfer of ownership or new legislation. The manuscripts arrived in 2011. In Korea, civic groups and scholars criticised the formula as preserving French ownership of objects taken by force; in France, some curators saw it as a precedent weakening inalienability.

The case thus demonstrates how the terms of restitution are shaped by the legal and institutional frameworks of holding states. It also anticipates later French debates, which led to specific laws for the return of objects to Benin and Senegal in 2020, and to the framework legislation discussed in 2025–2026, which seek to reconcile inalienability with the return of objects acquired through violence.

maps.caption-2: Then: Yuanmingyuan, Beijing (Qing China), China - Now: London, UK, Fontainebleau and other museums

fun.short: The Old Summer Palace in China was once full of amazing treasures, but British and French soldiers destroyed it during a war and took many of its treasures away. These precious items are now in museums far from China. Fun fact: The palace was so big and full of art that it took days to loot and burn it down!
fun.medium: The Old Summer Palace, or Yuanmingyuan, was once a grand royal residence in China, filled with art, gardens, and treasures. British and French forces destroyed it in 1860 during the Second Opium War, looting countless priceless artifacts. These treasures, which included paintings, sculptures, and luxury items, were taken from China and are now displayed in museums far from their homeland.  Fun fact: The palace was so vast and filled with so many valuable items that it took soldiers multiple days to loot and burn it to the ground! This act of looting wasn’t just about taking beautiful objects—it represented a violent assault on China’s cultural heritage and national pride, showing how colonialism targeted both the physical and symbolic centers of power in colonized nations.
fun.long: The Old Summer Palace, also known as Yuanmingyuan, was once the pinnacle of Chinese imperial grandeur, an architectural and artistic marvel covering over 800 acres. Built in the 18th century, the palace was renowned for its exquisite gardens, intricate pavilions, and priceless works of art that spanned centuries of Chinese history. The palace was a symbol of the power and cultural sophistication of the Qing Dynasty, housing a vast collection of rare artifacts, including jade sculptures, ancient manuscripts, silk paintings, and decorative treasures made of gold and silver. However, in 1860, during the Second Opium War, this magnificent complex became the target of British and French troops, who looted and destroyed the palace in one of the most devastating acts of cultural vandalism in history. Over the course of several days, European soldiers methodically stripped the palace of its treasures, filling ships with thousands of invaluable items that were later dispersed across European museums and private collections. The sheer scale of the looting was unprecedented; soldiers took everything from delicate porcelain vases to massive bronze statues, symbolizing the complete disregard for China's cultural heritage. Fun fact: The looting was so extensive that soldiers reportedly used carts to haul away the treasures, and it took multiple days to pillage the entire palace. After removing what they deemed valuable, the British and French forces set fire to the palace, leaving it in smoldering ruins and reducing a key symbol of China's cultural and historical identity to ash. The loss of the Old Summer Palace and its artifacts was not just a tragedy of cultural theft but also a deliberate assault on China's sovereignty and pride. The act of looting these precious objects symbolized the broader humiliation inflicted upon China during the era of unequal treaties, when European powers sought to assert control over China's economy, trade, and territory. The palace itself was a testament to Chinese artistry and craftsmanship, and its destruction was an affront to the centuries of cultural achievement it represented. The looting also played a critical role in shaping the global distribution of Chinese art, as many of the palace's treasures found their way into the collections of prestigious institutions such as the British Museum, the Louvre, and private collectors. This violent episode in China’s history continues to resonate today, as the country seeks the return of its looted treasures. For modern China, the loss of the Old Summer Palace’s artifacts is not merely a historical injustice but a lingering reminder of the national humiliation experienced during the Century of Humiliation when foreign powers imposed their will on China. The looted treasures, now displayed in foreign museums, are constant reminders of the imperial exploitation that once sought to diminish China's global standing.This act of plunder stands as a powerful example of how colonialism extended far beyond territorial conquest to include the systematic theft of cultural identity. By taking these priceless artifacts, colonial powers sent a message that their domination was not only political and military but also cultural. The looting of Yuanmingyuan exemplifies the lengths to which colonial forces would go to assert their superiority, using art and heritage as tools to impose their vision of global order, often at the expense of the colonized. The artifacts, stripped of their original cultural and historical context, were transformed into symbols of imperial might, showcased in European museums to celebrate the spoils of empire. Today, the debate over the restitution of these stolen treasures remains heated, with China pressing for the return of the Old Summer Palace artifacts as part of its broader effort to reclaim its cultural heritage. These calls for repatriation reflect the growing global acknowledgment of the wrongs committed during the colonial era and the desire to correct these historical injustices. The return of such treasures would not only restore a part of China’s cultural legacy but also serve as a symbolic act of historical reconciliation, recognizing the dignity and sovereignty of a nation that was once subjected to imperial plunder. The Old Summer Palace, though still in ruins, stands as a powerful reminder of the enduring impact of colonial exploitation on cultural identity and national pride.

British and French forces systematically removed countless artifacts from this royal palace in Beijing, leaving China’s cultural heritage scattered across foreign collections.
